knowledge_statements.statement_title: SGS Smooth-Gradient and Stochastic-Oracle Complexities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separate evaluation bounds for the smooth gradient and the stochastic first-order component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p_t,\theta_t\) be set by (8.1.39), and suppose \(D_X>0\) satisfies (8.1.53). With \(\beta_k,\gamma_k\) from (8.1.40) and (8.1.72) using \(\widetilde D=3D_X^2/4\), SGS finds a stochastic \(\varepsilon\)-solution using respectively
\[
\mathcal O\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{LD_X^2}{\varepsilon}}\right)
\]
evaluations of \(\nabla f\), and
\[
\mathcal O\!\left(\frac{(M^2+\sigma^2)D_X^2}{\varepsilon^2}+\sqrt{\frac{LD_X^2}{\varepsilon}}\right)
\]
evaluations of \(h'\).

If (8.1.57) also holds, a stochastic \((\varepsilon,\Lambda)\)-solution requires respectively
\[
\mathcal O\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{LD_X^2}{\varepsilon}\max\left\{1,\log\frac1\Lambda\right\}}\right)
\]
and
\[
\mathcal O\!\left(\frac{M^2D_X^2}{\varepsilon^2}\max\left\{1,\log^2\frac1\Lambda\right\}+\sqrt{\frac{LD_X^2}{\varepsilon}\max\left\{1,\log\frac1\Lambda\right\}}\right).
\]
The same bounds hold when \(X\) is bounded, \(\beta_k,\gamma_k\) follow (8.1.42), and (8.1.75) is used with \(\widetilde D=81D_X^2/32\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SGS separately bounds smooth-gradient and stochastic-component evaluations. Smooth-gradient cost has square-root dependence on 1/epsilon, while the stochastic-component cost has a leading 1/epsilon-squared term; the high-confidence bounds include the displayed logarithmic factors.
assumptions_latex: \text{Alternative schedule: }X\text{ is bounded, }\beta_k,\gamma_k\text{ follow (8.1.42), and }\widetilde D=81D_X^2/32

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Almost-sure convergence of the LMS recursion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded convergence guarantee for least-mean-squares stochastic approximation under the cited stochastic-approximation conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the LMS recursion for data \(z_k=h_k^T\theta^*+v_k\). Assume that \((v_k)\) are i.i.d. with mean zero and finite variance; \((h_k)\) are i.i.d. and independent of \((v_k)\); every component of \(\mathbb E[h_k\otimes h_k\otimes h_k\otimes h_k]\) is finite; conditions B.1--B.3 hold; \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k^2<\infty\); and \(\sup_k\mathbb E\|\widehat\theta_k\|^2<\infty\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Single-Sample Stochastic Gradient Ascent Update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic stochastic-gradient iteration for maximizing an expected or sample-driven objective, including its nonanticipativity requirement and the failure of deterministic samplewise line-search reasoning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W^n\) be the observation revealed at iteration \(n\), and suppose \(x^{n-1}\) and \(\alpha_{n-1}\) depend only on \(W^1,\ldots,W^{n-1}\). If the sample derivative \(\nabla_x F(x^{n-1},W^n)\) is computable, a stochastic gradient-ascent step is \[x^n=x^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-1}\nabla_xF(x^{n-1},W^n).\] Because an individual stochastic gradient can point away from an optimizer, maximizing the realized sample objective along this direction does not generally provide a valid deterministic line-search rule, and every positive step may worsen the underlying objective for a particular realization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At iteration n, choose the current point and stepsize using only observations through iteration n−1, then combine that point with the newly observed sample W^n to compute one sample gradient and take a stochastic gradient-ascent step. A single sample gradient can point away from the optimizer, so a deterministic line search based on that realization is not generally reliable and a positive step can worsen the true objective.

\nabla_xF(x^{n-1},W^n)\text{ is computable for the realized sample}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^n=x^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-1}\nabla_xF(x^{n-1},W^n),\quad\text{with no general guarantee that the realized direction is improving for the underlying objective.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Initialization and recursive MSE tracking for stochastic mean estimation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initial-step behavior and online squared-error smoothing, including the nonstationary-observation case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the stochastic mean update \(x^1=(1-\alpha_0)x^0+\alpha_0W(\omega^1)\), choosing \(\alpha_0=1\) gives \(x^1=W(\omega^1)\), eliminating dependence on \(x^0\); a smaller initial stepsize is appropriate only when \(x^0\) carries reliable prior information. Given iterates \(x^{m-1}\) and observations \(W(\omega^m)\), the empirical error is \[\operatorname{MSE}_n=\frac1n\sum_{m=1}^n\bigl(x^{m-1}-W(\omega^m)\bigr)^2.\] When the observation distribution changes over time, an online diagnostic is \[\operatorname{MSE}^n=(1-\beta_{n-1})\operatorname{MSE}^{n-1}+\beta_{n-1}\bigl(x^{n-1}-W(\omega^n)\bigr)^2,\] where \(\beta_{n-1}\) is a stepsize sequence and may equal \(\alpha_{n-1}\). Gradient and decision-variable units may differ, so stepsize calibration must account for their scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With initial stepsize one, the first stochastic mean update equals the first observation and ignores the initial guess. A smaller initial stepsize is justified when the initial guess is reliable. Performance can be measured by the average squared one-step prediction errors; for a changing observation distribution, those errors can instead be tracked by an exponentially smoothed recursion with its own stepsize, possibly the same stepsize used by the main iteration. Stepsize calibration must also account for differing gradient and decision-variable units.
assumptions_latex: \(x^0\) is an initial estimate and \(W(\omega^1),W(\omega^2),\ldots\) are sequential observations.
For recursive tracking, the observation distribution may vary with \(n\), and \(\beta_{n-1}\) is the smoothing stepsize.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stochastic quasi-Fejér sequence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition relative to a nonempty reference set W in Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sequence of random vectors \(\{\mathbf w^v\}_{v\ge0}\) is stochastic quasi-Fejér with respect to \(W\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) if \(\mathbb E\|\mathbf w^0\|^2<\infty\) and there exist random variables \(\gamma_v\ge0\) such that \(\sum_{v=0}^{\infty}\mathbb E[\gamma_v]<\infty\) and, for every \(w\in W\) and every \(v\ge0\), \[\mathbb E\!\left[\|w-\mathbf w^{v+1}\|^2\mid\mathbf w^0,\ldots,\mathbf w^v\right]\le \|w-\mathbf w^v\|^2+\gamma_v.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic stochastic-gradient recursion and its limiting gradient flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the smooth stochastic-gradient recursion and records its associated limiting ODE, Lyapunov identity, equilibrium set, conditional coercive-existence observation, and maximization sign convention. It does not assert convergence or impose unstated probabilistic conditions on the noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable with Lipschitz gradient. A stochastic-gradient scheme has the form
\[
x_{n+1}=x_n+a(n)\bigl[-\nabla f(x_n)+M_{n+1}\bigr],
\]
where the bracketed quantity is a noisy measurement of \(-\nabla f(x_n)\). Its limiting ODE is
\[
\dot x(t)=-\nabla f(x(t)).
\]
Along every solution,
\[
\frac{d}{dt}f(x(t))=-\|\nabla f(x(t))\|^2\le 0,
\]
with strict inequality whenever \(\nabla f(x(t))\ne0\), and the equilibrium set is \(H=\{x:\nabla f(x)=0\}\). If additionally \(f(x)\to\infty\) as \(\|x\|\to\infty\), then \(f\) attains a global minimum. For maximization, the sign of the gradient term is reversed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth stochastic-gradient iteration uses a noisy negative-gradient measurement. Its limiting system is negative-gradient flow, under which the objective decreases strictly away from critical points; those critical points are exactly the equilibria. Coercivity additionally ensures existence of a global minimizer. Reversing the gradient sign gives the maximization convention.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\text{ is continuously differentiable}
-\nabla f(x_n)+M_{n+1}\text{ is a noisy measurement of }-\nabla f(x_n)

\[
w(t+1)=w(t)-\frac{1}{t}H^{-1}\frac{\partial}{\partial w}\ell\!\left(f_{w(t)}(x_t),y_t\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient-Clipping Updates and Their Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pre-update gradient clipping, including norm, direction, stochastic-bias, and numerical-failure boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite gradient \(g\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and threshold \(v>0\), norm clipping uses \[\widetilde g=\begin{cases}g,&\|g\|\le v,\\v g/\|g\|,&\|g\|>v.\end{cases}\] Thus \(\|\widetilde g\|\le v\), and for finite nonzero \(g\), clipping preserves its direction. Element-wise clipping bounds individual components but generally changes direction. For a random minibatch gradient \(G\), clipping before averaging generally yields \(\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{clip}(G)]\ne\mathbb{E}[G]\) and is also generally not equivalent to clipping the full-data gradient. If the computed gradient is Inf or NaN, norm rescaling is undefined and a bounded random step is only a heuristic fallback.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Norm clipping bounds a finite gradient while preserving its direction. Element-wise clipping can change direction. Clipping minibatch gradients before averaging generally biases the estimate, and Inf or NaN gradients cannot be handled by the norm-rescaling formula.
assumptions_latex: g\text{ is finite for norm rescaling}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|\widetilde g\|\le v,\qquad g\ne0\Longrightarrow \widetilde g=cg\text{ for some }c>0,\qquad \mathbb{E}[\operatorname{clip}(G)]\ne\mathbb{E}[G]\text{ in general.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Iterate Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded algorithm with a qualitative comparison to unaveraged SGD. The extract supplies neither a new asymptotic rate nor the complete assumptions and constants behind the curvature-adaptivity claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For independent samples \(x_\ell\sim\alpha\), compute \(\widetilde{\mathbf g}^{(\ell+1)}=\widetilde{\mathbf g}^{(\ell)}+\tau_\ell\nabla_{\mathbf g}E^\varepsilon(\widetilde{\mathbf g}^{(\ell)},x_\ell)\) and report \(\mathbf g^{(\ell)}=\ell^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{\ell}\widetilde{\mathbf g}^{(k)}\). The average can be maintained recursively as \(\mathbf g^{(\ell+1)}=(\ell+1)^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf g}^{(\ell+1)}+\ell(\ell+1)^{-1}\mathbf g^{(\ell)}\). A displayed typical schedule is \(\tau_\ell=\tau_0/(1+\sqrt{\ell/\ell_0})\), which decays as \(\ell^{-1/2}\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Single-sample stochastic-gradient update and its descent limitation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sampled-gradient iteration with nonanticipative indexing, a newsvendor derivative example, and the failure of deterministic line-search reasoning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the sample derivative \(\nabla_xF(x,W^n)\) is available even though \(F\) or its exact gradient is not. If \(x^{n-1}\) and \(\alpha_{n-1}\) depend only on \(W^1,\ldots,W^{n-1}\), then the stochastic-gradient update is \[x^n=x^{n-1}-\alpha_{n-1}\nabla_xF(x^{n-1},W^n).\] For \(F(x,W)=p\min\{x,W\}-cx\), the sample derivative, away from \(x=W\), is \[\frac{\partial F(x,W)}{\partial x}=\begin{cases}p-c,&x<W,\\-c,&x>W.\end{cases}\] A sampled gradient need not point toward an optimizer of the true stochastic objective, so a positive step along it need not improve that objective and deterministic exact line-search reasoning does not apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a sample-path derivative is available, update the previous iterate by subtracting a stepsize times the derivative evaluated using the newest observation. The iterate and stepsize may use earlier observations but not the newest one before it is observed. In the newsvendor example, the sample derivative is p−c below realized demand and −c above it, with the equality case left unspecified. A single sampled gradient can point away from the true optimizer, so positive steps along it need not improve the true objective and cannot be selected by an ordinary deterministic exact line search.
assumptions_latex: \(\nabla_xF(x,W^n)\) exists at the sampled point used by the update.
\(x^{n-1}\) and \(\alpha_{n-1}\) are functions of \(W^1,\ldots,W^{n-1}\), not of \(W^n\).
For the newsvendor derivative formula, \(F(x,W)=p\min\{x,W\}-cx\) and \(x\ne W\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^n=x^{n-1}-\alpha_{n-1}\nabla_xF(x^{n-1},W^n),\qquad \nabla_xF(x^{n-1},W^n)\text{ need not be a descent direction for the true objective.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given p_0\in X with \Psi(p_0)-\Psi(x^*)\le\Delta_0, set \bar S=\lceil\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon)\rceil and choose \lambda>0 such that e^{-\lambda^2/3}+e^{-\lambda}\le\Lambda/\bar S. For s=1,\ldots,\bar S, minimize over \[\widehat X_s:=\{x\in X:V(p_{s-1},x)\le\widehat R_{s-1}^2:=\Delta_0/(\mu2^{s-1})\}\] by running \widehat N_s stochastic accelerated-gradient iterations from p_{s-1}, with \alpha_t=q_t=2/(t+1) and \gamma_t=\widehat\gamma_s t, where \[\widehat N_s=\left\lceil\max\left\{4\sqrt{\frac{2L}{\mu}},\frac{\max\{256(M^2+\sigma^2),288\lambda^2\sigma^2\}}{3\mu\Delta_0 2^{-(s+1)}}\right\}\right\rceil\] and \[\widehat\gamma_s=\min\left\{\frac1{4L},\left[\frac{3\Delta_0 2^{-(s-1)}}{2\mu(M^2+\sigma^2)\widehat N_s(\widehat N_s+1)^2}\right]^{1/2}\right\}.\] Set p_s=\bar x_{\widehat N_s}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the number of epochs from the desired tolerance and a confidence parameter satisfying the displayed tail allocation. At each epoch, restrict the problem to a shrinking Bregman neighborhood of the previous output, run the prescribed number of accelerated stochastic iterations, and use the resulting averaged iterate as the next epoch point. The source's isolated N_s in the scale formula is interpreted consistently as the defined epoch length hat N_s.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_s=\bar x_{\widehat N_s}\quad\text{after applying the prescribed accelerated method over }\widehat X_s.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f(x;\xi)]\) be convex on \(C\). Starting from \(x_0\in C\), iteration \(k\) samples \(\xi_k\), chooses \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k;\xi_k)\), and sets \[x_{k+1}=\Pi_C(x_k-\eta_k g_k),\qquad \eta_k>0.\] Analysis commonly requires \(\mathbb E[g_k\mid\mathcal F_k]\in\partial F(x_k)\) and a conditional second-moment bound. After \(K\) iterations, output \(x_K\) or a declared weighted average of the iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stochastic subgradient descent samples a subgradient, takes a subgradient step, and projects back onto the feasible convex set.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\eta>0\) and \(T\in\mathbb N_{>0}\), initialize \(\mathbf w^{(1)}=\mathbf 0\). Return \(\overline{\mathbf w}=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbf w^{(t)}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Without-Replacement Mini-Batches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-population unbiasedness and variance correction for a uniformly sampled subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_1,\ldots,g_N\in\mathbb R^d\ be a finite population with mean \(\bar g=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N g_i\. If \(B\ is uniformly sampled from all subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\ having cardinality \(b\, define \(\widehat g_B=b^{-1}\sum_{i\in B}g_i\. Then \[\mathbb E[\widehat g_B]=\bar g,\qquad \mathbb E\|\widehat g_B-\bar g\|^2=\frac{N-b}{bN}\,S^2,\] where \(S^2=(N-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\|g_i-\bar g\|^2\. Samples within the batch are dependent, and the finite-population correction makes the variance vanish when \(b=N\.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniformly sampled subset gives an unbiased finite-sum gradient, with variance reduced by the finite-population correction and zero variance for a full batch.
assumptions_latex: \(B\ is uniform over all subsets of size \(b\.
The vectors \(g_1,\ldots,g_N\ are fixed conditional on the current iterate.

children.title: Fixed Batch Sizes

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Batch Sizes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Statistical consequence of holding the independent mini-batch size constant across iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose iteration \(k\ uses an average \(\bar G_k\ of a fixed number \(b\ge1\ of conditionally independent, unbiased stochastic gradients, each having conditional variance at most \(\sigma^2\. Then \[\mathbb E[\bar G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla F(x_k),\qquad \mathbb E[\|\bar G_k-\nabla F(x_k)\|^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le\frac{\sigma^2}{b}\] at every iteration. Thus a fixed finite batch reduces variance by a constant factor but does not force the estimator noise to vanish with \(k\; convergence requiring vanishing accumulated noise must instead be supplied by the step-size policy or stronger assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed batch gives a constant variance-reduction factor, but the stochastic gradient noise generally does not vanish as iterations proceed.
assumptions_latex: The batch size \(b\ is fixed and finite.
Samples within every batch are conditionally independent and unbiased.
Single-sample conditional variance is bounded by \(\sigma^2\.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The batch variance is at most \(\sigma^2/b\ uniformly in \(k\ and need not converge to zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Growing Batch Sizes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded monotone batch policies in an infinite-sampling stochastic-gradient model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A growing batch-size policy is an integer sequence \(b_k\geq 1\) used in \(g_k=b_k^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{b_k}G(x_k,\xi_{k,j})\) such that \(b_{k+1}\geq b_k\) for every \(k\) and \(b_k\to\infty\). The associated stochastic-gradient update is \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_k g_k\). If the samples are conditionally independent and \(\mathbb E[G(x_k,\xi_{k,j})\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)\), then \(g_k\) remains conditionally unbiased while its conditional covariance is divided by \(b_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A growing-batch SGD policy uses nondecreasing batch sizes tending to infinity, preserving unbiasedness while progressively reducing independent sampling noise.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Batch Sizes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: History-dependent, nonanticipating batch selection for mini-batch SGD.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An adaptive batch-size policy selects an integer \(b_k\geq1\) that is measurable with respect to the pre-sampling history \(\mathcal F_k\), and then forms \(g_k=b_k^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{b_k}G(x_k,\xi_{k,j})\). A variance-controlled instance chooses the smallest admissible \(b\) whose variance estimate \(\widehat V_k(b)\) satisfies \(\widehat V_k(b)/b\leq\theta^2\max\{\|\widehat g_k(b)\|^2,\varepsilon_k^2\}\), where \(\theta>0\) and \(\varepsilon_k>0\). The update is \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_k\widehat g_k(b_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptive policy chooses each batch from current history, often increasing it until estimated gradient noise is small relative to the estimated signal.

knowledge_statements.title: Batch-Transition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stopping-time transitions between prescribed mini-batch levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(1\leq B_0<B_1<\cdots<B_m\) be prescribed batch levels and let \(0=\tau_0\leq\tau_1\leq\cdots\leq\tau_{m+1}=\infty\) be stopping times for the optimization filtration. A batch-transition regime is the policy \(b_k=B_r\) whenever \(\tau_r\leq k<\tau_{r+1}\). It is deterministic when every \(\tau_r\) is fixed in advance and adaptive when some \(\tau_r\) depends on observed iterates, gradients, or variance estimates. Nondecreasing levels ensure that every transition weakly increases sampling effort.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A batch-transition regime partitions iterations into phases, assigning a prescribed batch level to each phase and switching at deterministic or data-dependent stopping times.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau_r\) is a stopping time for each \(r\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projected independent mini-batch SGD and its oracle-call rate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded projected mini-batch SGD update, inverse-batch variance scaling, and expected smooth-convex oracle-call guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\in\mathbb N\), let \(\widetilde g_1(x_k),\ldots,\widetilde g_m(x_k)\) be conditionally independent, unbiased stochastic-gradient estimates given \(x_k\), and update \[x_{k+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal X}\!\left(x_k-\frac{\alpha}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m\widetilde g_i(x_k)\right).\] Suppose \(f\) is convex and \(\beta\)-smooth, \(\|\widetilde g(x)\|_2\leq B\), and the stepsize is selected by applying the smooth stochastic mirror-descent bound to the averaged oracle. Then \[\mathbb E\left\|\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\widetilde g_i(x)-\nabla f(x)\right\|_2^2=\frac1m\mathbb E\|\widetilde g_1(x)-\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\leq\frac{2B^2}{m}.\] After \(t/m\) iterations, using \(t\) original-oracle calls, the returned averaged point \(\widehat x\) satisfies \[\mathbb E f(\widehat x)-f(x^*)\leq\frac{2RB}{\sqrt t}+\frac{m\beta R^2}{t}.\] Consequently, if \(m\leq \frac{B}{R\beta}\sqrt t\), then \(\mathbb E f(\widehat x)-f(x^*)\leq3RB/\sqrt t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected mini-batch SGD averages m conditionally independent unbiased stochastic gradients per iteration. The estimator's mean-square error decreases proportionally to 1/m. With t total oracle calls, its expected smooth-convex suboptimality is at most 2RB over square root t plus m beta R squared over t; batches no larger than B square root t divided by R beta retain the 3RB over square root t guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \widetilde g_1(x_k),\ldots,\widetilde g_m(x_k)\text{ are conditionally independent and unbiased given }x_k.
t/m\text{ mini-batch iterations use }t\text{ calls to the original oracle}.
\text{The stepsize and radius parameter }R\text{ are those in the applicable smooth stochastic mirror-descent bound.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E\left\|\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\widetilde g_i(x)-\nabla f(x)\right\|_2^2\leq\frac{2B^2}{m},\qquad \mathbb E f(\widehat x)-f(x^*)\leq\frac{2RB}{\sqrt t}+\frac{m\beta R^2}{t};\quad m\leq\frac{B\sqrt t}{R\beta}\implies \mathbb E f(\widehat x)-f(x^*)\leq\frac{3RB}{\sqrt t}.

children.title: Sample-Parallel Throughput
children.top_down_role: Worker utilization and throughput during parallel batch evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Sample-Parallel Throughput
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Idealized synchronous throughput with balanced workers and logarithmic reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(p\) identical workers evaluate at most one sample gradient every \(c>0\) time units, a balanced batch of size \(b\) is partitioned across workers, and gradient reduction costs \(r\lceil\log_2 p\rceil\). Then one synchronous mini-batch requires at most \(T(b,p)=c\lceil b/p\rceil+r\lceil\log_2p\rceil\), giving throughput \(Q(b,p)=b/T(b,p)\). When communication is negligible and \(b\geq p\), \(Q(b,p)\) approaches \(p/c\); adding workers beyond \(b\) cannot reduce the evaluation term below \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balanced synchronous evaluation scales sample throughput nearly linearly up to the batch size, after which communication and insufficient samples limit further speedup.
assumptions_latex: Workers have equal evaluation cost and batches are balanced.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: ideal balanced-worker cost model with tree reduction
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A complexity bound is appropriate for this leaf, but the idealized hardware model has no citation. The phrase that a worker evaluates at most one sample every c time units describes a lower rate bound rather than the upper evaluation-time guarantee needed for the asserted upper bound on T(b,p).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proportional-fair scheduling and throughput recursion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers both sample-average and constant-gain discounted throughput estimates and the associated mean ODE.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For users $i=1,\ldots,r$ with known next-slot rates $r_{n+1,i}$ and constants $d_i>0$, select at time $n$ an index in $\arg\max_i r_{n+1,i}/(d_i+\theta_{n,i})$, randomizing among ties. With selection indicator $I_{n+1,i}$, update either $\theta_{n+1,i}=\theta_{n,i}+\frac{1}{n+1}(I_{n+1,i}r_{n+1,i}-\theta_{n,i})$ or, for constant $\epsilon>0$, $\theta_{n+1,i}^{\epsilon}=\theta_{n,i}^{\epsilon}+\epsilon(I_{n+1,i}^{\epsilon}r_{n+1,i}-\theta_{n,i}^{\epsilon})$. Under stationary rate statistics, the corresponding mean dynamics are $\dot\theta^i=\bar h_i(\theta)-\theta^i$, where $\bar h_i(\theta)=\mathbb E[r_i\mathbf 1\{r_i/(d_i+\theta^i)\ge r_j/(d_j+\theta^j),\ j\ne i\}]$; these dynamics are cooperative because increasing $\theta^j$ for $j\ne i$ cannot decrease $\bar h_i(\theta)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each slot, proportional-fair scheduling chooses a user maximizing its currently available rate divided by its accumulated throughput plus a positive offset, with randomized tie-breaking. Throughput can be updated by a sample-average recursion or a constant-gain discounted recursion. Under stationary rate statistics, the recursion has a cooperative mean ODE: increasing another user's throughput cannot reduce a given user's expected selected rate.

knowledge_statements.title: Statistical–Computational Crossover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Crossover defined from a deterministic-plus-sampling-error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the error after \(K\) iterations with batch size \(b\) obeys \(E_K(b)\leq D_K+V_K/b\), where \(D_K>0\) is the batch-independent optimization term and \(V_K/b\) is the sampling term. The statistical crossover batch is \(b_{\mathrm{stat}}=\lceil V_K/D_K\rceil\). For \(b\geq b_{\mathrm{stat}}\), sampling contributes no more than the deterministic term, so \(E_K(b)\leq2D_K\); further batch growth can improve this bound by at most \(V_K/b\). With \(p\)-way sample parallelism, the useful linear-scaling range ends by \(b_{\mathrm{cross}}=\min\{p,b_{\mathrm{stat}}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The crossover occurs when mini-batch sampling error falls below batch-independent optimization error or when the batch exhausts available sample parallelism.
assumptions_latex: At most \(p\) samples can be evaluated concurrently.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Batch Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous worker averaging with explicit straggler-dependent completion time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(p\) workers, a batch partition \(S_k=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{p}S_{k,i}\), iterate \(x_k\), and step size \(\eta_k>0\), worker \(i\) computes \(s_{k,i}=\sum_{j\in S_{k,i}}G(x_k,\xi_j)\) and count \(n_{k,i}=|S_{k,i}|\). After every worker returns, the coordinator forms \(g_k=(\sum_i s_{k,i})/(\sum_i n_{k,i})\) and sets \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_k g_k\). If worker times are \(T_{k,i}\) and reduction costs \(T_k^{\mathrm{red}}\), synchronous completion time is \(T_k=\max_iT_{k,i}+T_k^{\mathrm{red}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers compute disjoint gradient sums, a coordinator averages all returned samples, and each synchronous step waits for the slowest worker plus reduction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projected stochastic quasi-gradient iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines stochastic quasi-gradient estimates and the basic projected iteration when deterministic constraints are represented by the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_v=\sigma(x^0,\ldots,x^v)\). For convex \(g_i\), suppose \(\mathbb E[\eta_i(v)\mid\mathcal F_v]=g_i(x^v)+a_i(v)\) and \(\mathbb E[\beta_i(v)\mid\mathcal F_v]+b_i(v)\in\partial g_i(x^v)\), where \(a_i(v)\to0\) and \(\|b_i(v)\|\to0\). When all constraints are represented by \(X\), define \(\Pi_X(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\|x-y\|^2\) and iterate \(x^{v+1}=\Pi_X(x^v-\rho^v\beta_0(v))\). The estimate \(\beta_i(v)\) is called a stochastic quasi-gradient when \(b_i(v)\ne0\), and a stochastic subgradient when \(b_i(v)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conditional function and subgradient estimates may have biases that vanish asymptotically. With deterministic constraints incorporated into X, the method takes a stochastic quasi-gradient step and projects back onto X; zero subgradient bias yields a stochastic subgradient.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f(x)=\mathbb E[F(x,\xi)]\) be differentiable on a neighborhood of \(C\). Given \(x_0\in C\) and step sizes \(\eta_k>0\), draw \(\xi_k\), compute \(G_k=G(x_k,\xi_k)\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)\), and update \(x_{k+1}=\Pi_C(x_k-\eta_kG_k)\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Almost-sure optimality of projected stochastic quasi-gradient cluster points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A cluster-point convergence result for the projected stochastic quasi-gradient iteration; it establishes optimality of every subsequential limit, not necessarily convergence of the whole sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}g_0(x)\), where \(g_0\) is convex and continuous and \(X\) is convex and compact. For the projected stochastic quasi-gradient iterates \(\mathbf x^{v+1}=\Pi_X(\mathbf x^v-\rho^v\beta_0(v))\), define \(\gamma^0(v)=\inf_{x^*\in X^*}\beta_0(v)^T(\mathbf x^v-x^*)\). If, almost surely, \(\rho^v>0\), \(\sum_{v=0}^{\infty}\rho^v=\infty\), and \[\sum_{v=0}^{\infty}\mathbb E\!\left[\rho^v|\gamma^0(v)|+(\rho^v)^2\|\beta_0(v)\|^2\right]<\infty,\] then, almost surely, every subsequential limit \(\bar x(\omega)=\lim_i x^{v_i}(\omega)\) belongs to \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex continuous objective on a convex compact feasible set, if the projected stochastic quasi-gradient step sizes have infinite total mass while the expected quasi-gradient error and squared-step terms are summable, then every sample-path cluster point is optimal almost surely.
assumptions_latex: g_0:X\to\mathbb R\text{ is convex and continuous}
X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is convex and compact}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb P\!\left(\text{every cluster point of }\{\mathbf x^v\}\text{ lies in }X^*\right)=1

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Set Projection Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-iteration oracle cost of exact Euclidean projected stochastic methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(x_{k+1}=\Pi_C(x_k-\eta_kG_k)\). If producing \(G_k\) costs \(T_G(d)\), computing the exact Euclidean projection \(\Pi_C(y)=\arg\min_{x\in C}\|x-y\|_2^2/2\) costs \(T_{\Pi_C}(d)\), and vector arithmetic costs \(O(d)\), then one iteration costs \(T_G(d)+T_{\Pi_C}(d)+O(d)\) time and makes one stochastic-oracle call and one projection-oracle call. Thus \(K\) iterations cost \(K[T_G(d)+T_{\Pi_C}(d)+O(d)]\); projection dominates whenever \(T_{\Pi_C}(d)=\omega(T_G(d)+d)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each projected stochastic step needs one gradient-oracle call and one projection; expensive feasible-set projections can dominate total runtime.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional normed vector space, let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be convex. Let \(h:C\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(\mu\)-strongly convex for some \(\mu>0\), and define \(D_h(x,y)=h(x)-h(y)-\langle\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle\). Initialize \(x_0\in C\). At iteration \(k\), obtain an integrable dual-space random vector \(G_k\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]\in\partial f(x_k)\), choose \(\eta_k>0\), and set \(x_{k+1}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in C}\{\eta_k\langle G_k,x\rangle+D_h(x,x_k)\}\). After \(K\) steps, output a declared iterate or a declared weighted average of the feasible iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stochastic mirror descent minimizes a stochastic linearization of a convex objective plus a Bregman proximity term adapted to the geometry of the feasible set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stochastic Block Mirror Descent Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized single-block mirror updates with delayed blockwise accumulation of the weighted average; the normalized output requires a positive total weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $x_1\in X$, $\gamma_k>0$, $\theta_k\ge0$, and $p_i\in[0,1]$ satisfying $\sum_{i=1}^bp_i=1$, initialize $s_1=0$ and $u_i=1$. For $k=1,\ldots,N$, sample $i_k$ with $\Pr\{i_k=i\}=p_i$; set $s_{k+1}^{(i_k)}=s_k^{(i_k)}+x_k^{(i_k)}\sum_{j=u_{i_k}}^k\theta_j$, leave $s_{k+1}^{(i)}=s_k^{(i)}$ for $i\ne i_k$, and set $u_{i_k}=k+1$. Then choose $x_{k+1}^{(i_k)}\in\arg\min_{u\in X_{i_k}}\{\langle G_{i_k}(x_k,\xi_k),u\rangle+\gamma_k^{-1}V_{i_k}(x_k^{(i_k)},u)\}$ and leave every other block unchanged. After iteration $N$, add $x_N^{(i)}\sum_{j=u_i}^N\theta_j$ to $s_{N+1}^{(i)}$ for $i\ne i_N$ and output $\bar x_N=s_{N+1}/\sum_{k=1}^N\theta_k$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, SBMD samples one block, performs a stochastic mirror update on that block, leaves the other blocks unchanged, and updates delayed blockwise sums used to form a weighted average.
assumptions_latex: \sum_{k=1}^N\theta_k>0\quad\text{for the normalized output to be defined}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x_N=\frac{s_{N+1}}{\sum_{k=1}^N\theta_k}\quad\text{after the stated randomized block mirror updates and final accumulation.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected gap and estimator-error bounds for stochastic mirror descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded bounds for source-defined stochastic mirror-descent quantities. All symbols, estimators, assumptions, and the referenced constant-stepsize policy retain their source-defined meanings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose Assumptions 1--3 and Assumption 5 hold. Then
\[
\mathbb E[f^{*k}-f_*^k]\leq \frac{4D_X^2+(2M^2+3\sigma^2)\sum_{t=1}^k\gamma_t^2}{2\sum_{t=1}^k\gamma_t},
\]
\[
\mathbb E\left[\left|\bar f^k-f^{*k}\right|\right]\leq Q\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^k v_t^2},

and
\[
\mathbb E\left[\left|\underline f^k-f_*^k\right|\right]\leq \frac{D_X^2+(M^2+\sigma^2)\sum_{t=1}^k\gamma_t^2}{\sum_{t=1}^k\gamma_t}+(Q+2\sqrt{2}D_X\sigma)\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^k v_t^2}.

\mathbb E\left[\left|\bar f^k-f^{*k}\right|\right]\leq Qk^{-1/2},

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strongly convex expected-gap bound for stochastic block mirror descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equation-numbered strong-convexity and sampling assumptions remain by reference because the extract does not expand them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose (4.6.30) and (4.6.31) hold and, for every \(k\ge1\), \[\gamma_k\le\min\left\{\frac1{2\bar L},\frac b\mu\right\},\qquad \theta_{k+1}=\frac{b\gamma_k}{\Gamma_k}-\frac{(b-1)\gamma_{k+1}}{\Gamma_{k+1}},\] where \(\Gamma_1=1\) and \(\Gamma_k=\Gamma_{k-1}(1-\gamma_k\mu/b)\) for \(k\ge2\). Then, for every \(N\ge2\), \[\mathbb E[\phi(\bar x_N)-\phi(x_*)]\le\left(\sum_{k=2}^{N+1}\theta_k\right)^{-1}\left((b-\mu\gamma_1)\sum_{i=1}^bV_i(x_1^{(i)},x_*^{(i)})+(b-1)\gamma_1[\phi(x_1)-\phi(x_*)]+\sigma^2\sum_{k=1}^N\frac{\gamma_k^2}{\Gamma_k}\right),\] where \(x_*\) is the optimal solution of (4.6.53).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the referenced strongly convex and sampling conditions, compatible stepsizes, and recursively weighted averaging, the expected objective gap is controlled by the initial blockwise Bregman distance, initial objective gap, and weighted accumulated variance divided by the total output weight.
assumptions_latex: x_*\text{ is the optimal solution of (4.6.53).}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: High-probability bounds for stochastic block mirror descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equation-numbered hypotheses and parameter schedules remain by reference because the extract does not expand them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose (4.6.43) and (4.6.31) hold and \(X\) is bounded. (a) Under parameter choices (4.6.16), (4.6.25), and \(\widetilde D=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^bV_i(x_1^{(i)},x_*^{(i)})}\), for every \(\lambda>0\), \[\Pr\!\left\{f(\bar x_N)-f(x_*)\ge \frac{\sqrt{b\sum_{i=1}^bM_i^2\sum_{i=1}^bD_i}}{\sqrt{2N}}\left[1+(1+\lambda)\frac{\bar M^2}{\bar m^2}+8\lambda\frac{\bar M}{\bar m}\right]\right\}\le e^{-\lambda^2/3}+e^{-\lambda},\] where \(\bar m=\min_{1\le i\le b}M_i\) and \(x_*\) is any solution of (4.6.1). (b) Under the strongly convex parameter choices (4.6.33) and (4.6.38), for every \(\lambda>0\), \[\Pr\!\left\{f(\bar x_N)-f(x_*)\ge \frac{2(1+\lambda)b\sum_{i=1}^bM_i^2}{(N+1)\mu}\frac{\bar M^2}{\bar m^2}+\frac{8\sqrt2\lambda\bar M\sqrt{b\sum_{i=1}^bM_i^2\sum_{i=1}^bD_i}}{\bar m\sqrt{3N}}\right\}\le e^{-\lambda^2/3}+e^{-\lambda},\] where \(x_*\) is the optimal solution of (4.6.1).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the referenced conditions, boundedness, and prescribed parameter schedules, stochastic block mirror descent has explicit high-probability objective-gap bounds. The general nonsmooth threshold is order 1/sqrt(N); the strongly convex threshold contains 1/(N+1) and 1/sqrt(N) terms.
assumptions_latex: \text{In part (b), parameter choices (4.6.33) and (4.6.38) are used.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr\{f(\bar x_N)-f(x_*)\ge B_N(\lambda)\}\le e^{-\lambda^2/3}+e^{-\lambda},\quad \lambda>0,\text{ with the displayed case-specific }B_N(\lambda).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected Suboptimality Bound for RMDSA
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon expected objective bound for RMDSA under the preceding biased stochastic-oracle assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be bounded and \(N\ge1\). Under the preceding RMDSA stochastic-oracle assumptions, run \(N\) steps with \(\gamma_t=\sqrt{2\Omega}/(L\sqrt N)\) for every \(1\le t\le N\). Then \(\mathbf E[f(x^N)-\mathrm{Opt}]\le \sqrt{2\Omega}L/\sqrt N+2\sqrt{2\Omega}\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a bounded feasible set, N RMDSA steps with constant step size sqrt(2 Omega)/(L sqrt(N)) have expected suboptimality at most sqrt(2 Omega)L/sqrt(N) plus the bias term 2 sqrt(2 Omega) mu.
assumptions_latex: The preceding RMDSA oracle assumptions hold: the oracle noises are i.i.d., \(\mathbf E\|G(x,\xi)\|_*^2\le L^2<\infty\), and \(\|\mathbf E[G(x,\xi)]-f'(x)\|_*\le\mu\) for every \(x\in X\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected convergence rate of stochastic mirror descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An expected objective-gap bound for horizon-tuned stochastic mirror descent on a convex objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Phi\) be a mirror map that is \(1\)-strongly convex on \(\mathcal X\cap\mathcal D\) with respect to \(\|\cdot\|\), initialize \(x_1\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X\cap\mathcal D}\Phi(x)\), and define
\[
R^2=\sup_{x\in\mathcal X\cap\mathcal D}\Phi(x)-\Phi(x_1).
\]
If \(f\) is convex and \(\mathbb E\|\widetilde g(x)\|_*^2\leq B^2\) for every oracle query point, then for every \(t\geq1\), stochastic mirror descent with \(\eta=\frac{R}{B}\sqrt{\frac{2}{t}}\) satisfies
\[
\mathbb E f\!\left(\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^t x_s\right)-\min_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\leq RB\sqrt{\frac{2}{t}}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex objective, a 1-strongly convex mirror map with radius parameter R, and a stochastic oracle whose squared dual norm has expectation at most B squared, stochastic mirror descent with horizon-tuned step size achieves expected objective gap at most RB times the square root of 2/t at the uniform average of its iterates.
assumptions_latex: \Phi\text{ is }1\text{-strongly convex on }\mathcal X\cap\mathcal D\text{ with respect to }\|\cdot\|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projected SGD as Euclidean stochastic mirror descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-mirror specialization of stochastic mirror descent with time-varying step sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
With the Euclidean mirror map \(\Phi(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2\) and step sizes \((\eta_t)_{t\geq1}\), stochastic mirror descent reduces to projected stochastic gradient descent:
\[
x_{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal X}\!\left(x_t-\eta_t\widetilde g(x_t)\right),\qquad t\geq1.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the squared Euclidean mirror map, stochastic mirror descent is projected stochastic gradient descent: take a stochastic-gradient step with the current step size and project the result onto the feasible set.
assumptions_latex: (\eta_t)_{t\geq1}\text{ is a sequence of step sizes}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Explicit General-Convex SBMD Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected objective-gap bounds for importance sampling and uniform block sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume $\theta_k=\gamma_k$ and let $x_*$ be any solution. (a) If $X$ is bounded, $$p_i=\frac{\sqrt{D_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^b\sqrt{D_j}},\qquad \gamma_k=\gamma=\frac{\sqrt{2\sum_{i=1}^b\sqrt{D_i}}}{\sqrt{N\sum_{i=1}^bM_i^2}},$$ then $$\mathbb E[f(\bar x_N)-f(x_*)]\le\sqrt{\frac2N}\left(\sum_{i=1}^b\sqrt{D_i}\right)\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^bM_i^2}.$$ (b) If $p_i=1/b$ and, for some $\widetilde D>0$, $$\gamma_k=\gamma=\frac{\sqrt{2b}\,\widetilde D}{\sqrt{N\sum_{i=1}^bM_i^2}},$$ then $$\mathbb E[f(\bar x_N)-f(x_*)]\le\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^bM_i^2}\left(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^bV_i(x_1^{(i)},x_*^{(i)})}{\widetilde D}+\widetilde D\right)\frac{\sqrt b}{\sqrt{2N}}.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For bounded domains, importance sampling proportional to the square roots of the block diameters gives an explicit order-one-over-square-root-N expected gap. Uniform sampling with a constant tuned stepsize gives a corresponding bound involving the initial total Bregman distance and a free scale parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The expected-gap bounds in cases (a) and (b) hold under their respective stated sampling and stepsize choices.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected and high-probability guarantees for modified stochastic mirror descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-iteration guarantees for the source-defined averaged iterates of modified stochastic mirror descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume 0<\gamma_t\le (2L)^{-1} for every t\ge 1, and let \{x_{t+1}^{av}\}_{t\ge 1} be computed according to (4.1.23). Under Assumption 3, for every k\ge 1, \mathbb E[f(x_{k+1}^{av})-f^*]\le K_0(k), where K_0(k):=\left(\sum_{t=1}^k\gamma_t\right)^{-1}\left[D_X^2+\sigma^2\sum_{t=1}^k\gamma_t^2\right]. Under Assumptions 3 and 4, for every \lambda>0 and k\ge 1, \operatorname{Prob}\!\left\{f(x_{k+1}^{av})-f^*>K_0(k)+\lambda K_1(k)\right\}\le \exp(-\lambda^2/3)+\exp(-\lambda), where K_1(k):=\left(\sum_{t=1}^k\gamma_t\right)^{-1}\left[D_X\sigma\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^k\gamma_t^2}+\sigma^2\sum_{t=1}^k\gamma_t^2\right].
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the modified stochastic mirror-descent averages and the stated stepsize restriction, Assumption 3 gives the displayed expected objective-error bound. Adding Assumption 4 gives the displayed high-probability bound for every positive lambda and iteration k.
assumptions_latex: \text{Assumptions 3 and 4 hold for the probability bound}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall k\ge 1:\quad \mathbb E[f(x_{k+1}^{av})-f^*]\le K_0(k);\qquad \forall\lambda>0,\ k\ge 1:\quad \operatorname{Prob}\!\left\{f(x_{k+1}^{av})-f^*>K_0(k)+\lambda K_1(k)\right\}\le e^{-\lambda^2/3}+e^{-\lambda}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stochastic mirror-descent update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic stochastic mirror-descent iteration; the surrounding promise of later convergence results is not itself an algorithmic guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(G_t:=G(x_t,\xi_t)\). For \(t=1,2,\ldots\), stochastic mirror descent updates \[x_{t+1}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\left\{\gamma_t\langle G_t,x\rangle+V(x_t,x)\right\},\] where \(V\) is the prox-function associated with the distance-generating function \(\omega\), under the stated normalization \(\sigma_v=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, replace the exact subgradient by the stochastic-oracle output at the current point and minimize its stepsize-scaled linearization plus the prox term over X.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stochastic block mirror descent for composite optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The auxiliary accumulator update referenced as (4.6.13) is retained by reference because its formula is not included in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_1\in X\), stepsizes \(\gamma_k>0\), weights \(\theta_k\ge0\), and probabilities \(p_i\in[0,1]\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^bp_i=1\), initialize \(s_1=0\), \(u_i=1\), and \(\theta_1=0\). For \(k=1,\ldots,N\), sample \(i_k\) according to the prescribed block distribution, update the accumulators by (4.6.13), set \(u_{i_k}=k+1\), and define \[x_{k+1}^{(i)}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\arg\min_{z\in X_i}\left\{\langle G_i(x_k,\xi_k),z-x_k^{(i)}\rangle+\gamma_k^{-1}V_i(x_k^{(i)},z)+\chi_i(z)\right\},&i=i_k,\\x_k^{(i)},&i\ne i_k.\end{cases}\] Finally set \(s_{N+1}^{(i)}\leftarrow s_{N+1}^{(i)}+x_{N+1}^{(i)}\sum_{j=u_i}^{N+1}\theta_j\) for every block and output \[\bar x_N=\frac{s_{N+1}}{\sum_{k=1}^{N+1}\theta_k}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, sample one block and perform a composite mirror-proximal update on that block using its stochastic oracle, Bregman divergence, and separable regularizer; all other blocks remain unchanged. Return the prescribed weighted average assembled from the block accumulators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x_N=s_{N+1}\big/\sum_{k=1}^{N+1}\theta_k\text{ is produced after }N\text{ randomized single-block composite mirror updates.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: AC-SA one-step potential inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A pathwise one-step objective and Bregman-potential recurrence with stochastic error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x_{t-1},\bar x_{t-1})\in X^2\), and generate \((\underline x_t,x_t,\bar x_t)\in X^3\) by the AC-SA updates. If \[\frac{q_t(1-\alpha_t)}{\alpha_t(1-q_t)}=\frac1{1+\mu\gamma_t},\qquad 1+\mu\gamma_t>L\alpha_t\gamma_t,\] then for every \(x\in X\), \[\Psi(\bar x_t)\le(1-\alpha_t)\Psi(\bar x_{t-1})+\alpha_t l_\Psi(\underline x_t,x)+\frac{\alpha_t}{\gamma_t}\bigl[V(x_{t-1},x)-(1+\mu\gamma_t)V(x_t,x)\bigr]+\Delta_t(x),\] where \[l_\Psi(\underline x_t,x):=f(\underline x_t)+\langle f'(\underline x_t),x-\underline x_t\rangle+h(x)+\mu V(\underline x_t,x),\] \[\Delta_t(x):=\frac{\alpha_t\gamma_t(M+\|\delta_t\|_*)^2}{2[1+\mu\gamma_t-L\alpha_t\gamma_t]}+\alpha_t\langle\delta_t,x-x_{t-1}^+\rangle,\] and \[x_{t-1}^+:=\frac{\mu\gamma_t}{1+\mu\gamma_t}\underline x_t+\frac1{1+\mu\gamma_t}x_{t-1}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the coupling and stability conditions on the AC-SA parameters, each averaged objective value is bounded by the previous value, a composite lower model, a telescoping Bregman-potential difference, and an explicit stochastic-error term.
assumptions_latex: (\underline x_t,x_t,\bar x_t)\text{ are generated by AC-SA}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded one-step inequality for the iterates, divergence, and stochastic oracle defined in the surrounding mirror-descent setup.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that L\gamma_t<1 and define \delta_t:=G(x_t,\xi_t)-g(x_t), where g(x_t)=\mathbb E[G(x_t,\xi_t)]=\nabla f(x_t). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Accumulated AC-SA potential inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Telescopes the AC-SA one-step recurrence through iteration k.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{\bar x_t\}_{t\ge1}\) be generated by AC-SA, with parameters satisfying the coupling and stability relations \(\frac{q_t(1-\alpha_t)}{\alpha_t(1-q_t)}=(1+\mu\gamma_t)^{-1}\) and \(1+\mu\gamma_t>L\alpha_t\gamma_t\). Define \[\Gamma_1:=1,\qquad \Gamma_t:=(1-\alpha_t)\Gamma_{t-1}\quad(t\ge2).\] Then for every \(x\in X\) and \(k\ge1\), \[\Psi(\bar x_k)-\Gamma_k\sum_{t=1}^k\frac{\alpha_t}{\Gamma_t}l_\Psi(\underline x_t,x)\le \Gamma_k(1-\alpha_1)\Psi(\bar x_1)+\Gamma_k\sum_{t=1}^k\frac{\alpha_t}{\gamma_t\Gamma_t}\bigl[V(x_{t-1},x)-(1+\mu\gamma_t)V(x_t,x)\bigr]+\Gamma_k\sum_{t=1}^k\frac{\Delta_t(x)}{\Gamma_t},\] where \(l_\Psi\) and \(\Delta_t\) are the one-step model and stochastic-error terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying and summing the AC-SA one-step inequalities yields a weighted bound on the final objective relative to accumulated lower models, with Bregman-potential differences and stochastic errors weighted by the product factors Gamma.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected objective-gap bound for stochastic block mirror descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The assumptions referenced by equation numbers are preserved because their contents are not included in the extract.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Robust Mirror Descent Stochastic Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic-oracle assumptions and the resulting RMDSA modification of mirror descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi_1,\xi_2,\ldots\) be i.i.d. oracle noises. At query \(x_t\in\mathcal X\), the oracle returns \(G(x_t,\xi_t)\). Define \(g(x)=\mathbf E[G(x,\xi)]\), and assume for every \(x\in\mathcal X\) that \(\mathbf E\|G(x,\xi)\|_*^2\le L^2<\infty\) and \(\|g(x)-f'(x)\|_*\le\mu\). Robust mirror descent stochastic approximation replaces \(f'(x_t)\) in the mirror-descent iteration by \(G(x_t,\xi_t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The stochastic oracle returns noisy subgradient estimates with i.i.d. noise, uniformly bounded dual-norm second moment, and mean bias at most mu. RMDSA uses these estimates in place of the mirror-descent subgradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing \(f'(x_t)\) by \(G(x_t,\xi_t)\) in the mirror-descent iteration yields RMDSA.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Dual Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted regularized dual averaging for constrained stochastic convex optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(h:C\to\mathbb R\) be strongly convex. Initialize \(s_0=0\). For positive weights \(a_k\) and regularization scales \(\beta_k>0\), obtain \(G_k\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]\in\partial f(x_k)\), update \(s_{k+1}=s_k+a_kG_k\), and choose \(x_{k+1}=\arg\min_{x\in C}\{\langle s_{k+1},x\rangle+\beta_{k+1}h(x)\}\). After \(K\) oracle calls, output \(x_K\) or the declared weighted average \(\bar x_K=(\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}a_kx_k)/(\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}a_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stochastic dual averaging accumulates weighted stochastic subgradients in dual space and maps the cumulative vector back through strongly convex regularization.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Proximal Gradient Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean stochastic proximal-gradient iteration for a smooth expected loss plus a proper convex regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an initial point \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom} r\), at iteration \(t\geq 0\) obtain a random vector \(g_t\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[g_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=\nabla f(x_t)\), choose \(\alpha_t>0\), and set
\[
x_{t+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\alpha_t r}(x_t-\alpha_t g_t)
=\mathop{\arg\min}_{x\in\mathbb R^d}\left\{r(x)+\frac{1}{2\alpha_t}\lVert x-(x_t-\alpha_tg_t)\rVert^2\right\}.
\]
After a prescribed number \(T\) of oracle calls, output either \(x_T\) or a specified weighted average of \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace the smooth gradient by an unbiased stochastic estimate, take a forward step, and apply the proximal map of the nonsmooth regularizer.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and \(r:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\((\mathcal F_t)_{t\geq0}\) is the history filtration and \(x_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}\) is a stochastic forward step for \(f\) followed by a proximal step for \(r\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean proximal mapping of the scaled function alpha times r.
Stochastic gradient estimate at the current iterate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Composite upper estimate at an averaged iterate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A convex averaging and upper-model inequality used in AC-SA analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be convex, \(\Psi=f+h\), and suppose \(h\) is convex and
\[f(y)-f(x)-\langle f'(x),y-x\rangle\le \frac L2\|y-x\|^2+M\|y-x\|\qquad(x,y\in X).\]
If
\[\bar x_t=(1-\alpha_t)\bar x_{t-1}+\alpha_tx_t,\qquad \alpha_t\in[0,1],\quad \bar x_{t-1},x_t\in X,\]
then for every \(z\in X\),
\[\Psi(\bar x_t)\le(1-\alpha_t)\Psi(\bar x_{t-1})+\alpha_t\bigl[f(z)+\langle f'(z),x_t-z\rangle+h(x_t)\bigr]+\frac L2\|\bar x_t-z\|^2+M\|\bar x_t-z\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective at an averaged iterate is bounded by the weighted preceding objective and a linearized composite value, plus the mixed quadratic-linear upper-model error at the averaged point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Psi(\bar x_t)\le(1-\alpha_t)\Psi(\bar x_{t-1})+\alpha_t[f(z)+\langle f'(z),x_t-z\rangle+h(x_t)]+\frac L2\|\bar x_t-z\|^2+M\|\bar x_t-z\|.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected suboptimality bound for fixed-step stochastic gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex stochastic gradient regime with the source's condition L_g=0 and fixed step length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose stochastic gradient is run on a convex function \(f\) with \(L_g=0\) for \(T\) steps using a fixed step length \(\alpha>0\). Define \(\alpha_{\mathrm{opt}}=D_0/(B\sqrt{T+1})\) and \(\theta=\alpha/\alpha_{\mathrm{opt}}\). Then \[\mathbb{E}\!\left[f(\bar{x}^{T})-f^*\right]\leq \left(\frac{\theta}{2}+\frac{\theta^{-1}}{2}\right)\frac{BD_0}{\sqrt{T+1}}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For stochastic gradient on a convex objective with L_g = 0, after T fixed-step iterations the expected suboptimality of the averaged iterate is at most one half of theta plus one half of its reciprocal, multiplied by B D_0 divided by the square root of T+1, where theta is the chosen step length relative to the stated optimal step length.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Accelerated stochastic approximation iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The three updates defining one AC-SA iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_{t-1},\bar x_{t-1}\in X\), parameters \(q_t,\alpha_t,\gamma_t\), and an oracle sample \(\xi_t\), compute
\[\underline x_t=(1-q_t)\bar x_{t-1}+q_tx_{t-1},\]
\[x_t=\arg\min_{x\in X}\left\{\gamma_t\left[\langle G(\underline x_t,\xi_t),x\rangle+h(x)+\mu V(\underline x_t,x)\right]+V(x_{t-1},x)\right\},\]
and
\[\bar x_t=(1-\alpha_t)\bar x_{t-1}+\alpha_tx_t.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Forward–Backward Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic resolvent splitting for a cocoercive single-valued operator and a maximally monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_0\in\mathcal H\). At iteration \(t\geq0\), observe \(b_t\) with \(\mathbb E[b_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=B x_t\), choose \(\gamma_t>0\), and compute
\[
x_{t+1}=J_{\gamma_t A}(x_t-\gamma_t b_t),\qquad J_{\gamma_t A}=(I+\gamma_t A)^{-1}.
\]
Equivalently, the update satisfies \(0\in A x_{t+1}+b_t+\gamma_t^{-1}(x_{t+1}-x_t)\). A finite run returns \(x_T\), while asymptotic formulations study the entire adapted sequence \((x_t)_{t\geq0}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Estimate the forward operator stochastically, take an explicit step, and apply the resolvent of the maximally monotone backward operator.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) is maximally monotone, and \(B:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) is cocoercive.
\(x_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable and \(\mathbb E[\lVert b_t\rVert^2\mid\mathcal F_t]<\infty\).
The target problem is to find \(x_\star\) satisfying \(0\in A x_\star+B x_\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}\) is obtained by a stochastic forward evaluation of \(B\) and an implicit backward evaluation of \(A\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent of the scaled operator gamma A.

knowledge_statements.title: Heavy-Ball Stochastic Gradient Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical stochastic heavy-ball recursion with a velocity state and current-point gradient sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in\mathbb R^d\), initialize \(v_0=0\). For \(t\geq0\), sample \(g_t\) with \(\mathbb E[g_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=\nabla f(x_t)\), choose \(\alpha_t>0\) and momentum \(\beta_t\in[0,1)\), and update
\[
v_{t+1}=\beta_t v_t+g_t,\qquad x_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_t v_{t+1}.
\]
Equivalently, when \(\alpha_t=\alpha_{t-1}\), \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_tg_t+\beta_t(x_t-x_{t-1})\). After \(T\) iterations, output \(x_T\) or a declared average of the iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heavy-ball SGD exponentially carries past stochastic gradients in a velocity and steps opposite the resulting momentum direction.
assumptions_latex: \(x_t,v_t\) are \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable and \(g_t\) has finite conditional second moment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_t,v_t)\) obeys a stochastic first-order recursion with geometrically weighted gradient memory.

notation.meaning: Stochastic gradient sampled at the current iterate.

review_flags: authoritative stochastic heavy-ball source and exact normalization locator required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recursion is mathematically coherent and fits the heavy-ball stochastic-gradient container, including the stated constant-stepsize equivalence. Because stochastic heavy-ball conventions differ in velocity normalization, an authoritative source with an exact algorithm or equation locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Nesterov-Type Stochastic Momentum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Look-ahead stochastic momentum using a gradient sampled at an extrapolated point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_{-1}=x_0\in\mathbb R^d\), for \(t\geq0\) choose \(\beta_t\in[0,1)\) and \(\alpha_t>0\), form
\[
y_t=x_t+\beta_t(x_t-x_{t-1}),
\]
sample \(g_t\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[g_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=\nabla f(y_t)\), and update
\[
x_{t+1}=y_t-\alpha_t g_t.
\]
The method returns \(x_T\), \(y_T\), or a prespecified weighted average after \(T\) stochastic-gradient calls; the choice must be declared by the particular convergence guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extrapolate from the two latest iterates, evaluate a stochastic gradient at that look-ahead point, and step from the extrapolated point.
assumptions_latex: \(x_t,x_{t-1}\) are \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable and \(g_t\) has finite conditional second moment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}\) combines inertial extrapolation with a stochastic gradient evaluated at the extrapolated state \(y_t\).

notation.meaning: Stochastic gradient evaluated at the look-ahead point.

review_flags: Nesterov-type stochastic momentum has multiple inequivalent recursions; exact local variant needs an authoritative source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The look-ahead recursion is a plausible Nesterov-type stochastic momentum algorithm and fits the container, but several inequivalent stochastic Nesterov recursions exist. A source identifying this exact extrapolate-sample-update variant is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient Averaging States
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive weighted averaging state for stochastic gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((g_t)_{t\geq1}\subset\mathbb R^d\) be stochastic gradient observations and let \(a_t\in(0,1]\). A gradient averaging state is the adapted sequence \((m_t)_{t\geq0}\) defined by \(m_0=0\) and
\[
m_t=(1-a_t)m_{t-1}+a_tg_t.
\]
Consequently,
\[
m_t=\sum_{s=1}^{t}a_s\!\left(\prod_{j=s+1}^{t}(1-a_j)\right)g_s.
\]
For constant \(a_t=a\), the weight assigned to \(g_s\) at time \(t\) is \(a(1-a)^{t-s}\), so the state is an exponentially weighted, generally unnormalized average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient averaging state recursively combines the previous state with the newest stochastic gradient, yielding explicit geometrically decaying weights when the coefficient is constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_t\) is a causal weighted sum of \(g_1,\ldots,g_t\).

notation.meaning: Weight assigned to the new gradient observation.

review_flags: local intended averaging convention and supporting source are unspecified

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recursive expansion is correct and definition is an appropriate content kind for this state container. No evidence establishes that this particular normalized exponential-average convention is the intended local meaning of Gradient Averaging States.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive averaging of displacement or velocity observations in an inertial stochastic method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((u_t)_{t\geq1}\subset\mathbb R^d\) be velocity observations, such as \(u_t=x_t-x_{t-1}\), and let \(b_t\in(0,1]\). A velocity averaging state is the adapted sequence \((v_t)_{t\geq0}\) defined by \(v_0=0\) and
\[
v_t=(1-b_t)v_{t-1}+b_tu_t.
\]
Thus
\[
v_t=\sum_{s=1}^{t}b_s\!\left(\prod_{j=s+1}^{t}(1-b_j)\right)u_s.
\]
When \(b_t=b\), past velocities receive geometrically decreasing weights \(b(1-b)^{t-s}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A velocity averaging state filters observed displacements or velocities through a causal weighted recursion, with geometric memory under a constant averaging coefficient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_t\) is a causal weighted sum of the velocity observations \(u_1,\ldots,u_t\).

notation.meaning: Observed instantaneous velocity or iterate displacement.
Weight assigned to the newest velocity observation.

review_flags: velocity averaging may instead denote momentum itself in the intended source; exact convention requires evidence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recursion and its weighted-sum expansion are correct, and definition fits the terminal container. Evidence is needed because velocity averaging may denote an averaged displacement, a momentum state, or another inertial state under different conventions.

children.title: Coupled Averaging Effects
children.top_down_role: Stability and responsiveness consequences of combining averaged state mechanisms.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Averaging Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-state linear filtering effect when gradient and velocity averages are updated together.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(m_t=(1-a)m_{t-1}+ag_t\) and \(v_t=(1-b)v_{t-1}+bu_t\), where \(a,b\in(0,1]\) and \(m_0=v_0=0\). Then
\[
(m_t,v_t)=\sum_{s=1}^{t}\bigl(a(1-a)^{t-s}g_s,\;b(1-b)^{t-s}u_s\bigr).
\]
Hence the two states have distinct geometric memory lengths controlled by \(a\) and \(b\). If an iterate update uses \(d_t=m_t+\lambda v_t\), then \(d_t\) is the sum of two causal filters and cannot generally be represented by one geometric filter unless their decay factors coincide or the input sequences satisfy an additional relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupling gradient and velocity averages combines two filters with potentially different memory scales; generally their summed direction is not a single exponential average.
assumptions_latex: Both averaging states start from zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupled direction \(d_t=m_t+\lambda v_t\) contains two independently weighted histories, except in degenerate or specially related cases.

notation.meaning: Direction formed by coupling the two states.

review_flags: the algebraic property is precise, but the taxonomy's intended coupled averaging model lacks a source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed two-filter identity is algebraically correct, and property is the right mathematical role. The taxonomy's intended coupled averaging mechanism is not evidenced, so the claimed model and its interpretation cannot yet be tied reliably to this leaf.

children.title: Data-Adaptive Preconditioning Family

children.title: AdaGrad-Type Accumulated-Geometry Methods
children.top_down_role: Scalar, diagonal, and matrix accumulated-gradient scaling families.

knowledge_statements.title: AdaGrad-Type Accumulated-Geometry Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal AdaGrad with cumulative coordinatewise squared-gradient geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_1\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), \(s_0=0\), \(\delta>0\), and \(\eta>0\), for \(t=1,\ldots,T\) obtain a stochastic subgradient \(g_t\), set
\[
s_t=s_{t-1}+g_t\odot g_t,\qquad H_t=\operatorname{Diag}\!\bigl(\sqrt{s_t}+\delta\mathbf 1\bigr),
\]
and update
\[
x_{t+1}=\mathop{\arg\min}_{x\in X}\left\{\eta\langle g_t,x\rangle+\tfrac12\lVert x-x_t\rVert_{H_t}^{2}\right\}.
\]
After \(T\) oracle calls, output \(x_{T+1}\) or a prespecified average. Scalar and full-matrix variants replace \(H_t\) by their corresponding accumulated geometries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AdaGrad accumulates squared gradients and uses their square roots as an adaptive metric, reducing steps in coordinates with large historical gradients.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(g_t\) is an observed stochastic subgradient at \(x_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update is a projected stochastic first-order step in the cumulative gradient-dependent metric \(H_t\).

notation.meaning: Quadratic form z transpose H_t z.

children.title: RMSProp-Type Moving-Moment Scaling
children.top_down_role: Second-moment moving-average scaling in RMSProp-type methods.

knowledge_statements.title: RMSProp-Type Moving-Moment Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise RMSProp recursion using an exponential average of squared stochastic gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in\mathbb R^d\), initialize \(v_0=0\). For \(t\geq1\), sample a stochastic gradient \(g_t\) at \(x_{t-1}\), choose \(\rho\in[0,1)\), \(\alpha_t>0\), and \(\varepsilon>0\), and compute
\[
v_t=\rho v_{t-1}+(1-\rho)(g_t\odot g_t),\qquad
x_t=x_{t-1}-\alpha_t\,g_t\oslash(\sqrt{v_t}+\varepsilon\mathbf1).
\]
All square roots and divisions are coordinatewise. After \(T\) stochastic-gradient calls, return \(x_T\) or another output explicitly prescribed by the application.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: RMSProp divides each stochastic-gradient coordinate by a stabilized moving root-mean-square estimate of that coordinate's recent gradients.
assumptions_latex: \(g_t\in\mathbb R^d\) is a stochastic gradient observed at \(x_{t-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each coordinate is scaled by the reciprocal of its exponentially averaged recent root-mean-square gradient magnitude.

notation.meaning: Exponential moving average of coordinatewise squared gradients.

review_flags: authoritative RMSProp source and exact epsilon placement locator required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated recursion is a standard RMSProp-type algorithm and fits the terminal container. An authoritative locator is required because published and implementation variants differ in decay parameterization and whether epsilon is placed inside or outside the square root.

children.title: Adam-Type Moving-Moment Scaling
children.top_down_role: Coupled first-moment and second-moment scaling in Adam-type methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Adam-Type Moving-Moment Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adam recursion with bias-corrected first and second exponential gradient moments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in\mathbb R^d\), set \(m_0=v_0=0\). For \(t\geq1\), sample \(g_t\) at \(x_{t-1}\) and compute
\[
m_t=\beta_1m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_1)g_t,\qquad
v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)(g_t\odot g_t),
\]
\[
\widehat m_t=\frac{m_t}{1-\beta_1^t},\qquad
\widehat v_t=\frac{v_t}{1-\beta_2^t},\qquad
x_t=x_{t-1}-\alpha_t\widehat m_t\oslash(\sqrt{\widehat v_t}+\varepsilon\mathbf1).
\]
After \(T\) stochastic-gradient calls, output \(x_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adam combines bias-corrected moving averages of gradients and squared gradients, scaling the former by the stabilized square root of the latter.
assumptions_latex: \(g_t\in\mathbb R^d\) is a stochastic gradient at \(x_{t-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update uses a coordinatewise normalized, bias-corrected first-moment direction.

children.title: Moving-Moment Bias Correction
children.top_down_role: Finite-horizon corrections for initialized exponential moment estimates.

knowledge_statements.title: Moving-Moment Bias Correction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact zero-initialization correction for exponential moving moments under a stationary conditional mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z_1,z_2,\ldots\) be integrable random vectors with \(\mathbb E[z_t]=\mu\), and let \(q_0=0\) and \(q_t=\beta q_{t-1}+(1-\beta)z_t\) for a constant \(\beta\in[0,1)\). Then
\[
q_t=(1-\beta)\sum_{s=1}^{t}\beta^{t-s}z_s,
\qquad
\mathbb E[q_t]=(1-\beta^t)\mu.
\]
Therefore the corrected state \(\widehat q_t=q_t/(1-\beta^t)\) satisfies \(\mathbb E[\widehat q_t]=\mu\). Applied separately to gradient and squared-gradient observations, this yields the standard Adam corrections \(m_t/(1-\beta_1^t)\) and \(v_t/(1-\beta_2^t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-initialized exponential average is shrunk by one minus beta to the power t; dividing by that factor removes this initialization bias under stationarity.
assumptions_latex: \(z_t\) is integrable and has the same mean \(\mu\) for every \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat q_t=q_t/(1-\beta^t)\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\mu\).

children.title: Convergence-Sensitive Denominator Variants

knowledge_statements.title: Convergence-Sensitive Denominator Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: AMSGrad-style monotone second-moment denominator designed to prevent increases in effective coordinatewise steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(x_0\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) and \(m_0=v_0=\widehat v_0=0\). For \(t\geq1\), observe \(g_t\), choose \(\beta_{1,t}\in[0,1)\), \(\beta_2\in[0,1)\), and \(\alpha_t>0\), and set
\[
m_t=\beta_{1,t}m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_{1,t})g_t,
\]
\[
v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)(g_t\odot g_t),\qquad
\widehat v_t=\max\{\widehat v_{t-1},v_t\},
\]
where the maximum is coordinatewise. Update \(x_t\) by projecting \(x_{t-1}-\alpha_tm_t\oslash(\sqrt{\widehat v_t}+\varepsilon\mathbf1)\) onto \(X\), and output \(x_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AMSGrad replaces Adam's current second moment by its coordinatewise running maximum, preventing the adaptive denominator from decreasing.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(g_t\) is a stochastic gradient available at iteration \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat v_t\geq\widehat v_{t-1}\) coordinatewise, so the unregularized coordinatewise denominator is nondecreasing.

notation.meaning: Coordinatewise running maximum of second-moment states.

children.title: Normalized Stochastic Gradients
children.top_down_role: Direction-preserving magnitude normalization for stochastic gradients.

knowledge_statements.title: Normalized Stochastic Gradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SGD whose oracle direction is rescaled to unit norm, with a zero-gradient convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an initial point \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), stepsizes \(\eta_k>0\), and stochastic gradient samples \(g_k=G(x_k,\xi_k)\), define \(d_k=0\) when \(g_k=0\) and \(d_k=g_k/\lVert g_k\rVert_2\) otherwise. The normalized stochastic-gradient iteration is
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_k d_k.
\]
After a prescribed number \(K\) of oracle calls, output either the final iterate \(x_K\) or a stated average or randomized iterate. Normalization fixes every nonzero update length at \(\eta_k\); it does not generally preserve unbiasedness even when \(\mathbb{E}[g_k\mid x_k]=\nabla f(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Divide each nonzero sampled gradient by its Euclidean norm before stepping. This bounds the update length but generally turns an unbiased gradient sample into a biased direction.
assumptions_latex: \(\eta_k>0\) and the output convention are specified.

children.title: Clipped Stochastic Gradients
children.top_down_role: Magnitude truncation for stability under large stochastic gradients.

knowledge_statements.title: Clipped Stochastic Gradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean norm clipping at a fixed or predictable positive threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), stepsizes \(\eta_k>0\), thresholds \(\tau_k>0\), and samples \(g_k=G(x_k,\xi_k)\), set
\[
\widetilde g_k=\operatorname{clip}_{\tau_k}(g_k):=g_k\min\left\{1,\frac{\tau_k}{\lVert g_k\rVert_2}\right\},
\]
where the multiplier is defined as \(1\) when \(g_k=0\). Update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_k\widetilde g_k\) and return the prescribed final, averaged, or randomized iterate after \(K\) calls. Then \(\lVert\widetilde g_k\rVert_2\le\tau_k\), while conditional unbiasedness need not survive clipping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clip each sampled gradient to a threshold before applying the SGD step. The resulting direction has bounded norm, but clipping generally introduces conditional bias.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau_k>0\) is fixed in advance or measurable before observing \(g_k\).

children.title: Magnitude-Threshold Regimes
children.top_down_role: Threshold choices across noise, curvature, and scale regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Magnitude-Threshold Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise representation of Euclidean clipping below, at, and above its threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(g\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(\tau>0\), Euclidean clipping admits the regime decomposition
\[
\operatorname{clip}_{\tau}(g)=
\begin{cases}
g, & \lVert g\rVert_2\le\tau,\\
\tau g/\lVert g\rVert_2, & \lVert g\rVert_2>\tau.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus the small-magnitude regime leaves the stochastic gradient unchanged, the boundary \(\lVert g\rVert_2=\tau\) joins the formulas continuously, and the large-magnitude regime retains only the direction and caps the norm at \(\tau\). Equivalently, \(\lVert\operatorname{clip}_{\tau}(g)\rVert_2=\min\{\lVert g\rVert_2,\tau\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Below the threshold, clipping changes nothing; above it, clipping preserves direction and replaces the norm by the threshold. The two formulas agree at the boundary.
review_flags: exact representation is standard but no clipping-specific locator was supplied

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The piecewise representation is mathematically correct and fits the leaf, but no source with an inspectable clipping-specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Robustness–Bias Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Bias and stability consequences of aggressive magnitude control.

knowledge_statements.title: Robustness–Bias Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional bias and second-moment control induced by norm clipping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g\) be an integrable stochastic gradient with \(\mathbb{E}[g\mid x]=\nabla f(x)\), and let \(\widetilde g=\operatorname{clip}_{\tau}(g)\) for \(\tau>0\). Then
\[
\lVert\widetilde g\rVert_2\le\tau,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[\lVert\widetilde g\rVert_2^2\mid x]\le\tau^2,
\]
but its conditional bias is
\[
\mathbb{E}[\widetilde g\mid x]-\nabla f(x)
=-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(1-\frac{\tau}{\lVert g\rVert_2}\right)g\,\mathbf{1}_{\{\lVert g\rVert_2>\tau\}}\middle|x\right].
\]
Hence clipping limits the influence and second moment of large samples while generally introducing bias supported on the clipped tail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clipping uniformly bounds sample influence and second moments, but its expected direction is generally biased. The bias comes exactly from samples whose norms exceed the threshold.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is conditionally integrable and \(\mathbb{E}[g\mid x]=\nabla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[\lVert\widetilde g\rVert_2^2\mid x]\le\tau^2\), with the displayed tail-supported conditional bias.
review_flags: no supplied locator directly supports the clipping bias identity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The norm, second-moment, and tail-supported bias identities are correct under the stated assumptions, but the nontrivial bias formula lacks a cited source and locator.

children.title: Variance-Reduction Boundary
children.top_down_role: Interfaces from plain SGD to estimator-memory methods treated fully in the finite-sum optimization chapter.

knowledge_statements.title: Variance-Reduction Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between memoryless unbiased SGD oracles and finite-sum estimators with persistent control-variate state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite sum \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), plain SGD samples \(i_k\) and uses \(g_k=\nabla f_{i_k}(x_k)\), so \(\mathbb{E}[g_k\mid x_k]=\nabla f(x_k)\) but its conditional variance need not vanish at a minimizer. A method crosses the variance-reduction boundary when its estimator additionally uses persistent state—such as a reference full gradient or stored component gradients—to form \(v_k\) satisfying a decreasing or vanishing variance bound. Such estimator-memory constructions are not instances of memoryless plain SGD, even when the primal update remains \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_kv_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Plain SGD uses a fresh component gradient whose variance may persist at an optimum. Reference gradients or stored component gradients cross into finite-sum variance-reduction methods.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Persistent estimator state that controls or eliminates component-sampling variance marks departure from memoryless plain SGD.
review_flags: boundary wording requires chapter-level source alignment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record fits a failure-boundary container and appropriately distinguishes memoryless component sampling from persistent estimator-memory constructions, but this chapter boundary and the variance behavior need a finite-sum variance-reduction source.
