knowledge_statements.statement_title: Single-pass projected SGD bound for multicategory surrogate risk
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multicategory specialization of the expected averaged-iterate guarantee for projected stochastic subgradient descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \theta_0=0 and, for t=1,\ldots,n, set
\[
\theta_t=\Pi_D\!\left(\theta_{t-1}-\gamma_t\,\varphi(x_t)S'\!\left(y_t,\theta_{t-1}^{\top}\varphi(x_t)\right)^{\top}\right),
\]
where \Pi_D is the orthogonal projection onto \{\theta:\|\theta\|_{\mathrm F}\le D\}. Under the i.i.d. sampling setup, convexity of S(y,\cdot), \|\varphi(x)\|_2\le R, and \|S'(y,u)\|_2\le G, choose \gamma_t=D/(RG\sqrt n). Then the averaged iterate \bar\theta_n satisfies
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[\mathcal R_S(g^{(\bar\theta_n)})-\inf_{\|\theta\|_{\mathrm F}\le D}\mathcal R_S(g^{(\theta)})\right]\le \frac{DRG}{\sqrt n}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For i.i.d. multicategory data, projected stochastic subgradient descent over the Frobenius ball, using bounded features and bounded surrogate subgradients, achieves expected surrogate estimation error at most DRG divided by square root of n for the averaged iterate with constant step size D divided by RG square root of n.
assumptions_latex: \Pi_D\ \text{is the orthogonal projection onto }\{\theta:\|\theta\|_{\mathrm F}\le D\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Convex Stochastic Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected objective error for projected stochastic subgradient descent with constant stepsize and averaged output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex with minimizer \(x^*\), and suppose \(g_k\) satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[g_k\mid x_k]\in\partial f(x_k)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\lVert g_k\rVert_2^2\mid x_k]\le G^2\). For \(x_{k+1}=\Pi_X(x_k-\eta g_k)\), \(\eta>0\), and \(\bar x_K=K^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}x_k\),
\[
\mathbb{E}[f(\bar x_K)-f(x^*)]\le \frac{\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert_2^2}{2\eta K}+\frac{\eta G^2}{2}.
\]
Choosing \(\eta=\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert_2/(G\sqrt K)\) gives error at most \(G\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert_2/\sqrt K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaged projected stochastic subgradient descent achieves expected objective error proportional to one over the square root of the number of oracle calls.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(f\) is convex with a minimizer \(x^*\in X\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected convergence rate of weighted-average SGD for convex Lipschitz objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected objective-error guarantee for a convex, not necessarily smooth, objective using step-size-weighted averaging.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be convex and \(B\)-Lipschitz, and suppose that it admits a minimizer \(\theta_*\) with \(\|\theta_* -\theta_0\|_2\le D\). Suppose also that, for every \(s\ge1\), \(\mathbb E[g_s(\theta_{s-1})\mid\theta_{s-1}]=F'(\theta_{s-1})\) and \(\|g_s(\theta_{s-1})\|_2^2\le B^2\) almost surely. If \(\gamma_s=(D/B)/\sqrt{s}\) and \[\bar\theta_t=\frac{\sum_{s=1}^t\gamma_s\theta_{s-1}}{\sum_{s=1}^t\gamma_s},\] then \[\mathbb E[F(\bar\theta_t)-F(\theta_*)]\le DB\frac{2+\log t}{2\sqrt t}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex B-Lipschitz objective, unbiased bounded stochastic gradients and step sizes proportional to one over the square root of the iteration yield the stated expected objective-error bound for the weighted-average iterate.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Convex SGD
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected objective error for averaged SGD under convex smoothness and bounded stochastic-gradient variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and \(L\)-smooth with minimizer \(x^*\). Suppose \(g_k\) is conditionally unbiased and \(\mathbb{E}[\lVert g_k-\nabla f(x_k)\rVert_2^2\mid x_k]\le\sigma^2\). For \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta g_k\), a constant \(0<\eta\le 1/L\), and \(\bar x_K=K^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}x_k\),
\[
\mathbb{E}[f(\bar x_K)-f(x^*)]\le \frac{\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert_2^2}{2\eta K}+\frac{\eta\sigma^2}{2}.
\]
Thus a suitable horizon-dependent \(\eta\) yields the standard deterministic-transient plus \(O(\sigma/\sqrt K)\) stochastic term.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For smooth convex objectives, averaged SGD has a deterministic transient inversely proportional to stepsize times iterations and a noise term proportional to stepsize.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and a minimizer \(x^*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected-risk bound for smooth convex SGD
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparator-dependent guarantee for averaged SGD under pointwise smooth convex nonnegative losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that, for every \(z\), \(\ell(\cdot,z)\) is convex, \(\beta\)-smooth, and nonnegative. Then the averaged output of SGD satisfies, for every \(\mathbf w^\star\), \[\mathbb E[L_{\mathcal D}(\overline{\mathbf w})]\le\frac{1}{1-\eta\beta}\left(L_{\mathcal D}(\mathbf w^\star)+\frac{\|\mathbf w^\star\|^2}{2\eta T}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every sample loss is convex, beta-smooth, and nonnegative, averaged SGD obeys the stated expected population-risk bound relative to every comparator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\mathbf w^\star,\quad \mathbb E[L_{\mathcal D}(\overline{\mathbf w})]\le\frac{1}{1-\eta\beta}\left(L_{\mathcal D}(\mathbf w^\star)+\frac{\|\mathbf w^\star\|^2}{2\eta T}\right)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected Error Bound for Averaged SGD with Bounded Stochastic Subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General convex, potentially nonsmooth SGD rate with constant step size and averaged iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B,\rho>0\), let \(f\) be convex, and choose \(\mathbf w^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|\mathbf w\|\le B}f(\mathbf w)\). Run averaged SGD from \(\mathbf w^{(1)}=\mathbf0\) for \(T\in\mathbb N_{>0}\) iterations, with \(\mathbb E[\mathbf v_t\mid\mathbf w^{(t)}]\in\partial f(\mathbf w^{(t)})\), \(\|\mathbf v_t\|\le\rho\) almost surely for every \(t\), and \(\eta=B/(\rho\sqrt T)\). Then \(\mathbb E[f(\overline{\mathbf w})]-f(\mathbf w^\star)\le B\rho/\sqrt T\). Consequently, for every \(\epsilon>0\), \(T\ge B^2\rho^2/\epsilon^2\) suffices to make the expected suboptimality at most \(\epsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex objective, averaged SGD initialized at zero and using unbiased stochastic subgradients bounded almost surely by rho achieves expected error at most B rho divided by the square root of T when the constant step size is B divided by rho times the square root of T. Thus B squared rho squared divided by epsilon squared iterations suffice for expected error at most epsilon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[f(\overline{\mathbf w})]-f(\mathbf w^\star)\le\frac{B\rho}{\sqrt T},\qquad T\ge\frac{B^2\rho^2}{\epsilon^2}\Longrightarrow \mathbb E[f(\overline{\mathbf w})]-f(\mathbf w^\star)\le\epsilon.

children.title: Strongly Convex SGD

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex SGD
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mean-square SGD recursion and noise floor under strong convexity and smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(\mu\)-strongly convex and \(L\)-smooth with minimizer \(x^*\). Suppose \(g_k\) is conditionally unbiased and \(\mathbb{E}[\lVert g_k-\nabla f(x_k)\rVert_2^2\mid x_k]\le\sigma^2\). For constant-step SGD \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta g_k\) with \(0<\eta\le1/L\),
\[
\mathbb{E}\lVert x_K-x^*\rVert_2^2
\le (1-\mu\eta)^K\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert_2^2+\frac{\eta\sigma^2}{\mu}.
\]
Consequently, constant stepsizes converge geometrically to a noise neighborhood; decreasing stepsizes or suitable averaging are required for vanishing stochastic error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity gives geometric mean-square contraction under a constant stepsize, but persistent gradient noise leaves a neighborhood whose size is proportional to the stepsize.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted-average rate for strongly convex SGD
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An order-1/t objective-gap guarantee for projected SGD with decreasing step sizes and linearly weighted averaging.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be \(\alpha\)-strongly convex, let \(x^*\) be a minimizer of \(f\), and suppose the stochastic oracle satisfies \(\mathbb E\|\widetilde g(x)\|_*^2\leq B^2\). For every \(t\geq1\), SGD with
\[
\eta_s=\frac{2}{\alpha(s+1)}
\]
satisfies
\[
f\!\left(\sum_{s=1}^t\frac{2s}{t(t+1)}x_s\right)-f(x^*)\leq\frac{2B^2}{\alpha(t+1)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an alpha-strongly convex objective and a stochastic oracle with bounded expected squared dual norm, SGD using step size 2 divided by alpha times s+1 attains objective gap at most 2B squared divided by alpha times t+1 at the linearly weighted average of its iterates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Averaged SGD for Soft-SVM
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded algorithm stated for solving the referenced Soft-SVM objective; no convergence guarantee is included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\lambda>0\), \(T\in\mathbb N\), and training examples \((x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^m\). Initialize \(\theta^{(1)}=0\). For \(t=1,\ldots,T\), set \(w^{(t)}=(\lambda t)^{-1}\theta^{(t)}\), choose \(i\) uniformly from \([m]\), and set \(\theta^{(t+1)}=\theta^{(t)}+y_i x_i\) when \(y_i\langle w^{(t)},x_i\rangle<1\); otherwise set \(\theta^{(t+1)}=\theta^{(t)}\). Return \(\bar w=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T w^{(t)}\).

At iteration t, divide it by lambda times t to obtain the current weight vector, sample a training example uniformly, and add its signed feature vector to the auxiliary vector if its margin is below one. Otherwise leave the auxiliary vector unchanged. Return the average of the weight iterates.

children.title: Polyak–Łojasiewicz Regimes
children.top_down_role: Stochastic convergence regimes governed by gradient domination.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyak–Łojasiewicz Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global or region-restricted Polyak–Łojasiewicz gradient-dominance condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A differentiable function \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) with attained minimum value \(f^*\) satisfies the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition with parameter \(\mu>0\) on a set \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) if
\[
\frac12\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2^2\ge\mu\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)
\quad\text{for every }x\in D.
\]
The condition is global when \(D=\mathbb{R}^d\) and local when \(D\) is a proper validity region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The PL condition lower-bounds squared gradient norm by objective suboptimality on a specified region. It is global when that region is the whole space and local otherwise.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable and attains its minimum value \(f^*\).

notation.meaning: region on which the PL inequality holds

review_flags: no supplied locator specifically supports the PL condition

children.title: Error-Bound Regimes
children.top_down_role: Stochastic convergence regimes governed by residual-to-solution growth control.

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient error bound controlling distance to the minimizer set on a specified region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable with nonempty minimizer set \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}f\), and let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\). A gradient error bound with constant \(\kappa>0\) holds on \(D\) when
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\kappa\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2
\quad\text{for every }x\in D.
\]
The regime is global if \(D=\mathbb{R}^d\), and local if \(D\) is a neighborhood or sublevel set containing \(X^*\). For stochastic methods the inequality constrains the true gradient; transferring it to sampled gradients requires separate noise assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient error bound says distance to the solution set is controlled by the true gradient norm. It may hold globally or only near the solution set.
review_flags: no supplied locator identifies the intended gradient error-bound version

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record clearly selects the gradient error-bound notion and states it correctly, but several inequivalent error bounds exist; a source is needed to establish that this is the intended notion for the leaf.

children.title: Geometry Implication Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Implication and separation relationships among domination, growth, and error-bound conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometry Implication Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smooth global PL function need not be convex, establishing a boundary on geometry implications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(g(x)=x+\tfrac12\sin x\) and \(f(x)=g(x)^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). Since \(g'(x)=1+\tfrac12\cos x\ge\tfrac12\), \(g\) is strictly increasing, has the unique zero \(0\), and \(f^*=0\). Moreover,
\[
\frac12|f'(x)|^2=2g(x)^2g'(x)^2\ge\frac12 f(x),
\]
so \(f\) satisfies the global PL inequality with \(\mu=\tfrac12\). However,
\[
f''(x)=2g'(x)^2-g(x)\sin x
\]
is negative at \(x=\tfrac\pi2+2\pi m\) for all sufficiently large integers \(m\). Thus global PL geometry alone implies neither convexity nor strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A squared monotone nonlinear residual satisfies a global PL inequality yet is nonconvex. Therefore PL geometry alone does not imply convexity or strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) satisfies global PL with \(\mu=1/2\) but is not convex.
review_flags: self-contained counterexample lacks an external source locator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is internally correct and establishes that global PL does not imply convexity or strong convexity, but the nontrivial example has no external source locator.

children.title: Local Geometry Regimes
children.top_down_role: Guarantees available only within neighborhoods exhibiting favorable growth geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Geometry Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PL or gradient error-bound geometry restricted to a neighborhood or invariant sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable with attained minimum value \(f^*\), nonempty minimizer set \(X^*\), and region \(D\supseteq X^*\). A local PL regime holds on \(D\) if there exists \(\mu>0\) such that
\[
\frac12\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2^2\ge\mu\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)
\quad\text{for every }x\in D.
\]
A local gradient error-bound regime holds on \(D\) if there exists \(\kappa>0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\kappa\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2
\quad\text{for every }x\in D.
\]
A convergence guarantee using either local condition applies only while the iterates remain in \(D\); initialization in \(D\) alone does not ensure invariance under stochastic noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local PL and local gradient error-bound conditions are distinct inequalities that may hold on a restricted region. A stochastic convergence argument using either condition must ensure that its iterates remain in that region.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable, attains \(f^*\), and has nonempty minimizer set \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any guarantee based on a displayed local inequality requires \(x_k\in D\) throughout the analyzed horizon.
review_flags: no supplied locator supports the local geometry conditions or stochastic-invariance boundary

children.title: Composite Nonconvex Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Proximal and generalized-gradient stationarity regimes for composite objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Nonconvex Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal-gradient stationarity for a smooth nonconvex term plus a proper closed convex term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+h\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), where \(f\) is differentiable and \(h:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex. For \(\eta>0\), define the proximal-gradient mapping by \[G_\eta(x)=\eta^{-1}\!\left(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\eta h}(x-\eta\nabla f(x))\right).\] A point \(x\in\operatorname{dom}h\) is stationary exactly when \(G_\eta(x)=0\), equivalently \(0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial h(x)\). A random output \(X\) is expected \(\varepsilon\)-stationary when \(\mathbb{E}\|G_\eta(X)\|^2\leq\varepsilon^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composite stationarity is measured by the proximal-gradient mapping; its zeros satisfy the generalized first-order condition, and its expected squared norm defines stochastic approximate stationarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_\eta(x)=0\iff 0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial h(x)\), with approximate stationarity measured by \(\mathbb{E}\|G_\eta(X)\|^2\).

notation.meaning: Proximal mapping of the scaled function eta h.

children.title: Expected-Value Guarantees

knowledge_statements.title: Expected-Value Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expectation-mode guarantees for nonnegative stochastic error criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_T\) be the output of a stochastic optimization method after budget \(T\), and let \(M:\mathcal{X}\to[0,+\infty]\) be a measurable error criterion, such as objective gap, squared distance to a solution set, or squared stationarity residual. An expected-value guarantee at budget \(T\) is an inequality \[\mathbb{E}[M(X_T)]\leq B(T),\] where the expectation covers all algorithmic and oracle randomness. The method attains expected accuracy \(\varepsilon\) when \(B(T)\leq\varepsilon\); for squared residual conventions, the target may instead be written \(B(T)\leq\varepsilon^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expected-value guarantee bounds the mean of a specified measurable optimization error after a stated budget, with the accuracy convention declared explicitly.
assumptions_latex: \(X_T\) is a random element of a measurable space \(\mathcal{X}\).
\(M\) is measurable, nonnegative, and integrable at \(X_T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[M(X_T)]\leq B(T)\), with expected accuracy achieved whenever the declared threshold holds.

notation.meaning: Declared objective, distance, or stationarity error criterion.
Deterministic upper bound as a function of budget.

knowledge_statements.title: High-Probability Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Confidence-parameterized tail guarantees for a declared stochastic optimization error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_T\) be the output after budget \(T\), and let \(M:\mathcal{X}\to[0,+\infty]\) be measurable. A high-probability guarantee is a family of bounds indexed by \(\delta\in(0,1)\) such that \[\mathbb{P}\!\left(M(X_T)\leq B(T,\delta)\right)\geq 1-\delta.\] Equivalently, \(\mathbb{P}(M(X_T)>B(T,\delta))\leq\delta\). A claimed \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-guarantee must specify a budget \(T(\varepsilon,\delta)\) satisfying \(B(T(\varepsilon,\delta),\delta)\leq\varepsilon\), together with the randomness and tail assumptions covered by the probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A high-probability guarantee bounds a declared error with failure probability at most delta and states how the required budget depends on accuracy and confidence.

children.title: Almost-Sure Convergence

knowledge_statements.title: Almost-Sure Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robbins–Siegmund-type pathwise convergence criterion used in stochastic approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal{F}_k)\) be a filtration and let \(V_k,U_k,A_k,B_k\) be nonnegative, \(\mathcal{F}_k\)-measurable random variables satisfying \[\mathbb{E}[V_{k+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_k]\leq(1+A_k)V_k-U_k+B_k\quad\text{almost surely}.\] If \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}A_k<\infty\) and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}B_k<\infty\) almost surely, then \(V_k\) converges almost surely to a finite random variable and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}U_k<\infty\) almost surely. When \(U_k\) dominates a stationarity or distance residual, this yields its corresponding pathwise summability conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative stochastic Lyapunov sequence converges almost surely when its conditional drift has summable multiplicative and additive errors, and its descent terms are summable.
assumptions_latex: The displayed conditional drift inequality holds almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_k\) converges to a finite limit almost surely and \(\sum_k U_k<\infty\) almost surely.

children.title: Convergence in Probability

knowledge_statements.title: Convergence in Probability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence in probability for random optimization iterates or residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_n\) and \(X\) be random elements defined on a common probability space and taking values in a metric space \((S,d)\). The sequence \((X_n)\) converges in probability to \(X\), written \(X_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}X\), if for every \(\varepsilon>0\), \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}\!\left(d(X_n,X)>\varepsilon\right)=0.\] For a nonnegative scalar optimization residual \(R_n\), convergence in probability to zero means \(\mathbb{P}(R_n>\varepsilon)\to0\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iterates converge in probability when the chance of remaining farther than any fixed tolerance from the limit tends to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(X_n\) and \(X\) are random elements on one probability space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform continuity of the conditional allocation drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity assumption for the conditional mean service in proportional-fair stochastic allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\xi_n=\{R_l:l\le n\}\) and, for every \(i,n,\xi_n\), define
\[

\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Modes of convergence for real-valued random variables
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General definitions of convergence in probability, almost surely, in L^p, and in distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (X_n) and X be real-valued random variables on (\Omega,\mathcal A,\mathbb P). Convergence in probability means \mathbb P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\to0 for every \varepsilon>0. Almost-sure convergence means \mathbb P(\{\omega:X_n(\omega)\to X(\omega)\})=1. For 1\le p<\infty, convergence in L^p means X_n,X\in L^p and \int_\Omega|X_n-X|^p\,d\mathbb P\to0. Convergence in distribution means F_{X_n}(t)\to F_X(t) at every continuity point t of F_X, equivalently outside a countable exceptional set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergence in probability requires every fixed deviation probability to vanish; almost-sure convergence requires pointwise convergence with probability one; Lp convergence requires the pth-power error integral to vanish; and convergence in distribution requires convergence of distribution functions at continuity points of the limiting distribution.
assumptions_latex: (X_n)\text{ and }X\text{ are real-valued random variables on }(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mathbb P).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The four convergence modes are defined by the stated probability, almost-sure, }L^p\text{, and distribution-function conditions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero probability of convergence to a linearly unstable point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robbins–Monro nonconvergence under bounded, uniformly directionally exciting martingale-difference noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\widetilde\theta\) be a linearly unstable stationary point of the limiting ODE, and suppose that the mixed second-order partial derivatives of \(\bar g\) are continuous in a neighborhood of \(\widetilde\theta\). If \(\{\delta M_n\}\) is bounded and there exists \(K>0\) such that, for every \(n\) and every unit vector \(x\),
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[\max\{0,x^\top\delta M_n\}\right]\geq K,
\]
then the Robbins--Monro iterates have zero probability of converging to \(\widetilde\theta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the drift is twice differentiable with continuous mixed derivatives near a linearly unstable equilibrium, and the bounded noise supplies a uniformly positive amount of excitation in every direction at every iteration, then the stochastic-approximation iterates converge to that equilibrium with probability zero.
assumptions_latex: \text{The mixed second-order partial derivatives of }\bar g\text{ are continuous near }\widetilde\theta.
\exists K>0\ \forall n\ \forall x\in\mathbb R^r:\ \|x\|=1\implies \mathbb E[\max\{0,x^\top\delta M_n\}]\geq K.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence of a Noisy Gradient Recursion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General convergence and stationarity result for stochastic approximation with martingale-difference perturbations.

If a_k\geq0, \sum_k a_k=\infty, and \sum_k a_k^2\|R_{k+1}\|^2<\infty almost surely, then F(X_k) converges almost surely. If additionally \sum_k a_kR_{k+1} converges almost surely, then f(X_k)\to0 almost surely.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Large-Deviation Rate Integrand and Action Functional
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Legendre-transform rate density and path-space action for the stochastic-approximation interpolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \[H_1(\alpha,\psi,s)=h_0(s)H_0(h_1(s)\alpha,\psi),\qquad L(\beta,\psi,s)=\sup_{\alpha}\left\{\alpha'\bigl(\beta-\bar g(\bar\theta+\psi)\bigr)-H_1(\alpha,\psi,s)\right\}.\] For \(T>0\), define \[S(T,\phi)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int_0^T L(\dot\phi(s),\phi(s),s)\,ds,&\phi\text{ absolutely continuous},\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}\] Under (A10.3) and (A10.4), for every \(\delta_1>0\) there is \(\delta_2>0\) such that, for \(t\le T\), \[\left\lVert\dot\phi-\bar g(\bar\theta+\phi)\right\rVert\ge\delta_1\implies L(\dot\phi,\phi,t)\ge\delta_2,\] while \(L(\bar g(\bar\theta+\phi),\phi,t)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local rate function is the convex conjugate of the scaled cumulant function after centering by the mean drift. The action is its time integral along absolutely continuous paths and is infinity for all other paths. Under the two preceding scaling and cumulant assumptions, the rate is uniformly positive away from the mean drift and zero on the mean drift.
assumptions_latex: \text{Assumptions (A10.3) and (A10.4) hold for the positivity properties}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S(T,\phi)=\int_0^T L(\dot\phi(s),\phi(s),s)\,ds\text{ for absolutely continuous }\phi\text{ and }+\infty\text{ otherwise, with }L\text{ zero on and positive away from the mean drift.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Path-Space Large-Deviation Bounds for Constant-Step Stochastic Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the algorithm, assumptions, path sets, and action functional defined in the surrounding large-deviation framework.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume algorithm (10.1), let \(\epsilon_n=\epsilon\), and suppose (A10.1) and (A10.4) hold. Conditional on \(\theta^\epsilon(\epsilon q_\epsilon)=\theta_{q_\epsilon}^\epsilon=x\), for every admissible path set \(B_x\),
\[
-\inf_{\phi\in B_x^\circ}S(T,\phi)\le \liminf_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\epsilon\log P_x^\epsilon\!\left\{\theta^\epsilon(\epsilon q_\epsilon+\cdot)\in B_x\right\}
\le \limsup_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\epsilon\log P_x^\epsilon\!\left\{\theta^\epsilon(\epsilon q_\epsilon+\cdot)\in B_x\right\}
\le-\inf_{\phi\in\overline B_x}S(T,\phi).
\]
Moreover, there exists \(c>0\) such that, for sufficiently small \(\epsilon>0\) and sufficiently large \(n\),
\[
P_x^\epsilon\!\left\{\theta^\epsilon(\epsilon q_\epsilon+\cdot)\in B_{1,x}\right\}\le e^{-c/\epsilon}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated constant-step stochastic-approximation algorithm and assumptions, the scaled logarithmic probability of a path event is bounded below by the action infimum over the event interior and above by the action infimum over its closure. The specified escape event also has probability at most exponentially small in the inverse step size.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recurrence-driven convergence and exponential escape bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence theorem for the referenced stochastic-approximation state-perturbation algorithm under assumptions A9.1–A9.7.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume algorithms \((9.1)\) and \((5.1.1)\), assumptions \((A9.1)\)–\((A9.7)\), and \(\beta_n\to0\) uniformly in \(\omega\). If there exists \(\zeta>0\) such that, for every \(\rho>0\), \(\theta_n\in N_\rho(\bar\theta)\) infinitely often with probability \(\zeta\), then \(\theta_n\to\bar\theta\) with probability \(\zeta\). Moreover, if \(\operatorname{dist}(\bar\theta,\partial H)\ge\mu_1>0\), then there exists \(c>0\) such that, for all sufficiently large \(n\) and sufficiently small \(\mu\in(0,\mu_1)\), \[\mathbb P\!\left\{\theta_i\notin N_\mu(\bar\theta)\text{ for some }i\ge n\mid\theta_n\in N_{\nu(\mu/4)}(\bar\theta)\right\}\le e^{-c/\epsilon_n}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the referenced algorithmic assumptions and uniform decay of beta_n, visiting every neighborhood of the target infinitely often with probability zeta implies convergence to that target with probability zeta. If the target is separated from the boundary of H, then, when the process starts sufficiently close to it, the conditional probability of ever leaving a prescribed neighborhood after a sufficiently late iteration is at most exponential in minus one over epsilon_n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limiting Log-Moment-Generating Functional
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and regularity of the local cumulant functional for blockwise correlated noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L,G\subset\mathbb R^r\) be neighborhoods of \(0\), with \(\bar\theta+\bar G\subset H\), and let \(L\) be arbitrarily small. There exists a real function \(H_0(\alpha,\psi)\), continuous on \(L\times\bar G\), whose derivative with respect to \(\alpha\) is continuous on \(L\) for each fixed \(\psi\in\bar G\), such that for every \(T,\Delta>0\) with \(T/\Delta\in\mathbb N\), and every pair of functions \((\alpha(\cdot),\psi(\cdot))\) valued in \(L\times\bar G\) and constant on each \([i\Delta,(i+1)\Delta)\), \[\int_0^T H_0(\alpha(s),\psi(s))\,ds=\lim_{m,n\to\infty}\frac{\Delta}{m}\log E\exp\!\left(\sum_{i=0}^{T/\Delta-1}\alpha(i\Delta)'\sum_{j=im}^{im+m-1}\left[g_{n+j}(\bar\theta+\psi(i\Delta),\xi_{n+j})-\bar g(\bar\theta+\psi(i\Delta))\right]\right),\] where the joint limit exists along every manner in which \(m,n\to\infty\). A sufficient condition for this limit is that, for each fixed \(\alpha,\psi\), the conditional limits \[\lim_{m,n\to\infty}\frac1m\log E_n\exp\!\left(\alpha'\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}[g_{n+j}(\bar\theta+\psi,\xi_{n+j})-\bar g(\bar\theta+\psi)]\right)\] exist uniformly in \(\omega\) with probability one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On suitable neighborhoods, a continuous cumulant function H0 with continuous alpha-derivative represents the joint large-block limit of the scaled log moment-generating function for every piecewise-constant test pair. The joint limit must be independent of how both indices diverge; uniform almost-sure existence of the corresponding conditional block limits is sufficient.

(\alpha(\cdot),\psi(\cdot))\in L\times\bar G\text{ and is constant on each }[i\Delta,(i+1)\Delta)

There exists a function \(\bar H_2(\alpha)\), continuous and differentiable on a neighborhood \(L\) of the origin, such that for admissible \(\alpha(\cdot),T,\Delta\), either
\[
\int_0^T\bar H_2(\alpha(s))\,ds\ge\limsup_{m,n\to\infty}\frac{\Delta}{m}\log E\exp\!\left(\sum_{i=0}^{T/\Delta-1}\alpha'(i\Delta)\sum_{j=im}^{im+m-1}\delta M_{n+j}\right),
\]
or, almost surely,
\[
\bar H_2(\alpha)\ge\limsup_{m,n\to\infty}\frac1m\log E_n\exp\!\left(\alpha'\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\delta M_{n+j}\right),
\]
where the latter limsup is uniform in \(\omega\) outside a null set. With \(\bar H_1\) from (A10.5), set
\[
\bar H(\alpha,\psi)=\tfrac12\bar H_1(2\alpha,\psi)+\tfrac12\bar H_2(2\alpha),
\]
and define \(\bar L\) and \(\bar S\) from this \(\bar H\) as in the preceding large-deviation construction. Under these definitions, inequalities (10.9) and (10.11) remain valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The martingale-increment component admits a continuous differentiable upper bound on its asymptotic log moment-generating function. Averaging its scaled bound with the observation-noise bound yields a combined cumulant majorant and hence a combined rate function and action, for which the preceding large-deviation inequalities remain valid.
assumptions_latex: \bar H_2\text{ is continuous and differentiable on a neighborhood }L\text{ of }0.
\text{Either the unconditional integrated bound or the almost-sure conditional uniform bound holds.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar H(\alpha,\psi)=\frac12\bar H_1(2\alpha,\psi)+\frac12\bar H_2(2\alpha),\quad \bar L,\bar S\text{ are induced as before, and (10.9), (10.11) remain valid.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Modes of convergence for random variables
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines almost-sure, mean-square, and in-probability convergence, gives the source's componentwise extension to random vectors, and records that almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sequence \(\{X_i\}\) converges almost surely to \(X\) if \(\Pr(\lim_{i\to\infty}X_i=X)=1\); it converges in mean square if \(\lim_{i\to\infty}\mathbb E[(X_i-X)^2]=0\); and it converges in probability if, for every \(\delta>0\), \(\lim_{i\to\infty}\Pr(|X_i-X|\ge\delta)=0\). For random vectors, the source defines each mode by componentwise convergence. Moreover, almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Almost-sure convergence means that the sequence converges to the target with probability one. Mean-square convergence means that the expected squared error tends to zero. Convergence in probability means that the probability of an error exceeding any fixed positive tolerance tends to zero. The source applies these definitions componentwise to random vectors, and almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability.
assumptions_latex: For mean-square convergence, \(\mathbb E[(X_i-X)^2]\) is defined for each relevant \(i\).
For convergence in probability, the limit condition holds for every \(\delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X_i\to X\ \text{almost surely}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad X_i\to X\ \text{in probability}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Almost-Supermartingale Convergence Principle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General stochastic convergence lemma for adapted descent recursions with summable errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (\mathcal F_k) be a filtration. Let (Y_k) be adapted and uniformly bounded below, and let (A_k) and (B_k) be adapted nonnegative random variables. If \mathbb E[Y_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]\leq Y_k-A_k+B_k and \sum_k B_k<\infty almost surely, then (Y_k) converges almost surely and \sum_k A_k<\infty almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an adapted process uniformly bounded below, a conditional expected-descent inequality with nonnegative descent terms and almost-surely summable errors implies almost-sure convergence of the process and summability of the descent terms.
assumptions_latex: Y_k\text{ is }\mathcal F_k\text{-adapted and uniformly bounded below}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recurrence and invariant-set limits under eventual Lyapunov drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic-approximation limit-set theorem when strict Lyapunov drift is guaranteed only outside a nonzero level set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the conditions of Theorem 4.2, except that \(c(\delta)>0\) and \(c_0(\delta)>0\) are required only for \(\delta\geq\lambda_0\). Then, for every \(\lambda>\lambda_0\), \(Q_\lambda\) is a recurrence set for \((\theta_n)\). If the asymptotic rate of change in (4.9) is zero almost surely for \(\Delta=2\lambda_0\), then almost surely every limit trajectory of \((\theta^n)\) lies in an invariant set of (4.11) contained in \(Q_{\lambda_0}\). If each \(G(\theta)=\{\bar g(\theta)\}\), \(\bar g\) is a gradient, and (A2.6) holds, then outside a null set the iterates converge to a single stationary set \(S_i\). Otherwise, under the additional hypotheses of Theorem 2.5 or its corollary, the algorithm's limit points are almost surely contained in the chain-recurrent set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the Lyapunov drift conditions of the preceding theorem hold only above level lambda-zero, every higher Lyapunov sublevel set is recurrent. With the stated zero asymptotic-change condition, limit trajectories lie in an invariant set inside the lambda-zero sublevel set. A singleton gradient mean field yields convergence to one stationary set under the cited gradient condition; under the alternative cited hypotheses, all limit points are chain recurrent.
assumptions_latex: \text{The conditions of Theorem 4.2 hold except for the modified positivity range below.}
\text{For the limit-trajectory conclusion, the asymptotic rate of change of (4.9) is zero a.s. for }\Delta=2\lambda_0.
\text{For stationary-set convergence: }G(\theta)=\{\bar g(\theta)\},\ \bar g\text{ is a gradient, and (A2.6) holds}.
\text{For the alternative conclusion, the additional conditions of Theorem 2.5 or its corollary hold.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\lambda>\lambda_0,\ Q_\lambda\text{ is recurrent};\quad \operatorname{LimTraj}(\theta^n)\subseteq\mathcal I((4.11))\cap Q_{\lambda_0}\ \text{a.s.};\quad \text{in the stated special cases, convergence is to one stationary set or the limit points are chain recurrent a.s.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Three-Component Cumulant Majorant for Locally Linearized Stochastic Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A large-deviation condition decomposing martingale noise, equilibrium observation noise, and local derivative fluctuations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exist functions \(\bar H_3(\alpha)\) and \(\bar H_4(\alpha,\psi)\) with, respectively, the continuity and differentiability properties required of \(\bar H_2\) in (A10.6) and \(\bar H_0\) in (A10.4). The bounds (10.19) or (10.20) hold for \(\bar H_3\) after replacing \(\delta M_n\) by \(g_n(\bar\theta,\xi_n)\), and the bounds (10.14) or (10.15) hold for \(\bar H_4\) after replacing the centered observation term by
\[
[g'_{n,\theta}(\bar\theta,\xi_{n+j})-A]\psi.
\]
Define
\[
\bar H(\alpha,\psi)=\frac13\left[\bar H_2(3\alpha)+\bar H_3(3\alpha)+\bar H_4(3\alpha,\psi)\right],
\]
\[
\bar L(\beta,\psi)=\sup_\alpha\left[\alpha'(\beta-A\psi+O(|\psi|^2))-\bar H(\alpha,\psi)\right],
\]
and let \(\bar S\) be the action induced by this \(\bar L\). In a sufficiently small neighborhood of the origin, the linear term \(A\psi\) strictly dominates \(O(|\psi|^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate smooth cumulant majorants are assumed for equilibrium observations and local derivative fluctuations, in addition to the martingale-noise majorant. Their equally weighted scaled sum defines a combined cumulant bound; its convex conjugate uses the local drift expansion, whose linear term dominates the quadratic-order remainder near the equilibrium.

\bar H_4\text{ has the regularity of }\bar H_0\text{ in (A10.4).}
\text{The corresponding unconditional or almost-sure conditional uniform log-MGF bounds hold.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Log-MGF Majorant and Induced Action Functional
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient large-deviation condition for the centered observation-noise component in the surrounding stochastic-approximation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists \(\bar H_1(\alpha,\psi)\), with the continuity and differentiability properties required of \(H_0\) in (A10.4), such that for every \(\Delta>0\), \(T>0\) with \(T/\Delta\in\mathbb N\), and admissible \(\alpha(\cdot),\psi(\cdot)\), either
\[
\int_0^T\bar H_1(\alpha(s),\psi(s))\,ds\ge\limsup_{m,n\to\infty}\frac{\Delta}{m}\log E\exp\!\left(\sum_{i=0}^{T/\Delta-1}\alpha'(i\Delta)\sum_{j=im}^{im+m-1}\bigl[g_{n+j}(\bar\theta+\psi(i\Delta),\xi_{n+j})-\bar g(\bar\theta+\psi(i\Delta))\bigr]\right),
\]
or, almost surely for each \(\alpha,\psi\),
\[
\bar H_1(\alpha,\psi)\ge\limsup_{m,n\to\infty}\frac1m\log E_n\exp\!\left(\alpha'\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}[g_{n+j}(\bar\theta+\psi,\xi_{n+j})-\bar g(\bar\theta+\psi)]\right),
\]
with the latter limsup uniform in \(\omega\) outside a null set. Setting \(\bar H=\bar H_1\), define
\[
\bar L(\beta,\psi)=\sup_\alpha\{\alpha'(\beta-\bar g(\bar\theta+\psi))-\bar H(\alpha,\psi)\},
\]
and define \(\bar S(T,\phi)\) from \(\bar L\) in the same manner as \(S(T,\phi)\) is defined from \(L\).

Its convex conjugate defines the local rate function, from which the path action is constructed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constrained stochastic-approximation convergence through ODE limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded theorem under the referenced step-size, noise, and constraint-set conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the step-size condition (5.1.1), conditions (A5.2.1)--(A5.2.3), one of the constraint-set conditions (A4.3.1)--(A4.3.3), and \(E|\beta_n|\to0\). Every subsequence of \(\{(\theta^n(\cdot),Z^n(\cdot))\}\) has a further subsequence that is almost surely equicontinuous in the extended sense on a sequence of intervals tending to infinity, and its limits satisfy ODE (2.2). If (2.2) has a unique limit point \(\bar\theta\) that is Lyapunov-asymptotically stable, then, for every \(\mu,T>0\), \(P\{\sup_{t\le T}|\theta^n(t)-\bar\theta|>\mu\}\to0\). More generally, there exist \(\mu_n\to0\) and \(T_n\to\infty\) such that \(P\{\sup_{t\le T_n}\operatorname{dist}(\theta^n(t),L_H)\ge\mu_n\}\to0\); moreover, for every \(\delta>0\), the fraction of time spent in the \(\delta\)-neighborhood of \(L_H\) converges to one in probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the referenced step-size, noise, and constraint assumptions, every interpolated-process subsequence has a further almost surely extended-equicontinuous subsequence whose limits solve the limiting ODE. A unique Lyapunov-asymptotically-stable ODE limit point gives uniform convergence in probability on every fixed horizon. More generally, the process approaches the ODE limit set over growing horizons, and the fraction of time spent near that set tends to one in probability.

knowledge_statements.title: Convergence in Distribution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak convergence of random optimization outputs on a metric state space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_n\) and \(X\) be random elements taking values in a metric space \(S\), with laws \(\mu_n\) and \(\mu\). The sequence \((X_n)\) converges in distribution to \(X\), written \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\), if \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_n)]=\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X)]\] for every bounded continuous function \(\varphi:S\to\mathbb{R}\). Equivalently, the probability measures \(\mu_n\) converge weakly to \(\mu\). The variables need not be realized on a common probability space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outputs converge in distribution when expectations of every bounded continuous test function converge to those under the limiting law.
assumptions_latex: \(X_n\) and \(X\) take values in a metric space \(S\).
All test functions \(\varphi:S\to\mathbb{R}\) are bounded and continuous.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Central limit theorem for stationary values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic normality of empirical model values evaluated at convergent composite strong d-stationary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose Assumptions 10.5.1 and 10.5.2 hold. Let \(\{x^{N;\varepsilon}\}\) be composite \(\varepsilon\)-strong d-stationary points of the sampled problems associated with \(\{\omega^s\}_{s=1}^{\infty}\subset\widehat\Omega\). Assume \(x^{N;\varepsilon}\to x^\infty\in\mathcal D\) almost surely, and that for some \(\varepsilon'\in(0,\varepsilon/2]\), \(x^\infty\) is the unique minimizer of \(R_{x^\infty;\varepsilon'}(\bullet,x^\infty)\) on \(X\). If \(\mathcal L(x^\infty;\bullet)\) is square integrable, then \[\sqrt N\bigl(\mathcal M_N(x^{N;\varepsilon})-\mathcal M(x^\infty)\bigr)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N\!\left(0,\operatorname{Var}[\mathcal L(x^\infty;\widetilde\omega)]\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated structural assumptions, let the sampled points be composite epsilon-strong d-stationary points and converge almost surely to x-infinity in the admissible set. If x-infinity uniquely minimizes the indicated localized population residual model for some epsilon-prime at most epsilon/2, and its loss is square integrable, then the square-root-N normalized empirical stationary-value error converges in distribution to a centered normal law with the stated variance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak limit of sample-average optimal values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Central-limit theorem for the optimal value of a sample-average stochastic program over a compact feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) be compact. Assume that there exists \(\widetilde x\in X\) with \(\mathbb E[\theta(\widetilde x,\widetilde\omega)]<\infty\), and that there exists a measurable \(C:\Omega\to\mathbb R_+\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[C(\widetilde\omega)^2]<\infty\) and \[|\theta(x^1,\omega)-\theta(x^2,\omega)|\le C(\omega)\|x^1-x^2\|\quad\forall x^1,x^2\in X\] for almost every \(\omega\). If \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\mathbb E[\theta(x,\widetilde\omega)]\), then \[\sqrt N\bigl(\theta_{\min}^N-\theta_{\min}^*\bigr)\xrightarrow{d}\inf_{x\in S}\mathbb G_x,\] where each \(\mathbb G_x\) is normally distributed as \(\mathcal N(0,\operatorname{Var}[\theta(x,\widetilde\omega)])\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a compact feasible set, suppose the integrand is integrable at one feasible point and is almost surely Lipschitz on the feasible set with a square-integrable random Lipschitz modulus. Then the square-root-N normalized error in the sample-average optimal value converges in distribution to the infimum, over the population minimizer set, of the associated centered Gaussian process; each marginal has variance equal to the variance of the integrand at that minimizer.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Total variation convergence and absolute continuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational measure-convergence definitions. Radon–Nikodym representation is stated conditionally because the extract omits a general hypothesis ensuring existence of the derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mu_n,\mu\in\mathcal P(S)\), write \(\mu_n\to\mu\) in total variation when \(\sup_{f\in C_b(S),\,\lVert f\rVert_\infty\leq1}\left|\int f\,d\mu_n-\int f\,d\mu\right|\to0\). In the source's regular state-space setting, this implies convergence of the integrals for every bounded measurable \(f:S\to\mathbb R\). A probability measure \(\mu\) is absolutely continuous with respect to a positive measure \(\lambda\), written \(\mu\ll\lambda\), if \(\lambda(B)=0\Rightarrow\mu(B)=0\) for every Borel set \(B\). Whenever a Radon\text{--}Nikodym derivative \(\Lambda=d\mu/d\lambda\) exists, \(\int f\,d\mu=\int f\Lambda\,d\lambda\) for every integrable \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total variation convergence uniformly controls integrals over bounded continuous test functions and, in the stated regular setting, implies convergence for bounded measurable tests. Absolute continuity means every lambda-null Borel set is also mu-null. When a Radon–Nikodym density exists, it represents integration against mu relative to lambda.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ satisfies the source's regular state-space assumptions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{TV}}\mu\Rightarrow\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu\ \forall f\text{ bounded measurable};\qquad \Lambda=\frac{d\mu}{d\lambda}\Rightarrow\int f\,d\mu=\int f\Lambda\,d\lambda.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence in Distribution and Tightness in Finite Dimensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional convergence and tightness criteria for finite-dimensional random variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $A_n,A$ be $\mathbb{R}^k$-valued random variables with laws $P_n,P_A$. Then $A_n\Rightarrow A$ if the joint distribution functions converge at every continuity point of the distribution function of $A$; equivalently, $\mathbb{E}F(A_n)\to\mathbb{E}F(A)$ for every bounded continuous $F:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}$. The family $\{P_n\}$ is tight if $\lim_{K\to\infty}\sup_nP(\lVert A_n\rVert\ge K)=0$. If $\lVert A_n\rVert<\infty$ almost surely for every $n$, this is equivalent to requiring that for every $\mu>0$ there exist finite $M_\mu,K_\mu$ such that $P(\lVert A_n\rVert\ge K_\mu)\le\mu$ for all $n\ge M_\mu$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergence in distribution is convergence of joint distribution functions at continuity points, equivalently convergence of expectations for every bounded continuous test function. Tightness is uniform vanishing of the probability outside sufficiently large bounded sets, with an equivalent eventual tail-bound formulation when every random variable is almost surely finite.
assumptions_latex: A_n,A\text{ are }\mathbb{R}^k\text{-valued random variables on a common probability space}
\lVert A_n\rVert<\infty\ \text{a.s. for every }n\text{ in the eventual-tail characterization}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A_n\Rightarrow A\iff \mathbb{E}F(A_n)\to\mathbb{E}F(A)\ \forall F\in C_b(\mathbb{R}^k),\qquad \{P_n\}\text{ tight}\iff\lim_{K\to\infty}\sup_nP(\lVert A_n\rVert\ge K)=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Tightness Criterion in Skorokhod Path Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient compact-containment and increment conditions for processes on the whole or nonnegative time axis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $A_n(\cdot)$ have paths in $D(-\infty,\infty)$. Suppose that for every $\delta>0$ and every $t$ in a dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$ there is a compact $K_{\delta,t}\subset\mathbb{R}$ with $\inf_nP(A_n(t)\in K_{\delta,t})\ge1-\delta$, and that for every $T>0$, $\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\limsup_n\sup_{|\tau|\le T}\sup_{0\le s\le\delta}\mathbb{E}\min\{|A_n(\tau+s)-A_n(\tau)|,1\}=0$. Then $\{A_n(\cdot)\}$ is tight in $D(-\infty,\infty)$. For $D[0,\infty)$, the same conclusion holds with $0\le\tau\le T$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence of càdlàg processes is tight when its values are uniformly concentrated in compact sets at a dense collection of times and its expected truncated increments vanish uniformly on compact time intervals. On the nonnegative time axis, the increment condition is restricted to nonnegative base times.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{A_n(\cdot)\}\text{ is tight in }D(-\infty,\infty);\text{ on }D[0,\infty)\text{ replace }|\tau|\le T\text{ by }0\le\tau\le T.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tightness and moment bounds for normalized stochastic-approximation iterates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers diminishing-step and constant-step normalized errors near a stable equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume algorithm (5.1), (A4.5), and (A5.1)--(A5.7). Suppose \(P\succ0\) is symmetric and, as \(\theta\to\bar\theta\), \[V(\theta)=(\theta-\bar\theta)'P(\theta-\bar\theta)+o(|\theta-\bar\theta|^2).\] Then \(\{(\theta_n-\bar\theta)/\sqrt{\epsilon_n}\}\) is tight. If additionally some symmetric \(P_1\succ0\) satisfies \(V(\theta)\ge(\theta-\bar\theta)'P_1(\theta-\bar\theta)\) for every \(\theta\), then \[\sup_n E\frac{|\theta_n-\bar\theta|^2}{\epsilon_n}<\infty.\] For constant step \(\epsilon_n=\epsilon\), if the corresponding interpolated processes \(\theta^\epsilon(\cdot)\) converge weakly, possibly after shifts of time origin, to the constant process \(\bar\theta\), then there are finite \(n_\epsilon\) such that \(\{(\theta_n^\epsilon-\bar\theta)/\sqrt\epsilon:n\ge n_\epsilon,\epsilon\}\) is tight; under the global quadratic lower bound, \[\limsup_{\epsilon\to0}\sup_{n\ge n_\epsilon}E\frac{|\theta_n^\epsilon-\bar\theta|^2}{\epsilon}<\infty.\] Moreover, \(n_\epsilon\) may be chosen so that \(e^{-\lambda_1\epsilon n_\epsilon}|\theta_0-\bar\theta|=O(\sqrt\epsilon)\) for any \(0<\lambda_1<\lambda\), with \(\lambda_1\) arbitrarily close to \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated stochastic-approximation and Lyapunov assumptions, the error divided by the square root of the step size is tight. A global quadratic lower bound on the Lyapunov function also gives a uniform normalized second-moment bound. Corresponding tail tightness and moment bounds hold for constant steps after an explicitly scaled burn-in period.
assumptions_latex: For the second-moment conclusions, \(P_1=P_1'\succ0\) and \(V(\theta)\ge(\theta-\bar\theta)'P_1(\theta-\bar\theta)\) for all \(\theta\).
In the constant-step regime, \(\theta^\epsilon(\cdot)\Rightarrow\bar\theta\), possibly after shifting time origins.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left\{\frac{\theta_n-\bar\theta}{\sqrt{\epsilon_n}}\right\}\text{ is tight},\qquad \sup_nE\frac{|\theta_n-\bar\theta|^2}{\epsilon_n}<\infty\text{ under the global lower bound, with the analogous constant-step tail conclusions and }e^{-\lambda_1\epsilon n_\epsilon}|\theta_0-\bar\theta|=O(\sqrt\epsilon).

knowledge_statements.title: Probabilistic Implication Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict implication boundaries among almost-sure, probability, and distributional convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For random elements in a metric space, \[X_n\to X\ \text{almost surely}\ \Longrightarrow\ X_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}X\ \Longrightarrow\ X_n\xrightarrow{d}X.\] Neither converse holds in general. If independent events \((A_n)\) satisfy \(\mathbb{P}(A_n)=1/n\) and \(X_n=\mathbf{1}_{A_n}\), then \(X_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0\) but \(X_n\) does not converge almost surely. If \(X,X_1,X_2,\ldots\) are independent Bernoulli random variables with parameter \(1/2\), then \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\), while \(\mathbb{P}(|X_n-X|>1/2)=1/2\), so convergence in probability fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability, which implies convergence in distribution; independent Bernoulli constructions show both reverse implications fail.
assumptions_latex: All variables in each implication share a metric state space.
The event sequence in the first counterexample is independent.
The Bernoulli variables in the second counterexample are mutually independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The implications \(\mathrm{a.s.}\Rightarrow\mathbb{P}\Rightarrow d\) hold, but both converses fail without additional assumptions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-SFO-budget RSMD bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimizes the constant batch size under the conditions of the preceding RSMD corollary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume all conditions of Corollary 6.6 and fix a total SFO budget \(\bar N\). For \(\widetilde D>0\), choose
\[
m=\left\lceil\min\left\{\max\left\{1,\frac{\sigma\sqrt{6\bar N}}{4L\bar D}\right\},\bar N\right\}\right\rceil.
\]
Then
\[
\frac{\mathbb E\|g_{X,R}\|^2}{L}\le \mathcal B_{\bar N},
\]
where
\[
\mathcal B_{\bar N}:=\frac{16LD_\Psi^2}{\bar N}+\frac{4\sqrt6\sigma}{\sqrt{\bar N}}\left(\frac{D_\Psi^2}{\widetilde D}+\widetilde D\max\left\{1,\frac{\sqrt6\sigma}{4L\widetilde D\sqrt{\bar N}}\right\}\right).
\]
If additionally \(f\) is convex and \(x^*\) is optimal, then
\[
\mathbb E[\Psi(x_R)-\Psi(x^*)]\le \mathcal C_{\bar N},
\]
where
\[
\mathcal C_{\bar N}:=\frac{4LV(x_1,x^*)}{\bar N}+\frac{\sqrt6\sigma}{\sqrt{\bar N}}\left(\frac{V(x_1,x^*)}{\bar D}+\frac{\widetilde D}{3}\max\left\{1,\frac{\sqrt6\sigma}{4L\widetilde D\sqrt{\bar N}}\right\}\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the preceding RSMD conditions, the displayed batch-size allocation for a fixed SFO budget yields the stated expected stationarity bound. If f is convex, it also yields the stated expected objective-gap bound. The distinction between the extracted symbols bar D and tilde D is preserved.
assumptions_latex: \bar N\text{ is the fixed total number of SFO calls}
\text{For the objective bound: }f\text{ is convex and }x^*\text{ is optimal}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{\mathbb E\|g_{X,R}\|^2}{L}\le \mathcal B_{\bar N},\qquad \mathbb E[\Psi(x_R)-\Psi(x^*)]\le \mathcal C_{\bar N}\text{ in the convex case}

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Number of stochastic-oracle calls needed to attain a declared accuracy criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a stochastic oracle \(\mathcal{O}\) that, for a query \(x\), returns random information such as \(g(x,\xi)\). For an algorithm producing \(X_N\) after at most \(N\) oracle calls and an error criterion \(M\), its expected stochastic oracle complexity is \[N_{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon)=\inf\{N\in\mathbb{N}:\mathbb{E}[M(X_N)]\leq\varepsilon\}.\] Its high-probability oracle complexity is \[N_{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon,\delta)=\inf\{N\in\mathbb{N}:\mathbb{P}(M(X_N)\leq\varepsilon)\geq1-\delta\}.\] Batched calls are counted individually unless the oracle model explicitly assigns unit cost to a batch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stochastic oracle complexity counts the oracle responses required to meet a stated expected or high-probability error target under an explicit call-cost convention.
assumptions_latex: The oracle interface and the cost of one call are specified.
\(M\) is a declared nonnegative measurable error criterion.
The guarantee mode is either expected or high probability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complexity is the least oracle-call budget meeting the declared \(\varepsilon\) or \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) criterion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constant-Step Stochastic Mirror-Descent Work Prescription
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-horizon prescription. The integer-rounding operators in the extracted horizon formulas are corrupted and are not asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a problem \(F\in\widetilde D_{r,l}^{a,v_0}\) and a requested averaged relative error \(v\) satisfying \(v_0<v<1\), run \(N\) iterations of (3.1)--(3.2) with a constant displacement \(\rho>0\) and return \((x^N,l^N)\). Writing \(\delta=v-v_0\), the extracted unambiguous step-size prescription is
\[\rho=\frac{1}{2L}\rho_{V,V_I,r}(\delta),\qquad \rho_{V,V_I,r}(\delta)=\min\left\{\gamma_{V,r}\left(\frac{\delta}{6}\right),\gamma_{V_I,r}\left(\frac{\delta}{6}\right)\right\}.\]
The laboriousness is \(N\): \(N-1\) oracle questions and one output operation. The corrupted horizon display is based on the quantity \(4/[\delta\rho_{V,V_I,r}(\delta)]\). In the Hilbert case with \(r\ge2\), the extract gives \(\rho=2v/L\) and a horizon obtained by an unresolved integer rounding of \(v^{-2}\).

Its counted work is N, consisting of N−1 oracle calls and one output operation. The extraction identifies the real-valued quantities underlying the horizon choices, but not their exact integer-rounding convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Sample Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Number of data samples required to attain a stochastic optimization accuracy target.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle–Sample Accounting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conversion between iteration, oracle-call, and sample-use counts under batching and reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose iteration \(k\) makes \(q_k\) stochastic-oracle calls, call \(j\) consumes \(b_{k,j}\) sample occurrences, and \(D_{k,j}\) is the set of distinct sample identities used by that call. After \(T\) iterations, the exact accounting identities are \[N_{\mathrm{oracle}}(T)=\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}q_k,\qquad N_{\mathrm{sample}}(T)=\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\sum_{j=1}^{q_k}b_{k,j},\] and \[N_{\mathrm{distinct}}(T)=\left|\bigcup_{k=0}^{T-1}\bigcup_{j=1}^{q_k}D_{k,j}\right|.\] Hence oracle and sample complexities coincide only when every call consumes exactly one sample occurrence; distinct-sample complexity can be smaller under reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle calls, consumed sample occurrences, and distinct samples obey separate counts; they coincide only under one-new-sample-per-call accounting.
assumptions_latex: Each iteration has a finite number \(q_k\) of oracle calls.
Every call has a declared batch size and set of sample identities.
Repeated sample occurrences are counted in \(N_{\mathrm{sample}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{oracle}}=N_{\mathrm{sample}}\) when \(b_{k,j}=1\) for every call, while \(N_{\mathrm{distinct}}\leq N_{\mathrm{sample}}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Epoch Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum SGD complexity measured in completed full-data epochs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\), and suppose that each completed epoch processes every index exactly once. If \(K_\varepsilon\) is the least number of completed epochs after which the reported output \(\widehat x\) satisfies an accuracy criterion \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\), then \(K_\varepsilon\) is the epoch complexity. The component-gradient count at that epoch boundary is \(nK_\varepsilon\), apart from separately counted initialization or validation work. If an oracle-call guarantee holds after every call count at least \(N_\varepsilon\), then stopping at the next completed epoch gives the upper bound \(K_\varepsilon\le \lceil N_\varepsilon/n\rceil\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epoch complexity counts completed traversals of all n components. An N-call guarantee converts to at most ceiling(N/n) epochs only when it remains valid at the next epoch boundary.
assumptions_latex: Each completed epoch evaluates every component exactly once.
\(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\) specifies the required output accuracy.
For the ceiling conversion, the guarantee holds at every call count at least \(N_\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The boundary evaluation count is \(nK_\varepsilon\), and \(K_\varepsilon\le\lceil N_\varepsilon/n\rceil\) under the stated persistent-guarantee condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Pass Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum oracle cost normalized by dataset size, including partial traversals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\), let \(N_\varepsilon\) be the total number of component-oracle calls made before the reported output satisfies \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\). The pass complexity is \(P_\varepsilon=N_\varepsilon/n\). This normalization permits fractional passes and applies whether indices are visited cyclically, by reshuffling, or by sampling with replacement, provided repeated calls are counted with multiplicity. If \(T_\varepsilon\) is the number of iterations performed and iteration \(t\) uses a mini-batch of size \(b_t\), then \(N_\varepsilon=\sum_{t=0}^{T_\varepsilon-1}b_t\) and \(P_\varepsilon=n^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^{T_\varepsilon-1}b_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pass complexity is total component-oracle calls divided by dataset size, with repeated samples counted and partial passes allowed.
assumptions_latex: Every sampled component in a mini-batch incurs one component-oracle call.

knowledge_statements.title: Streaming-to-Finite-Data Translation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation of streaming oracle counts to empirical finite-sum pass counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_n(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\). Conditional on the fixed dataset, draw \(I_t\) independently and uniformly from \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and set \(g_t=\nabla f_{I_t}(x_t)\). Then \(\mathbb E[g_t\mid x_t,F_n]=\nabla F_n(x_t)\), so a streaming analysis requiring \(T_\varepsilon\) independent unbiased oracle calls applies conditionally to this with-replacement empirical oracle whenever its remaining moment assumptions hold. Its finite-data cost is \(T_\varepsilon\) component-gradient evaluations, equivalently \(T_\varepsilon/n\) passes. This translation does not by itself justify random-reshuffling or without-replacement guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform with-replacement sampling turns an empirical finite sum into an unbiased streaming oracle; T calls equal T/n passes, but reshuffling requires separate analysis.
assumptions_latex: Indices are conditionally independent and uniform with replacement.
The streaming theorem's conditional moment assumptions hold for the empirical oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[g_t\mid x_t,F_n]=\nabla F_n(x_t)\) and the normalized data cost is \(T_\varepsilon/n\) passes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth convex averaged-SGD objective bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The averaged iterate is the preceding definition $\widetilde x(n)=n^{-1}\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}x(m)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f$ be convex and $\beta$-smooth, without assuming strong convexity. Assume its nonempty minimizer set $\mathcal M$ is closed and convex, $\mathbb E[\|M(k)\|^2]\le\sigma^2<\infty$ for every $k$, and $D:=\min_{y\in\mathcal M}\|x(0)-y\|$. For $n>0$, set $\eta:=\frac D\sigma\sqrt{\frac2n}$ and use the constant step $a(m)\equiv a:=(\beta+1/\eta)^{-1}$ for every $m\le n$. Then, for every $x^*\in\mathcal M$, $\mathbb E[f(\widetilde x(n))]-f(x^*)\le\frac{\beta D^2}{2n}+\sqrt{\frac2n}D\sigma$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth convex objective with a nonempty minimizer set and bounded noise variance, a horizon-dependent constant step gives an averaged expected objective gap bounded by beta D squared over 2n plus square root of 2/n times D sigma.

children.title: Parallel Runtime Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Runtime Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Critical-path wall-clock complexity for parallel stochastic first-order execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an accuracy event \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\). For an execution DAG that produces an output satisfying this event, let \(W_\varepsilon\) be its total unit-time work and \(D_\varepsilon\) its critical-path length. On \(P\) identical processors under a greedy scheduler, the parallel runtime obeys \(T_P(\varepsilon)\le W_\varepsilon/P+D_\varepsilon\), up to a scheduler-independent constant and separately charged communication costs. Every schedule also satisfies \(T_P(\varepsilon)\ge\max\{W_\varepsilon/P,D_\varepsilon\}\). Consequently, the achievable speedup is limited by both available parallelism \(W_\varepsilon/D_\varepsilon\) and any communication or synchronization added to the critical path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel time is controlled by work per processor and critical-path depth; speedup stops when depth, communication, or synchronization dominates.
assumptions_latex: The computation is represented by a finite precedence DAG.
Processors are identical and execute ready unit-cost tasks greedily.
Communication not encoded in the DAG is accounted for separately.

notation.meaning: total work needed to attain accuracy epsilon

children.title: Synchronization Complexity
children.top_down_role: Barrier, communication-round, and coordination costs during parallel execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Synchronization Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Number and latency cost of global coordination events before certified accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a parallel stochastic first-order method, define a synchronization event as a barrier or collective operation that no participating worker can pass until its required messages arrive. If \(S_\varepsilon\) such events occur before the output satisfies \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\), then \(S_\varepsilon\) is the synchronization complexity. If these events are sequentially ordered on a common critical path and event \(s\) has latency \(\lambda_s\), their critical-path contribution is \(C_{\mathrm{sync}}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{s=1}^{S_\varepsilon}\lambda_s\). If \(\lambda_s\ge\lambda>0\) for every counted event, then every such execution satisfies \(T_P(\varepsilon)\ge\lambda S_\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Synchronization complexity counts blocking coordination events. When the events are sequential on one critical path, their latencies add and impose a runtime floor.
assumptions_latex: Each counted synchronization event blocks participating workers until its required messages arrive.
The counted events are sequentially ordered on a common critical path.
Event latency \(\lambda_s\) includes required communication and waiting.
\(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\) defines attainment of the target accuracy.

total latency of the sequential synchronization events

children.title: Staleness-Induced Runtime Costs
children.top_down_role: Runtime penalties associated with delayed worker information.

knowledge_statements.title: Staleness-Induced Runtime Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Runtime overhead caused by delayed gradients and their iteration inflation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In asynchronous SGD, write the update as \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t g(x_{t-d_t};\xi_t)\), where \(0\le d_t\le\tau\). Let \(N_\varepsilon(\tau)\) be the number of committed updates required to satisfy \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\), and let \(c_t(\tau)\) be the wall-clock cost of update \(t\), including contention and retries. The staleness-induced runtime cost relative to fresh execution is
\[C_{\mathrm{stale}}(\varepsilon,\tau)=\sum_{t=0}^{N_\varepsilon(\tau)-1}c_t(\tau)-\sum_{t=0}^{N_\varepsilon(0)-1}c_t(0).\]
It includes both iteration inflation and per-update systems overhead; bounded delay alone does not imply that this difference is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Staleness cost is the runtime difference between delayed and fresh executions, combining extra optimization updates with contention, retries, and changed per-update cost.
assumptions_latex: Asynchronous updates use gradients delayed by \(d_t\le\tau\).
Fresh and delayed executions use the same target event \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\).
All committed-update costs are measured on a common wall-clock model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{stale}}(\varepsilon,\tau)\) decomposes into update-count inflation and changed per-update execution costs.

notation.meaning: gradient delay at committed update t
updates required under maximum delay tau
runtime difference relative to fresh execution

children.title: Parallel Scaling Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Worker-count regimes limited by serial work, communication, or load imbalance.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Scaling Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Work-depth, communication, and serial-fraction limits on SGD speedup.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an accuracy-producing execution has total unit-time work \(W_\varepsilon\), one-processor reference time \(T_1(\varepsilon)=W_\varepsilon\), dependency depth \(D_\varepsilon\), unavoidable communication time \(C_\varepsilon(P)\), and unavoidable nonoverlappable serial time \(sT_1(\varepsilon)\) for some \(s\in[0,1]\). Then any \(P\)-processor implementation satisfies \[T_P(\varepsilon)\ge\max\{W_\varepsilon/P,D_\varepsilon,C_\varepsilon(P),sT_1(\varepsilon)\}.\] Hence the speedup \(S_P=T_1(\varepsilon)/T_P(\varepsilon)\) satisfies \[S_P\le\min\{P,T_1(\varepsilon)/D_\varepsilon,T_1(\varepsilon)/C_\varepsilon(P),1/s\},\] with the last term omitted when \(s=0\). Strong scaling saturates when dependency depth, communication, or serial work dominates \(W_\varepsilon/P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a unit-work serial baseline, parallel speedup is limited by processor count, dependency depth, communication, and the reciprocal nonoverlappable serial fraction.
assumptions_latex: All compared executions satisfy the same accuracy event.
The one-processor reference time satisfies \(T_1(\varepsilon)=W_\varepsilon\) in the unit-cost work model.
\(D_\varepsilon\), \(C_\varepsilon(P)\), and \(sT_1(\varepsilon)\) are individually unavoidable runtime lower bounds.
The serial time \(sT_1(\varepsilon)\) cannot overlap parallel work.

notation.meaning: speedup relative to the one-processor reference execution
total unit-time work required for the accuracy event
fraction of one-processor time that is unavoidable and nonoverlappable

children.title: Stochastic First-Order Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Information-theoretic boundaries for stochastic convex and nonconvex optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic First-Order Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical oracle lower-bound regimes for convex and smooth nonconvex stochastic optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the stochastic first-order oracle model, worst-case query complexity depends on the function class. For convex \(G\)-Lipschitz objectives over a domain with initial distance at most \(R\), attaining \(\mathbb E[F(\widehat x)-F^*]\le\varepsilon\) requires \(\Omega(G^2R^2/\varepsilon^2)\) oracle calls in general. For \(\mu\)-strongly convex objectives with gradient-noise variance at most \(\sigma^2\), the stochastic term is \(\Omega(\sigma^2/(\mu\varepsilon))\). For smooth nonconvex objectives with smoothness \(L\), initial gap \(\Delta\), and variance \(\sigma^2\), obtaining \(\mathbb E\|\nabla F(\widehat x)\|\le\varepsilon\) has a canonical stochastic lower-bound scale \(\Omega(\sigma^2L\Delta/\varepsilon^4)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case stochastic first-order complexity scales quadratically in convex accuracy, linearly in inverse strongly convex accuracy, and quartically for nonconvex gradient-norm accuracy.
assumptions_latex: The oracle returns unbiased stochastic first-order information with the stated variance control.
The algorithm is measured by worst-case expected oracle queries over the specified class.
The convex and nonconvex regimes are interpreted separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The respective lower-bound scales are \(\Omega(G^2R^2/\varepsilon^2)\), \(\Omega(\sigma^2/(\mu\varepsilon))\), and \(\Omega(\sigma^2L\Delta/\varepsilon^4)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No sources are supplied for three nontrivial lower bounds. Authoritative results are required to fix the oracle model, randomized-algorithm scope, dimension or parameter regimes, and the nonconvex norm-versus-squared-norm accuracy convention.

children.title: Objective-Value Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Value Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-probability bounds certifying the objective value of an SGD output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f(x;\xi)]\), and let \(\widehat x\) be independent of a validation sample \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m\). An objective-value certificate at confidence \(1-\delta\) is a random interval \([L_m,U_m]\), computable from the validation data and declared concentration assumptions, such that
\[\mathbb P\{L_m\le F(\widehat x)\le U_m\}\ge1-\delta.\]
Its width \(U_m-L_m\) quantifies certified evaluation uncertainty. It certifies objective accuracy relative to a target value \(v\) when the relevant one-sided bound holds, for example \(U_m\le v+\varepsilon\). Independence may be replaced only by a concentration argument valid for adaptive reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A validation-based confidence interval certifies the population objective at the SGD output; comparison of its upper endpoint with a target yields an accuracy certificate.
assumptions_latex: The validation observations satisfy a stated concentration condition.
The output is independent of validation data, unless adaptive concentration is used.

children.title: Optimality-Gap Certificates
children.top_down_role: Accuracy evidence based on primal, dual, or primal-dual gaps.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimality-Gap Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual or lower-bound certificates for convex stochastic optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be a proper closed convex objective with optimum \(F^*\). Suppose a computable random upper bound \(U\) and lower bound \(L\) satisfy \(\mathbb P\{F(\widehat x)\le U\text{ and }L\le F^*\}\ge1-\delta\). Then \(G=U-L\) is an optimality-gap certificate: whenever \(G\le\varepsilon\),
\[\mathbb P\{F(\widehat x)-F^*\le\varepsilon\}\ge1-\delta.
\]
In a primal-dual formulation, \(U=F(\widehat x)\) and \(L=D(\widehat y)\) are admissible when \(\widehat x\) and \(\widehat y\) are feasible and weak duality gives \(D(\widehat y)\le F^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid objective upper bound minus a valid optimum lower bound certifies suboptimality; a feasible primal-dual gap is the standard instance.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, closed, convex, and attains its optimum.
The upper and lower bounds are jointly valid with probability at least \(1-\delta\).
Any primal-dual specialization satisfies primal and dual feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G=U-L\le\varepsilon\) certifies \(F(\widehat x)-F^*\le\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\).

notation.meaning: certified upper bound on the candidate objective
certified lower bound on the optimal value

children.title: Distance-to-Solution Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Distance-to-Solution Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-probability certification of distance from an SGD output to the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be proper, closed, and convex on a closed convex set \(X\), with nonempty solution set \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}F(x)\). A radius \(r\ge0\), computed from declared stochastic observations and assumptions, is a \((1-\delta)\)-confidence distance certificate for \(\widehat x\in X\) if
\[\mathbb P\{\operatorname{dist}(\widehat x,X^*)\le r\}\ge1-\delta.
\]
For example, if \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex and a valid gap certificate gives \(F(\widehat x)-F^*\le\varepsilon\), then \(r=\sqrt{2\varepsilon/\mu}\) is a distance certificate on the same event.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distance certificate bounds the output's distance to the solution set with stated confidence; strong convexity converts an objective-gap certificate into such a radius.
assumptions_latex: The convex solution set \(X^*\) is nonempty.
The claimed radius is measurable from the certificate data.
For the conversion example, \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P\{\operatorname{dist}(\widehat x,X^*)\le r\}\ge1-\delta\), with \(r=\sqrt{2\varepsilon/\mu}\) under strong convexity and an \(\varepsilon\)-gap certificate.

children.title: Certificate Conversion Regimes
