knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Conversion Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversions among objective-gap, distance, and residual certificates under convex regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be convex with nonempty minimizer set \(X^*\), and write \(\Delta(x)=F(x)-F^*\). Certificate conversions require additional geometry. If \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex, then \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\sqrt{2\Delta(x)/\mu}\). If \(F\) is \(G\)-Lipschitz on its domain, then \(\Delta(x)\le G\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\). If \(F\) is differentiable and \(L\)-smooth, then \(\|\nabla F(x)\|^2\le2L\Delta(x)\). Each deterministic implication preserves the confidence level of the source stochastic certificate; reversing any implication generally requires a corresponding error-bound, growth, or strong-convexity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity, Lipschitz continuity, and smoothness convert gap, distance, and gradient certificates; confidence is preserved, while reverse conversions need extra error-bound geometry.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is convex and attains its minimum.
Each displayed conversion uses its stated regularity condition.
The source certificate is valid on an event of probability at least \(1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On the source event, \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\sqrt{2\Delta(x)/\mu}\), \(\Delta(x)\le G\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\), or \(\|\nabla F(x)\|^2\le2L\Delta(x)\), as applicable.

children.title: Gradient-Norm Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Norm Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-probability first-order certificate for smooth unconstrained stochastic optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, let \(X\) be a possibly random candidate iterate, and let \(U\) be a data-dependent statistic satisfying \(\mathbb{P}(\|\nabla F(X)\|\le U)\ge 1-\alpha\). Declaring success when \(U\le\varepsilon\) is a level-\(1-\alpha\) gradient-norm certificate: \[\mathbb{P}\bigl(U\le\varepsilon\ \text{and}\ \|\nabla F(X)\|>\varepsilon\bigr)\le\alpha.\] Thus an accepted certificate verifies \(\varepsilon\)-stationarity except on an event of probability at most \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid upper confidence bound on the gradient norm certifies approximate stationarity whenever that bound is at most the requested tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) upper-bounds \(\|\nabla F(X)\|\) with probability at least \(1-\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Statistical upper bound on the gradient norm.

children.title: Gradient-Mapping Certificates
children.top_down_role: First-order stopping evidence adapted to constraints or composite structure.

notation.meaning: Proximal operator of eta times h.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite first-order certificate based on the proximal-gradient mapping.

source_refs.locator: 10.2 The Proximal Gradient Method p. 270

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F=f+h\), \(\eta>0\), and \(\varepsilon\ge 0\), define the gradient mapping by \[G_\eta(x)=\eta^{-1}\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\eta h}(x-\eta\nabla f(x))\bigr).\] A verified inequality \(\|G_\eta(x)\|\le\varepsilon\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-gradient-mapping certificate. Moreover, \(G_\eta(x)=0\) holds if and only if \(0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial h(x)\); hence the zero certificate is equivalent to first-order stationarity for the composite problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal-gradient mapping measures composite stationarity; a mapping norm at most the nonnegative tolerance certifies an approximate fixed point, and a zero norm exactly characterizes stationarity.
knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Mapping Certificates

source_witnesses.locator: 10.2 The Proximal Gradient Method p. 270

children.title: Proximal-Residual Certificates
children.top_down_role: Stopping evidence based on proximal fixed-point residuals.

notation.meaning: Distance from zero to the set A(y).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent fixed-point certificate for a monotone inclusion.

source_refs.locator: 2.6 Proximal point method p. 44
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:\mathbb{R}^d\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^d\) be maximally monotone, let \(\eta>0\), let \(\varepsilon\ge0\), and let \(J_{\eta A}=(I+\eta A)^{-1}\). Define \[r_\eta(x)=\eta^{-1}\|x-J_{\eta A}(x)\|.\] The inequality \(r_\eta(x)\le\varepsilon\) is a proximal-residual certificate. If \(y=J_{\eta A}(x)\), then \(\eta^{-1}(x-y)\in A(y)\), so \(\operatorname{dist}(0,A(y))\le r_\eta(x)\). In particular, \(r_\eta(x)=0\) if and only if \(0\in A(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scaled displacement from a point to its resolvent image certifies a nearby inclusion residual at a specified nonnegative tolerance and vanishes exactly at a solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal-Residual Certificates

source_witnesses.locator: 2.6 Proximal point method p. 44
source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

children.title: Residual Comparison Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Comparison Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of composite stationarity residuals under Lipschitz smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+h\), let \(y=\operatorname{prox}_{\eta h}(x-\eta\nabla f(x))\), and let \(G_\eta(x)=(x-y)/\eta\). If \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then \[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(y))\le(1+L\eta)\|G_\eta(x)\|.\] If additionally \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial h\), then \[\|G_\eta(x)\|\le\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x)).\] Consequently, gradient-mapping and subdifferential residuals are comparable, although generally evaluated at different points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For smooth-plus-convex objectives, the gradient-mapping norm bounds a stationarity residual at the proximal point and is itself bounded by the residual at the original point.

notation.meaning: Composite limiting subdifferential, equal here to gradient f plus convex subdifferential h.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-sample and asymptotic confidence regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded confidence-set construction using finite-sample distance laws or asymptotic normality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_n(r)=\{x:\|X_n-x\|_D^2\le r\}\). If \(\|X_n-x^*\|_D^2\) has distribution function \(G_n\), then \(\mathbb P\{x^*\in C_n(\varepsilon)\}=G_n(\varepsilon)\). Thus, whenever a quantile \(q_{n,1-\alpha}\) satisfies \(G_n(q_{n,1-\alpha})=1-\alpha\), \(C_n(q_{n,1-\alpha})\) has confidence level \(1-\alpha\). If \(\|z\|_D^2=z^\top Dz\) with \(D\succ0\), \(\sqrt n(X_n-x^*)\Rightarrow N(0,V)\), and \(G_{D,V}\) is the distribution function of \(Z^\top DZ\) for \(Z\sim N(0,V)\), then \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P\{\|X_n-x^*\|_D^2\le\varepsilon/n\}=G_{D,V}(\varepsilon)\). Consequently, at a continuity quantile \(q_{1-\alpha}=G_{D,V}^{-1}(1-\alpha)\), \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P\{\|X_n-x^*\|_D^2\le q_{1-\alpha}/n\}=1-\alpha\). Under consistency and the additional regularity required for plug-in quantiles, the corresponding limit holds with \(V\) replaced by \(\widehat V_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A known distance distribution yields an exact confidence set when its selected quantile attains the desired probability. Under asymptotic normality, quadratic-distance confidence sets have squared radius equal to an appropriate normal-quadratic-form quantile divided by n. An estimated covariance may be substituted when consistency and quantile regularity justify the plug-in construction.
assumptions_latex: \|X_n-x^*\|_D^2\text{ has distribution function }G_n\text{ for the finite-sample claim}
\|z\|_D^2=z^\top Dz,\quad D\succ0\text{ for the asymptotic quadratic-distance claim}
\widehat V_n\to V\text{ together with conditions ensuring plug-in quantile validity when }\widehat V_n\text{ is used}

children.title: Statistical Stopping Rules

knowledge_statements.title: Statistical Stopping Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-inspection stopping using a confidence bound on a stationarity measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix deterministic inspection times \(1\le t_1<\cdots<t_K\), error allocations \(\alpha_k>0\) with \(\sum_{k=1}^K\alpha_k\le\alpha\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). At inspection \(t_k\), construct an upper confidence bound \(U_k\) satisfying \(\mathbb{P}(R(x_{t_k})>U_k)\le\alpha_k\). Stop at the first \(t_k\) for which \(U_k\le\varepsilon\), and output \(x_{t_k}\); otherwise return no certificate. The probability of stopping with \(R(x_{t_k})>\varepsilon\) is at most \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inspect predetermined iterates, stop when a multiplicity-adjusted upper confidence bound falls below tolerance, and control the probability of a false stationarity declaration.
assumptions_latex: \(t_1,\ldots,t_K\) are fixed before observing the inspection data.

notation.meaning: Upper confidence bound at inspection k.
Error probability assigned to inspection k.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Bonferroni-calibrated fixed-inspection confidence bounds control false stopping

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Bonferroni-calibrated fixed-inspection algorithm is correct and fits Statistical Stopping Rules, but it has no authoritative citation with an inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic fixed-width stopping family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition of shrinking-width asymptotic coverage for stochastic stopping rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family of stopping times \((\tau_{\varepsilon,\alpha})\) is called a family of asymptotic fixed-width stopping times if \(\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\mathbb P\{\|X_{\tau_{\varepsilon,\alpha}}-x^*\|_D^2\le\varepsilon\}\ge1-\alpha\). The sets \(C_\varepsilon=\{x:\|X_{\tau_{\varepsilon,\alpha}}-x\|_D^2\le\varepsilon\}\) are called asymptotic fixed-width confidence sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stopping-time family is asymptotically fixed-width when its limiting coverage is at least 1 minus alpha as the prescribed width shrinks to zero. The corresponding sets centered at the stopped iterates are asymptotic fixed-width confidence sets.
assumptions_latex: (\tau_{\varepsilon,\alpha})\text{ is a family of stopping times}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-width stopping time and confidence set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition for stochastic-approximation iterates under the stated distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\tau_{\varepsilon,\alpha}\) be a stopping time such that \(\mathbb P\{\|X_{\tau_{\varepsilon,\alpha}}-x^*\|_D^2\le\varepsilon\}=1-\alpha\). Then \(\tau_{\varepsilon,\alpha}\) is called a fixed-width stopping time, and \(C=\{x:\|X_{\tau_{\varepsilon,\alpha}}-x\|_D^2\le\varepsilon\}\) is called a fixed-width confidence set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stopping time is called fixed-width when the stopped iterate is within the prescribed squared-distance tolerance of the true solution with probability 1 minus alpha. The corresponding set centered at the stopped iterate is its fixed-width confidence set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \tau_{\varepsilon,\alpha}\text{ is a fixed-width stopping time and }C=\{x:\|X_{\tau_{\varepsilon,\alpha}}-x\|_D^2\le\varepsilon\}\text{ is a fixed-width confidence set}

children.title: Sequential Stopping Rules
children.top_down_role: Termination criteria based on evidence accumulated during repeated monitoring.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Stopping Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive stopping based on an anytime-valid upper confidence sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\ge1}\) be a filtration, let \(x_t\) be \(\mathcal{F}_t\)-measurable, and suppose \((U_t)_{t\ge1}\) satisfies \[\mathbb{P}\bigl(\forall t\ge1:\ R(x_t)\le U_t\bigr)\ge1-\alpha.\] Define the stopping time \(\tau=\inf\{t\ge1:U_t\le\varepsilon\}\), with \(\inf\varnothing=\infty\). If \(\tau<\infty\), output \(x_\tau\); otherwise continue sampling. Then \(\mathbb{P}(\tau<\infty,\ R(x_\tau)>\varepsilon)\le\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An anytime-valid upper confidence sequence permits adaptive stopping while retaining the prescribed probability of a correct stationarity certificate.
assumptions_latex: \((U_t)\) simultaneously upper-bounds \(R(x_t)\) with probability at least \(1-\alpha\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: simultaneous coverage remains valid at data-dependent stopping times

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The anytime-valid stopping rule and its false-certificate guarantee are correct and algorithm is the appropriate content kind, but no authoritative confidence-sequence or sequential-inference source is cited.

children.title: Confidence Calibration
children.top_down_role: Calibration of stopping evidence to target reliability levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Confidence Calibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Error-budget calibration for repeated stochastic stationarity checks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For inspection events \(E_t=\{R(x_t)>U_t\}\), choose deterministic error levels \(\alpha_t>0\) satisfying \(\sum_{t\ge1}\alpha_t\le\alpha\). If each marginal construction obeys \(\mathbb{P}(E_t)\le\alpha_t\), then \[\mathbb{P}\bigl(\exists t\ge1:R(x_t)>U_t\bigr)\le\sum_{t\ge1}\alpha_t\le\alpha.\] Therefore the bounds are jointly valid at confidence \(1-\alpha\), and any stopping rule that accepts only when \(U_t\le\varepsilon\) has false-certificate probability at most \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocate a summable error budget across inspections; the resulting bounds are simultaneously valid and can safely support adaptive stopping.

notation.meaning: Confidence-bound failure event at time t.
Error budget assigned to time t.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: countable union bound provides simultaneous confidence calibration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The summable error-budget calibration follows from the countable union bound and fits the Confidence Calibration leaf, but the record supplies no authoritative source or locator.

children.title: Optional-Stopping Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Validity limits caused by adaptive inspection or data-dependent termination.

knowledge_statements.title: Optional-Stopping Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ville-type time-uniform boundary for a sub-gamma process.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((S_t,\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\ge0}\) be adapted and let \((V_t)_{t\ge0}\) be predictable and nonnegative. Suppose that for a fixed \(\lambda>0\), \(M_t=\exp\{\lambda S_t-\psi(\lambda)V_t\}\) is a nonnegative supermartingale with \(M_0\le1\). For \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), define \[b_t(\alpha,\lambda)=\frac{\log(1/\alpha)+\psi(\lambda)V_t}{\lambda}.\] Then \(\mathbb{P}(\exists t\ge0:S_t\ge b_t(\alpha,\lambda))\le\alpha\). Consequently the same boundary remains valid when evaluated at any stopping time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative exponential supermartingale yields a time-uniform crossing boundary whose error probability remains controlled under optional stopping.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Ville inequality applied to a nonnegative exponential supermartingale

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated boundary is a correct Ville-inequality consequence of the assumed nonnegative supermartingale, and theorem is the correct terminal role. An authoritative source with a theorem, section, or page locator is nevertheless required.

children.title: Uniform Iterate Averaging

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Iterate Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-history arithmetic averaging of stochastic-approximation iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given iterates \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\in\mathbb{R}^d\), initialize \(\bar x_1=x_1\) and update \[\bar x_t=\bar x_{t-1}+\frac{1}{t}(x_t-\bar x_{t-1}),\qquad t=2,\ldots,T.\] Output \(\bar x_T\). Equivalently, \(\bar x_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T x_t\). Every iterate receives weight \(1/T\), so the procedure is the uniform full-history averaging policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain the arithmetic mean of all iterates using an online recursion and return that mean after the final iteration.

children.title: Weighted Iterate Averaging
children.top_down_role: Full-history averaging with nonuniform iterate contributions.

notation.meaning: Weighted average through time t whenever the cumulative weight is positive.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-history averaging with deterministic nonnegative iterate weights.

source_refs.locator: 8.3 The Stochastic Projected Subgradient Method p. 221

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(T\ge1\), iterates \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\in\mathbb{R}^d\), and deterministic weights \(w_t\ge0\) with \(W_T=\sum_{t=1}^T w_t>0\), define \[\bar x_T^{(w)}=\frac{1}{W_T}\sum_{t=1}^T w_t x_t.\] For an online implementation, set \(W_0=0\), update \(W_t=W_{t-1}+w_t\), let \(t_0=\min\{t:w_t>0\}\), initialize \(\bar x_{t_0}^{(w)}=x_{t_0}\), and for \(t>t_0\) update \[\bar x_t^{(w)}=\bar x_{t-1}^{(w)}+\frac{w_t}{W_t}\bigl(x_t-\bar x_{t-1}^{(w)}\bigr).\] Output \(\bar x_T^{(w)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Form a convex combination of the full iterate history using prescribed nonnegative weights, initializing the running mean at the first positively weighted iterate and then applying the weighted-mean recursion.

children.title: Weight-Schedule Regimes
children.top_down_role: Polynomial, recency-sensitive, or gain-linked weighting families.

knowledge_statements.title: Weight-Schedule Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity regimes for normalized full-history averaging weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonnegative weights \((w_t)_{t\ge1}\), write \(W_T=\sum_{t=1}^T w_t\) and \(q_{T,t}=w_t/W_T\). A diffuse full-history schedule satisfies \[W_T\to\infty,\qquad \max_{1\le t\le T}q_{T,t}\to0.\] Its variance concentration is measured by \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}(T)=(\sum_{t=1}^T q_{T,t}^2)^{-1}=W_T^2/\sum_{t=1}^T w_t^2\). For polynomial weights \(w_t=t^p\) with \(p>-1/2\), \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}(T)/T\to(2p+1)/(p+1)^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular averaging schedule has diverging total weight and no dominant iterate; its squared normalized weights determine an effective sample size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{t\le T}q_{T,t}\to0\), with \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}(T)=W_T^2/\sum_{t=1}^T w_t^2\) and polynomial-weight limit \((2p+1)/(p+1)^2\).

notation.meaning: Weight of iterate t after normalization at horizon T.
Effective sample size induced by normalized weights.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: normalized-weight diffuseness and inverse squared-weight concentration characterize averaging schedules

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diffuseness conditions, effective-sample-size expression, and polynomial-weight limit are mathematically coherent and condition is a reasonable role for the schedule-regime leaf. The quantitative asymptotic claim requires an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Tail-Averaging Transient Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Averaging restricted to later iterates to reduce transient effects.

children.title: Tail Iterate Averaging
children.top_down_role: Averaging policies restricted to a terminal segment of the iterate history.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail Iterate Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform averaging after discarding an initial stochastic-approximation transient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given iterates \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and a burn-in index \(b\in\{0,\ldots,T-1\}\), define the tail length \(m=T-b\) and output \[\bar x_{b:T}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{t=b+1}^{T}x_t.\] Online computation initializes \(z_{b+1}=x_{b+1}\) and updates \(z_t=z_{t-1}+(x_t-z_{t-1})/(t-b)\) for \(t>b+1\). The discarded prefix contributes zero weight and each retained iterate receives weight \(1/m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discard the first b iterates, uniformly average the remaining tail, and return the resulting mean to reduce initialization transients.

notation.meaning: Uniform average over the retained tail.

source_refs.locator: 8.3 The Stochastic Projected Subgradient Method p. 221

source_witnesses.locator: 8.3 The Stochastic Projected Subgradient Method p. 221

children.title: Burn-In Selection
children.top_down_role: Choice of the transient period excluded before averaging begins.

knowledge_statements.title: Burn-In Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion for selecting the discarded prefix in tail-averaged stochastic approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given iterates \(x_0,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d\), choose a burn-in index \(b\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and form \(\bar x_{b:n}=(n-b)^{-1}\sum_{k=b+1}^{n}x_k\). For a target \(x_\star\), an oracle mean-square-error burn-in is any \[b_n^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\le b<n}\left\{\left\|\mathbb E[\bar x_{b:n}]-x_\star\right\|^2+\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\operatorname{Cov}(\bar x_{b:n})\right)\right\}.\] Thus burn-in selection balances removal of initialization bias against the variance increase caused by reducing the retained sample size \(n-b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select the discarded prefix by minimizing the tail average’s squared bias plus covariance trace; longer burn-in reduces initialization effects but leaves fewer iterates for variance reduction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b_n^\star\) minimizes the mean-square error of \(\bar x_{b:n}\) over admissible burn-in indices.

notation.meaning: average of iterates retained after burn-in

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: bias-variance decomposition of the mean-square error gives the stated oracle selection criterion
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The oracle MSE criterion is mathematically coherent, all notation is introduced, and condition is a suitable content kind for this terminal container. However, the record has no inspectable citation or source locator supporting its use as a burn-in selection criterion for tail-averaged stochastic approximation.

children.title: Transient–Variance Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Finite-time balance between transient removal and retained-sample variability.

knowledge_statements.title: Transient–Variance Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact bias–variance tradeoff induced by changing the retained tail of an iterate sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every burn-in \(b<n\), the tail average satisfies \[\mathbb E\|\bar x_{b:n}-x_\star\|^2=\|\mathbb E\bar x_{b:n}-x_\star\|^2+\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\operatorname{Cov}(\bar x_{b:n})\right).\] Increasing \(b\) can suppress the transient component \(\|\mathbb E\bar x_{b:n}-x_\star\|^2\), but it does not universally improve total error: under weak dependence in a stationary tail with long-run covariance \(V\), the variance term is asymptotically \(\operatorname{tr}(V)/(n-b)\). Consequently, discarding more iterates trades smaller transient bias for a shorter effective sample and potentially larger variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tail averaging decomposes into transient bias and sampling variance. Discarding more early iterates can reduce bias, but the shorter retained tail typically increases variance.
assumptions_latex: For the asymptotic variance assertion, the retained stationary tail obeys a central limit theorem with long-run covariance \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tail length and transient suppression must be balanced because the two mean-square-error components generally move in opposite directions.

notation.meaning: long-run covariance of the stationary or locally stationary tail

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact bias-variance identity plus the standard long-run-covariance scaling for sample means
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact bias-variance identity fits the property container. The long-run covariance approximation additionally requires a clearly specified joint regime for the retained length n-b and a source stating the relevant dependence and central-limit assumptions. No citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Forgetting-Based Averaging Family
children.top_down_role: Forgetting-based averages for tracking and constant-gain regimes.

children.title: Exponential Iterate Averaging
children.top_down_role: Recency-weighted averaging with exponentially decaying historical influence.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Iterate Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive iterate averaging with geometrically decaying weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input iterates \(x_0,x_1,\ldots\in\mathbb R^d\), forgetting parameters \(\beta_k\in(0,1]\), and initialize \(y_0=x_0\). For \(k\ge1\), update \[y_k=(1-\beta_k)y_{k-1}+\beta_k x_k.\] Equivalently, \(y_k=w_{0,k}x_0+\sum_{i=1}^k w_{i,k}x_i\), where \(w_{0,k}=\prod_{j=1}^k(1-\beta_j)\) and \(w_{i,k}=\beta_i\prod_{j=i+1}^k(1-\beta_j)\). The weights are nonnegative and sum to one. At a prescribed stopping index \(n\), output \(y_n\). For constant \(\beta_k=\beta\), the weight of an observation \(r\) steps old is proportional to \((1-\beta)^r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain a recursive convex combination of the current iterate and the previous average. Constant forgetting gives geometrically decaying weights to older iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_n\) is a convex, exponentially forgetting average of \(x_0,\ldots,x_n\).

notation.meaning: forgetting or averaging parameter at iteration k
weight assigned at time k to iterate i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: unrolling the exponential-smoothing recursion yields the displayed normalized weights
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recursion and its unrolled convex weights are correct, and algorithm is the appropriate content kind. Geometric or exponential decay is guaranteed for constant beta, whereas arbitrary varying beta_k produces product-form forgetting that need not be geometric. An inspectable source is also absent.

children.title: Moving-Window Iterate Averaging
children.top_down_role: Averaging over a finite rolling segment of recent iterates.

knowledge_statements.title: Moving-Window Iterate Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform averaging over a fixed or time-varying trailing window.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input iterates \(x_0,x_1,\ldots\in\mathbb R^d\) and window lengths \(m_k\in\{1,\ldots,k+1\}\). At iteration \(k\), compute \[y_k=\frac1{m_k}\sum_{i=k-m_k+1}^{k}x_i.\] For a constant window \(m_k=m\) once \(k\ge m-1\), the update can be implemented recursively as \(y_k=y_{k-1}+m^{-1}(x_k-x_{k-m})\). At a prescribed stopping index \(n\), output \(y_n\). Iterates older than \(m_n-1\) steps receive zero weight, while all retained iterates receive weight \(1/m_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Average only the most recent window of iterates. A fixed window admits a constant-cost update by adding the newest iterate and removing the oldest.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_n\) is the uniform average of the final \(m_n\) iterates.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct definition and algebraic recursion for a trailing arithmetic mean

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The window-average definition fits the algorithm container. For a fixed window m, the recursive update involving x_{k-m} is valid from k at least m, not at the first index k=m-1 where the full window becomes available. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Technical noise conditions for maximal-window stochastic-approximation averaging.

children.title: Forgetting-Horizon Regimes
children.top_down_role: Effective memory choices for stationary, drifting, or constant-gain settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Forgetting-Horizon Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of exponential averaging by its effective memory relative to elapsed time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constant forgetting \(\beta\in(0,1]\), define the effective horizon \(h_\beta=1/\beta\); exponential weights beyond age \(r\) have total mass \((1-\beta)^{r+1}\). For a sequence \(\beta_n\downarrow0\), the regimes are: \(n\beta_n\to\infty\), where \(h_{\beta_n}=o(n)\) and averaging is localized to a vanishing fraction of the history; \(n\beta_n\to c\in(0,\infty)\), where the horizon is of order \(n\); and \(n\beta_n\to0\), where the nominal horizon exceeds the observed history and forgetting is negligible over \(n\) steps. A moving window has the analogous classification after replacing \(h_{\beta_n}\) by \(m_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective memory is about the inverse forgetting rate. It may cover a vanishing, fixed-order, or effectively complete fraction of the observed history.
assumptions_latex: For the window analogue, \(1\le m_n\le n+1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The limits of \(n\beta_n\), equivalently of \(h_{\beta_n}/n\), determine the finite-, macroscopic-, and full-history regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Normality of Averaged Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyak–Ruppert central limit theorem for a locally stable finite-dimensional stochastic approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\gamma_{k+1}(h(x_k)+\xi_{k+1})\) converge in probability to \(x_\star\), where \(h(x_\star)=0\), \(h(x)=H(x-x_\star)+o(\|x-x_\star\|)\), and every eigenvalue of \(H\) has positive real part. Suppose \(\xi_{k+1}\) is a martingale difference, its conditional covariance converges in probability to \(\Gamma\), a local Lindeberg condition holds, and \(\gamma_k=a k^{-\alpha}\) with \(a>0\) and \(1/2<\alpha<1\). For \(\bar x_n=n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^n x_k\), \[\sqrt n(\bar x_n-x_\star)\Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,H^{-1}\Gamma H^{-\mathsf T}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under local stability, martingale-noise, and diminishing-gain conditions, the equally averaged approximation is asymptotically normal with the sandwich covariance.
assumptions_latex: The recursion converges to a locally differentiable stable root with nonsingular Jacobian \(H\).
The martingale noise satisfies conditional covariance convergence and a local Lindeberg condition.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the mean field at the stable root
limiting conditional covariance of the local martingale noise

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical finite-dimensional Polyak-Ruppert central limit theorem under local stability and martingale-noise hypotheses
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind and sandwich-covariance conclusion match the asymptotic-normality container, but this central-limit theorem is sensitive to localization, noise-remainder, moment, stability, and convergence-rate hypotheses not fully stated here. An authoritative theorem-level citation is required to determine whether the listed assumptions suffice.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Efficiency of Averaged Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gain-robust sandwich covariance and its recursive-estimation efficiency interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the hypotheses of the Polyak–Ruppert central limit theorem, the averaged estimator has limiting covariance \(V_{\mathrm{PR}}=H^{-1}\Gamma H^{-\mathsf T}\), which does not depend on the scalar gain multiplier \(a>0\) when \(1/2<\alpha<1\). Hence averaging attains the standard sandwich covariance for the estimating equation \(h(x_\star)=0\). Whenever the underlying statistical experiment has information bound \(H^{-1}\Gamma H^{-\mathsf T}\), the averaged approximation is asymptotically efficient. In particular, for a correctly specified likelihood score with \(H=\Gamma=I(x_\star)\), its limiting covariance is \(I(x_\star)^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polyak–Ruppert averaging removes first-order dependence on the gain multiplier and attains the sandwich benchmark; for likelihood scores this becomes inverse Fisher information.
assumptions_latex: The averaged-approximation central limit theorem holds with nonsingular \(H\).
Efficiency is asserted only when the model’s information lower bound equals the displayed sandwich covariance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_{\mathrm{PR}}=H^{-1}\Gamma H^{-\mathsf T}\), and this covariance is efficient whenever it equals the experiment-specific information bound.

notation.meaning: asymptotic covariance of the averaged approximation
Fisher information at the target parameter

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the Polyak-Ruppert sandwich covariance is gain-robust and coincides with inverse Fisher information in the correctly specified score case

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Time Polyak–Ruppert Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete demonstration that asymptotic efficiency does not remove finite-sample initialization bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the noise-free scalar approximation \(x_{k+1}=(1-a/(k+1))(x_k-x_\star)+x_\star\) with \(0<a<1\). Then \[x_k-x_\star=(x_0-x_\star)\prod_{j=1}^{k}\left(1-\frac a j\right)=\frac{x_0-x_\star}{\Gamma(1-a)}k^{-a}(1+o(1)).\] Consequently, the full Polyak–Ruppert average satisfies \[\bar x_n-x_\star=\frac{x_0-x_\star}{(1-a)\Gamma(1-a)}n^{-a}(1+o(1)).\] If \(a<1/2\), this deterministic transient exceeds the canonical \(n^{-1/2}\) stochastic scale. Thus asymptotic covariance claims alone do not guarantee good finite-time behavior without suitable gains or burn-in.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar recursion shows that a poorly scaled harmonic gain leaves initialization bias larger than the root-n fluctuation scale, so averaging alone need not ensure good finite-time performance.
assumptions_latex: The displayed recursion is deterministic, so its error isolates the transient component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(a<1/2\), the full-average transient is \(\Theta(n^{-a})\), larger than \(n^{-1/2}\).

notation.meaning: arithmetic mean of the first n iterates

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the product identity follows from the gamma-function ratio and directly exhibits the finite-time transient

knowledge_statements.title: Raw-Iterate Central-Limit Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Central-limit scalings for unaveraged stochastic approximation with polynomial or harmonic gains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\gamma_{k+1}(h(x_k)+\xi_{k+1})\), assume convergence to \(x_\star\), local linearization \(h(x)=H(x-x_\star)+o(\|x-x_\star\|)\), stable \(H\), and martingale noise with limiting covariance \(\Gamma\) and a Lindeberg condition. If \(\gamma_k=a k^{-\alpha}\), \(1/2<\alpha<1\), then \(\gamma_k^{-1/2}(x_k-x_\star)\Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,\Sigma)\), where \(H\Sigma+\Sigma H^{\mathsf T}=\Gamma\). If \(\alpha=1\) and every eigenvalue of \(aH-\tfrac12I\) has positive real part, then \[\sqrt{k}(x_k-x_\star)\Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,V),\quad (aH-\tfrac12I)V+V(aH^{\mathsf T}-\tfrac12I)=a^2\Gamma.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Raw iterates have gain-dependent Gaussian limits. Subharmonic powers use inverse-square-root gain scaling, while harmonic gains require an additional spectral threshold.
assumptions_latex: The recursion converges to a locally stable differentiable root.
The martingale noise has limiting covariance \(\Gamma\) and satisfies a Lindeberg condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The raw-iterate limit is Gaussian with covariance determined by the regime-specific Lyapunov equation.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Covariance Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lyapunov and integral representations of the raw-iterate limiting covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) have eigenvalues with positive real parts and let \(\Gamma\succeq0\). The continuous Lyapunov equation \[H\Sigma+\Sigma H^{\mathsf T}=\Gamma\] has the unique symmetric positive-semidefinite solution \[\Sigma=\int_0^\infty e^{-Ht}\Gamma e^{-H^{\mathsf T}t}\,dt.\] This \(\Sigma\) is the covariance appearing in the raw-iterate limit \(\gamma_k^{-1/2}(x_k-x_\star)\Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,\Sigma)\) for the subharmonic-gain regime. If \(\Gamma\succ0\), then \(\Sigma\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The raw-iterate covariance is the unique positive-semidefinite solution of a Lyapunov equation and equals an integral of noise covariance propagated by the local stable dynamics.
assumptions_latex: Every eigenvalue of \(H\) has positive real part.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Sigma=\int_0^\infty e^{-Ht}\Gamma e^{-H^{\mathsf T}t}\,dt\) uniquely solves \(H\Sigma+\Sigma H^{\mathsf T}=\Gamma\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard continuous Lyapunov equation and semigroup integral representation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Lyapunov equation and semigroup integral are internally consistent, and representation is the correct content kind. The linear-algebra claim is standard, but its identification with the raw-iterate asymptotic covariance inherits the unsourced central-limit theorem. No inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Local Noise Geometry
children.top_down_role: Directional covariance features of stochastic perturbations near limiting states.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Noise Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional covariance geometry of stochastic-approximation innovations at a limiting solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi_{k+1}\in\mathbb R^d\) be the martingale innovation in a stochastic approximation converging to \(x_\star\). Its local noise covariance is a symmetric matrix \(\Gamma\succeq0\) satisfying \[\mathbb E[\xi_{k+1}\xi_{k+1}^{\mathsf T}\mid\mathcal F_k]\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}\Gamma\] on trajectories approaching \(x_\star\). For every direction \(u\in\mathbb R^d\), the local directional noise variance is \(u^{\mathsf T}\Gamma u\). The range of \(\Gamma\) is the noise-excited subspace, and its null space consists exactly of directions having zero limiting innovation variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local noise geometry is encoded by the limiting conditional covariance: its quadratic form gives directional variance, its range gives excited directions, and its null space gives noise-free directions.
assumptions_latex: The conditional covariance converges in probability along trajectories approaching \(x_\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u^{\mathsf T}\Gamma u\) is the limiting noise variance in direction \(u\), with zero variance exactly when \(u\in\ker\Gamma\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: covariance quadratic forms, ranges, and null spaces give the standard directional geometry of square-integrable noise
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition fits the local-noise-geometry container, and the quadratic-form and null-space claims are correct for a symmetric positive-semidefinite limiting covariance. A source should confirm the martingale-difference convention under which the displayed conditional second moment is the conditional covariance and should provide a specific locator.

children.title: Curvature–Covariance Interaction
children.top_down_role: Influence of local objective geometry on limiting dispersion.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature–Covariance Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral filtering of local noise by symmetric positive-definite curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the local drift \(H\) is symmetric positive definite with eigendecomposition \(H=Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)Q^{\mathsf T}\), and write \(\widetilde\Gamma=Q^{\mathsf T}\Gamma Q\). The raw-iterate covariance solving \(H\Sigma+\Sigma H=\Gamma\) obeys \[(Q^{\mathsf T}\Sigma Q)_{ij}=\frac{\widetilde\Gamma_{ij}}{\lambda_i+\lambda_j}.\] The Polyak–Ruppert covariance \(V_{\mathrm{PR}}=H^{-1}\Gamma H^{-1}\) obeys \[(Q^{\mathsf T}V_{\mathrm{PR}}Q)_{ij}=\frac{\widetilde\Gamma_{ij}}{\lambda_i\lambda_j}.\] Thus weak-curvature directions amplify asymptotic fluctuations, with different spectral filters for raw and averaged iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the curvature eigenbasis, raw and averaged covariances divide noise components by curvature-dependent factors; small eigenvalues therefore amplify fluctuations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Curvature filters local noise through denominators \(\lambda_i+\lambda_j\) for raw iterates and \(\lambda_i\lambda_j\) for Polyak–Ruppert averages.

notation.meaning: eigenvalues of the local curvature or drift matrix
noise covariance expressed in the curvature eigenbasis

knowledge_statements.title: Gain-Sensitive Covariance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Raw-iterate central-limit covariance for linearized stochastic approximation with gain \(\gamma/n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_{n+1}=x_n-(\gamma/n)(H(x_n-x_\star)+\xi_{n+1}+r_n)\), where \(H\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\), \(\gamma>0\), and the martingale-difference noise has limiting conditional covariance \(\Sigma\). If every eigenvalue of \(\gamma H\) has real part greater than \(1/2\) and the remainder is negligible at the central-limit scale, then \(\sqrt n(x_n-x_\star)\) converges in distribution to a centered normal vector with covariance \(V_\gamma\), where \[ (\gamma H-\tfrac12 I)V_\gamma+V_\gamma(\gamma H^{\mathsf T}-\tfrac12 I)=\gamma^2\Sigma. \] Thus both the stability threshold and asymptotic covariance depend on the gain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For gain γ/n, a raw-iterate Gaussian limit exists beyond a gain-dependent stability threshold, and its covariance solves a gain-dependent continuous Lyapunov equation.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb E[\xi_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=0\) and \(\mathbb E[\xi_{n+1}\xi_{n+1}^{\mathsf T}\mid\mathcal F_n]\to\Sigma\) in probability.
\(\sqrt n\,r_n\to0\) in probability locally along the recursion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sqrt n(x_n-x_\star)\Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,V_\gamma)\), with \(V_\gamma\) satisfying the displayed Lyapunov equation.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the mean field at the stable root

children.title: Constant-Gain Stationary Behavior
children.top_down_role: Invariant distributions and steady-state fluctuations under persistent gains.

knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Gain Stationary Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local linear constant-gain behavior around a stable stochastic-approximation equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(e_{n+1}=(I-\gamma H)e_n-\gamma\xi_{n+1}\), with constant \(\gamma>0\), independent centered noise of covariance \(\Sigma\), and \(\rho(I-\gamma H)<1\). The Markov chain has a unique stationary law whenever the noise has a finite second moment. Its stationary mean is zero and its covariance \(P_\gamma\) is the unique positive-semidefinite solution of \[ P_\gamma=(I-\gamma H)P_\gamma(I-\gamma H)^{\mathsf T}+\gamma^2\Sigma. \] If \(H\) is Hurwitz in the positive-stable convention, then \(P_\gamma=O(\gamma)\) as \(\gamma\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stable constant-gain linear recursion approaches an invariant distribution whose covariance solves a discrete Lyapunov equation and is typically proportional to the small gain.
assumptions_latex: \((\xi_n)\) are independent, centered, and have covariance \(\Sigma\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The invariant covariance is the unique \(P_\gamma\succeq0\) satisfying the displayed discrete Lyapunov equation.
review_flags: Supplied stochastic-optimization locators do not specifically support invariant-distribution and stationary-covariance claims.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The discrete Lyapunov covariance claim fits constant-gain stationary behavior, but independence, centering, and a common covariance do not explicitly make the noise identically distributed. Without time-homogeneous noise, the recursion need not define a time-homogeneous Markov chain with a stationary law. A source and a precise i.i.d. or time-homogeneity hypothesis are required.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Timescale Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupled stochastic approximation with a fast variable \(y_n\) and slow variable \(x_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given initial states \((x_0,y_0)\in\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^q\), step sizes \((a_n,b_n)\), mean fields \(h,g\), and observed perturbations \(M_{n+1},N_{n+1}\), iterate \[ x_{n+1}=x_n+a_n\bigl(h(x_n,y_n)+M_{n+1}\bigr),\qquad y_{n+1}=y_n+b_n\bigl(g(x_n,y_n)+N_{n+1}\bigr). \] Impose \(a_n/b_n\to0\), so \(y_n\) evolves on the faster clock. Run until a prescribed iteration or residual criterion is met, and output \((x_n,y_n)\), or the slow component \(x_n\) when it is the target variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Update two coupled variables with diminishing gains whose ratio tends to zero, making one recursion asymptotically faster than the other.
assumptions_latex: \((M_{n+1},N_{n+1})\) are adapted martingale-difference perturbations with controlled conditional second moments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed updates define a two-timescale stochastic-approximation procedure with \(y_n\) on the fast clock.
review_flags: No two-timescale stochastic-approximation source locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm correctly represents a fast-slow stochastic approximation with y on the faster clock when a_n/b_n tends to zero, and the algorithm content kind fits the terminal container. No inspectable two-timescale stochastic-approximation citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Multilevel Timescale Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite hierarchy of coupled stochastic recursions with level-specific gains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For levels \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(z_n^{(i)}\in\mathbb R^{d_i}\). A multilevel stochastic-approximation system is represented by \[ z_{n+1}^{(i)}=z_n^{(i)}+a_n^{(i)}\bigl(h_i(z_n^{(1)},\ldots,z_n^{(m)})+M_{n+1}^{(i)}\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m. \] With the ordering from slowest to fastest, require \(a_n^{(i)}/a_n^{(i+1)}\to0\) for every \(i<m\). On level \(i\)'s clock, faster coordinates are treated through their equilibrated responses, while slower coordinates are asymptotically frozen.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multilevel system couples several stochastic recursions whose adjacent gain ratios vanish, producing an ordered hierarchy of effective clocks.
assumptions_latex: Each \(M_{n+1}^{(i)}\) is an adapted martingale difference with controlled conditional second moment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupled recursion admits an ordered slow-to-fast clock representation determined by the gain-ratio hierarchy.

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Timescale Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested equilibrium reduction for a finite slow-to-fast stochastic-approximation hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the multilevel recursion with levels ordered from slowest to fastest. It is a nested timescale system if, for each \(i=m,m-1,\ldots,2\), the frozen faster subsystem has a designated asymptotically stable equilibrium map \(\lambda_i(z^{(1)},\ldots,z^{(i-1)})\). Define these maps recursively after substituting \(z^{(j)}=\lambda_j(z^{(1)},\ldots,z^{(j-1)})\) for every \(j>i\). The reduced drift at level \(i-1\) is then obtained by inserting all faster equilibrium maps into \(h_{i-1}\). This recursive substitution distinguishes nested reduction from mere coexistence of multiple gains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A timescale hierarchy is nested when each faster subsystem has a stable equilibrium map that can be recursively substituted into every slower drift.
assumptions_latex: Every frozen faster subsystem has a specified asymptotically stable equilibrium map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The hierarchy defines successive reduced mean fields by recursive substitution of \(\lambda_m,\lambda_{m-1},\ldots,\lambda_2\).

notation.meaning: equilibrium response of level i to slower coordinates
unreduced mean field at level i

review_flags: The exact nested-equilibrium convention requires a dedicated multiscale stochastic-approximation source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is locally appropriate, but the exact recursive convention for equilibrium maps and reduced drifts depends on a formal multiscale setup. No source is supplied to confirm that convention or its required frozen-system hypotheses.

children.title: Scale-Separation Hierarchies
children.top_down_role: Relative gain regimes governing separation among multiple clocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Separation Hierarchies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic gain-ratio condition defining a strict hierarchy of stochastic-approximation clocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_n^{(i)}>0\) be the gain of level \(i\), with levels indexed from slowest to fastest. A strict scale-separation hierarchy holds when \[ \frac{a_n^{(i)}}{a_n^{(i+1)}}\longrightarrow0,\qquad i=1,\ldots,m-1. \] Equivalently, for cumulative clocks \(t_n^{(i)}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k^{(i)}\), a bounded interval on clock \(i\) contains asymptotically unbounded elapsed time on clock \(i+1\). The pairwise adjacent conditions imply \(a_n^{(i)}/a_n^{(j)}\to0\) whenever \(i<j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Successive gains are strictly separated when each slower gain is negligible relative to the next faster gain; this orders all clocks transitively.
assumptions_latex: Levels are indexed from slowest to fastest.

notation.meaning: cumulative algorithmic time of level i

review_flags: No multiple-timescale stochastic-approximation locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Adjacent gain-ratio separation does imply all pairwise gain-ratio limits by multiplication. The asserted equivalence with elapsed cumulative time over bounded clock intervals generally needs additional regularity on the gain sequences and clock interpolation. A multiple-timescale source is required to establish the intended formulation.

children.top_down_role: Dependence and feedback transmitted across stochastic timescales.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Scale Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block representation of interactions among stochastic-approximation levels with distinct gains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Stack the level states as \(z_n=(z_n^{(1)},\ldots,z_n^{(m)})\), define \(A_n=\operatorname{diag}(a_n^{(1)}I_{d_1},\ldots,a_n^{(m)}I_{d_m})\), and write \[ z_{n+1}=z_n+A_n\bigl(h(z_n)+M_{n+1}\bigr). \] Cross-scale coupling is present when some off-diagonal block derivative \(D_jh_i(z)\) is nonzero for \(i\ne j\). In a linearization at an equilibrium \(z_\star\), the block Jacobian \(J=(D_jh_i(z_\star))_{i,j}\) records the direction and strength of these interactions, while \(A_n\) assigns their timescale-dependent magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-scale coupling consists of off-diagonal dependence between level drifts; a block Jacobian records the interactions and a diagonal gain matrix records their clocks.
assumptions_latex: Each \(h_i\) is differentiable near the equilibrium \(z_\star\).
The state partition \(\mathbb R^{d_1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb R^{d_m}\) matches the gain levels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The off-diagonal blocks \(D_jh_i(z_\star)\) characterize local cross-scale coupling.

notation.meaning: derivative of level i drift with respect to level j state
block Jacobian of the coupled mean field

review_flags: No source specifically addressing cross-scale coupling was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The block representation and off-diagonal Jacobian criterion match local cross-scale coupling, and representation is an appropriate content kind. No supporting source with a specific cross-scale or multilevel linearization locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Event-time filtrations for asynchronous processor updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information available immediately before and immediately after an indexed asynchronous update event.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each processor \(\alpha\), let \((\mathcal F_{n,\alpha})_n\) and \((\mathcal F^+_{n,\alpha})_n\) be nondecreasing families of \(\sigma\)-algebras. The pre-event algebra \(\mathcal F_{n,\alpha}\) measures at least \(\theta_0\), every \(Y_{j-1,\gamma}\) with \(T_{j,\gamma}<T_{n+1,\alpha}\), and every \(T_{j,\gamma}\) with \(T_{j,\gamma}\le T_{n+1,\alpha}\). The post-event algebra \(\mathcal F^+_{n,\alpha}\) measures at least \(\theta_0\), every \(Y_{j-1,\gamma}\) with \(T_{j,\gamma}\le T_{n+1,\alpha}\), and every \(T_{j,\gamma}\) with \(T_{j,\gamma}\le T_{n+1,\alpha}\). Define \(E_{n,\alpha}[\,\cdot\,]=E[\,\cdot\mid\mathcal F_{n,\alpha}]\) and \(E^+_{n,\alpha}[\,\cdot\,]=E[\,\cdot\mid\mathcal F^+_{n,\alpha}]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each processor, the pre-update information includes the initial state, observations strictly preceding the processor's next event, and event times up to and including that event. The post-update information also includes observations occurring at that event. The associated symbols denote conditional expectations with respect to these two nondecreasing filtrations.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge0\) and processor indices \(\alpha,\gamma\) range over the asynchronous system.
\(T_{j,\gamma}\) is the real time of update \(j\) at processor \(\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_{n,\alpha}=E[\,\cdot\mid\mathcal F_{n,\alpha}]\) and \(E^+_{n,\alpha}=E[\,\cdot\mid\mathcal F^+_{n,\alpha}]\), where the two filtrations contain the stated strict- and non-strict-event histories.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shared-component asynchronous agreement-update model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a distributed block iteration combining delayed agreement messages with processor-local computations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb R^n=\prod_{\ell=1}^m\mathbb R^{n_\ell}\) and let each of \(p\) processors maintain \(x^i(t)=(x_1^i(t),\ldots,x_m^i(t))\). For each component \(\ell\), let \(\varnothing\ne C_\ell\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\) be its computing processors, with processor-update times \(T_\ell^i\). Communication of component \(\ell\) uses a directed graph \(G_\ell=(N,A_\ell)\); for \((j,i)\in A_\ell\), the receive-time set \(T_\ell^{ij}\) is infinite and a message received at \(t\in T_\ell^{ij}\) contains \(x_\ell^j(\tau_\ell^{ij}(t))\), where \(1\le \tau_\ell^{ij}(t)\le t\). Set \(T_\ell^{ii}=\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) and \(\tau_\ell^{ii}(t)=t\). With \(\gamma_\ell^i(t)>0\), \(s_\ell^i(t)\in\mathbb R^{n_\ell}\), and \(s_\ell^i(t)=0\) whenever \(i\notin C_\ell\) or \(t\notin T_\ell^i\), the iteration initialized by arbitrary \(x^i(1)\in\mathbb R^n\) is
\[
x_\ell^i(t+1)=\sum_{\{j:\,t\in T_\ell^{ij}\}}a_\ell^{ij}(t)x_\ell^j(\tau_\ell^{ij}(t))+\gamma_\ell^i(t)s_\ell^i(t),
\]
where \(a_\ell^{ij}(t)\ge0\) and \(\sum_{\{j:\,t\in T_\ell^{ij}\}}a_\ell^{ij}(t)=1\) for every \(i,\ell,t\). If no external message is received, this reduces to \(x_\ell^i(t+1)=x_\ell^i(t)+\gamma_\ell^i(t)s_\ell^i(t)\); if no computation occurs, it reduces to the underlying agreement iteration obtained by omitting the final update term.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each processor maintains a local copy of every vector block. A block update is the sum of a convex combination of possibly delayed local copies received from communicating processors and a positive-stepsize local computation. Processors not assigned to a block, or inactive at that time, contribute no local computation. With no received external message the rule is a local computational update; with no computation it is the underlying agreement iteration.
assumptions_latex: (j,i)\in A_\ell\implies T_\ell^{ij}\text{ is infinite},\qquad t\in T_\ell^{ij}\implies 1\le\tau_\ell^{ij}(t)\le t.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asynchronous stochastic-approximation recursion with delayed component information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines componentwise stochastic approximation with random sparse activation, local update clocks, delayed component observations, and an update-frequency condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $Y_n\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$ be the random set of components updated at time $n$, let $0\leq\tau_{ji}(n)\leq n$ denote the delay of component $j$ used when updating component $i$, and define $v(i,n)=\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}I\{i\in Y_m\}$. Then, for $1\leq i\leq d$ and $n\geq0$,
\[
x_{n+1}(i)=x_n(i)+a(v(i,n))I\{i\in Y_n\}\left[h_i\!\left(x_{n-\tau_{1i}(n)}(1),\ldots,x_{n-\tau_{di}(n)}(d)\right)+M_{n+1}(i)\right].
\]
If $\liminf_{n\to\infty}v(i,n)/n>0$, then component $i$ is updated infinitely often. Irreducibility of $(Y_n)$ as a Markov chain on the finite power set of $\{1,\ldots,d\}$ is sufficient for this positive lower update frequency. The stated controlled-Markov condition, under which every stationary policy induces an irreducible chain with all stationary state probabilities bounded below by a common $\delta>0$, is a further sufficient condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each event, only the components in the random set Y_n are updated. Component i selects its stepsize using its local update count and evaluates its drift using possibly delayed values of all components. Positive asymptotic lower update frequency implies infinitely many updates of each component; the stated irreducible Markov and uniformly positive controlled-Markov activation conditions are sufficient.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shifted sequences and clock interpolations for asynchronous updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition of time-shifted coordinates for one processor in a decreasing-step asynchronous recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\sigma\ge 0\), \(n\ge 0\), and processor \(\alpha\), let \(p_\alpha(\sigma)+n\) index the \((n+1)\)-st update at or after \(\sigma\). Define \(\delta\tau_{n,\alpha}^{\sigma}=\delta\tau_{p_\alpha(\sigma)+n,\alpha}\), \(\epsilon_{n,\alpha}^{\sigma}=\epsilon_{p_\alpha(\sigma)+n,\alpha}\), \(Y_{n,\alpha}^{\sigma}=Y_{p_\alpha(\sigma)+n,\alpha}\), \(t_{n,\alpha}^{\sigma}=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\epsilon_{i,\alpha}^{\sigma}\), and \(\tau_{n,\alpha}^{\sigma}=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\epsilon_{i,\alpha}^{\sigma}\delta\tau_{i,\alpha}^{\sigma}\). With \(\theta_{0,\alpha}^{\sigma}=\theta_{p_\alpha(\sigma),\alpha}\), set \(\theta_{n+1,\alpha}^{\sigma}=\Pi_{[a_\alpha,b_\alpha]}(\theta_{n,\alpha}^{\sigma}+\epsilon_{n,\alpha}^{\sigma}Y_{n,\alpha}^{\sigma})\). Define \(\theta_\alpha^{\sigma}(t)=\theta_{n,\alpha}^{\sigma}\) for \(t\in[t_{n,\alpha}^{\sigma},t_{n+1,\alpha}^{\sigma})\); define \(\widehat\theta_\alpha^{\sigma}(t)=\theta_{n,\alpha}^{\sigma}\) and \(N_\alpha^{\sigma}(t)=t_{n,\alpha}^{\sigma}\) for \(t\in[\tau_{n,\alpha}^{\sigma},\tau_{n+1,\alpha}^{\sigma})\); and define \(\tau_\alpha^{\sigma}(t)=\tau_{n,\alpha}^{\sigma}\) for \(t\in[t_{n,\alpha}^{\sigma},t_{n+1,\alpha}^{\sigma})\). Then \(N_\alpha^{\sigma}(\tau_\alpha^{\sigma}(t))=t_{n,\alpha}^{\sigma}\) on the latter interval, \(\theta_\alpha^{\sigma}(t)=\widehat\theta_\alpha^{\sigma}(\tau_\alpha^{\sigma}(t))\), and \(\widehat\theta_\alpha^{\sigma}(t)=\theta_\alpha^{\sigma}(N_\alpha^{\sigma}(t))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting at the first processor update at or after a real-time shift, the update data and iterates are reindexed. Piecewise-constant interpolations are then defined on cumulative step-size time and step-size-weighted real time, with clock-change identities relating the two representations.
assumptions_latex: \(p_\alpha(\sigma)\) indexes the first update of processor \(\alpha\) at or after real time \(\sigma\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The shifted recursion and interpolations satisfy \(N_\alpha^{\sigma}(\tau_\alpha^{\sigma}(t))=t_{n,\alpha}^{\sigma}\), \(\theta_\alpha^{\sigma}=\widehat\theta_\alpha^{\sigma}\circ\tau_\alpha^{\sigma}\), and \(\widehat\theta_\alpha^{\sigma}=\theta_\alpha^{\sigma}\circ N_\alpha^{\sigma}\) on their stated intervals.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discounted frozen-parameter noise condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A summability and second-moment condition for centered asynchronous stochastic-approximation updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(n\), let \(I_{i,\alpha}^{\epsilon}(\theta,n)\) indicate an update at \(i\ge n\) when the parameter is held at \(\theta\) from iterate \(n\), and define \[\Gamma_{n,\alpha}^{\epsilon,d}(\theta)=\epsilon\sum_{i=n}^{\infty}(1-\epsilon)^{i-n}\widehat E_n^{\epsilon}\!\left[\widehat g_{i,\alpha}^{\epsilon}(\theta,\widehat\xi_{i,\alpha}^{\epsilon})-\bar g_\alpha(\theta)\right]I_{i,\alpha}^{\epsilon}(\theta,n).\] For every \(\theta\), \(\alpha\), and \(n\), and all sufficiently small \(\epsilon>0\), the sum of the absolute values of its summands is integrable and \[\mathbb E\left|\Gamma_{n,\alpha}^{\epsilon,d}(\widehat\theta_n^{\epsilon})\right|^2=O(\epsilon^2)\left(\mathbb EV(\widehat\theta_n^{\epsilon})+1\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The discounted sum of centered updates under frozen parameters and sparse activation is absolutely integrable and has second moment of order epsilon squared times one plus the expected Lyapunov value.

children.title: Random Activation Models
children.top_down_role: Randomized selection of components or agents eligible to update.

knowledge_statements.title: Random Activation Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate or block activation represented by an adapted random diagonal mask.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_n\in\mathbb R^d\) and let \(S_{n+1}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\) be a random active set. Define the mask \(D_{n+1}=\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf1_{\{i\in S_{n+1}\}})\). A random activation model specifies the conditional law of \(S_{n+1}\) given \(\mathcal F_n\), equivalently the activation probabilities \(p_{n,i}=\mathbb P(i\in S_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n)\) together with any within-step dependence. Only coordinates selected by \(D_{n+1}\) may change; inactive coordinates remain equal to their preceding values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random active set, or its diagonal mask, determines which coordinates may update at each iteration and specifies their conditional activation probabilities.
assumptions_latex: \(S_{n+1}\) is measurable with respect to the information available at iteration \(n+1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((I-D_{n+1})(x_{n+1}-x_n)=0\), so every inactive coordinate is unchanged.

notation.meaning: conditional activation probability of coordinate i

children.title: Partial-Update Recursions
children.top_down_role: Stochastic recursions that modify only selected state components per event.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Update Recursions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Masked stochastic-approximation update for randomly selected coordinates or blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in\mathbb R^d\), gains \(\alpha_n>0\), a stochastic direction oracle \(G(x_n,\xi_{n+1})\), and activation masks \(D_{n+1}\), perform \[ x_{n+1}=x_n-\alpha_nD_{n+1}G(x_n,\xi_{n+1}). \] Equivalently, coordinate \(i\) is updated by \(x_{n+1,i}=x_{n,i}-\alpha_nG_i(x_n,\xi_{n+1})\) when \(i\) is active and is otherwise unchanged. Stop at a prescribed iteration or residual threshold and output the latest iterate or a specified weighted average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, multiply the stochastic direction by an activation mask so only selected coordinates or blocks are updated.
assumptions_latex: \(D_{n+1}\) is an adapted diagonal zero-one mask, or its block-diagonal analogue.
\(G(x_n,\xi_{n+1})\) is measurable at the update time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{n+1}-x_n=-\alpha_nD_{n+1}G(x_n,\xi_{n+1})\) has support only on the active coordinates.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For active sets \(S_n\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\), define the update count \(\nu_i(n)=\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbf1_{\{i\in S_k\}}\). Uniform asymptotic coverage holds if there exists \(\eta>0\) such that \[ \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\nu_i(n)}{n}\ge\eta\quad\text{almost surely for every }i. \] A stronger bounded-window regime requires an integer \(B\ge1\) such that \(\bigcup_{k=n}^{n+B-1}S_k=\{1,\ldots,d\}\) for every \(n\). Either condition rules out permanent starvation; bounded-window coverage implies uniform asymptotic coverage with \(\eta\ge1/B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coverage requires every coordinate to activate persistently; bounded-window coverage guarantees at least one activation per coordinate in every fixed-length window.

children.title: Sparse-Update Effects
children.top_down_role: Stability and speed consequences of infrequent component updates.

assumptions_latex: Conditional on \(\mathcal F_n\), the indicators \(\delta_{n+1,1},\ldots,\delta_{n+1,d}\) are mutually independent Bernoulli variables and are independent of \(G_{n+1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The effective drift is multiplied by \(P\), and conditionally independent Bernoulli masking contributes coordinatewise variance proportional to \(p_i(1-p_i)\) when the unmasked direction is deterministic.

notation.meaning: diagonal matrix of conditional activation probabilities

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mean drift and fluctuation changes induced by conditionally independent coordinate thinning.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_{n+1}=\operatorname{diag}(\delta_{n+1,1},\ldots,\delta_{n+1,d})\), where, conditional on \(\mathcal F_n\), the indicators are mutually independent Bernoulli variables and are independent of the stochastic direction. Let \(P=\mathbb E[D_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=\operatorname{diag}(p_1,\ldots,p_d)\). For the increment \(\Delta x_n=-\alpha_nD_{n+1}G_{n+1}\), \[ \mathbb E[\Delta x_n\mid\mathcal F_n]= -\alpha_nP\,\mathbb E[G_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]. \] Hence sparse activation scales coordinatewise mean drift by \(p_i\). If \(G_{n+1}=g\) is deterministic conditional on \(\mathcal F_n\), masking adds conditional covariance \(\alpha_n^2\operatorname{diag}(p_i(1-p_i)g_i^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditionally independent coordinate thinning scales each mean update by its activation probability and adds diagonal sampling covariance when the unmasked direction is deterministic.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Step-Size and Moment Condition for Random Delays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Delay-tail and step-size compatibility assumption for asynchronous stochastic approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist \(\eta>0\) and a nonnegative integer-valued random variable \(\bar\tau\) such that \(a(n)=o(n^{-\eta})\), \(\bar\tau\) stochastically dominates every \(\tau_{k\ell}(n)\), and \(\mathbb{E}[\bar\tau^{1/\eta}]<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: There exist eta greater than zero and a nonnegative integer-valued random variable bar-tau such that the step size is little-o of n to the minus eta, bar-tau stochastically dominates all delays tau indexed by k, l, and n, and its 1/eta moment is finite.
assumptions_latex: \bar\tau\text{ is a nonnegative integer-valued random variable}

children.title: Delayed Information Models
children.top_down_role: Updates based on information received after a communication or computation lag.

knowledge_statements.title: Delayed Information Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic approximation whose update uses a state observed at an earlier iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\tau_n\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\) be an adapted delay. A delayed-information stochastic-approximation model has the form \[ x_{n+1}=x_n-\alpha_nD_{n+1}\bigl(G(x_{n-\tau_n},\xi_{n+1})+\varepsilon_{n+1}\bigr), \] where \(D_{n+1}\) selects the updated coordinates or blocks. The information age at update \(n+1\) is \(\tau_n\); the current-information model is recovered when \(\tau_n=0\). A bounded-delay regime imposes \(\sup_n\tau_n<\infty\), whereas an unbounded random-delay regime permits arbitrarily large \(\tau_n\) subject to separate tail or moment conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A delayed-information recursion evaluates its update direction at an earlier iterate; bounded and unbounded-delay regimes differ through restrictions on the information age.
assumptions_latex: \(0\le\tau_n\le n\) and \(x_{n-\tau_n}\) is available when update \(n+1\) is formed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update direction is based on the stale state \(x_{n-\tau_n}\), with staleness measured by \(\tau_n\).

notation.meaning: stochastic direction computed from delayed information

children.title: Stale Information Models
children.top_down_role: Updates based on state or gradient information whose age affects relevance.

knowledge_statements.title: Stale Information Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Read-at-time, apply-at-time model for asynchronous stochastic approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=H_1\times\cdots\times H_m\) be a product space and let \(x^k=(x_1^k,\ldots,x_m^k)\in H\) denote the global state at logical time \(k\in\mathbb N\). A stale-information model associates the update applied at time \(k\) with a read vector \(\hat x^k\in H\) satisfying \(\hat x_i^k=x_i^{k-d_{k,i}}\), where \(d_{k,i}\in\{0,\ldots,k\}\). Given a stepsize \(\alpha_k\ge0\), a sampled input \(\xi_k\) in a measurable space \(\Xi\), a block update map \(G_i:H\times\Xi\to H_i\), and the canonical embedding \(U_i:H_i\to H\), a corresponding asynchronous step may be written as \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\alpha_kU_{i_k}G_{i_k}(\hat x^k,\xi_k)\). The read is componentwise consistent when each \(\hat x_i^k\) equals a value attained previously by component \(i\); the assembled vector \(\hat x^k\) need not equal any single past global iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stale-information model evaluates an asynchronous block update using component values attained at earlier logical times. Different components may come from different past times, so the assembled read vector need not be a past global iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\hat x_i^k=x_i^{k-d_{k,i}}\) with \(d_{k,i}\in\{0,\ldots,k\}\), and the update is evaluated at \(\hat x^k\).

notation.meaning: age of component i used by update k
canonical embedding of block i into the product space
sampled input used at update k

children.title: Bounded-Delay Regimes
children.top_down_role: Asynchronous settings with uniformly controlled information lags.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Delay Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform deterministic delay condition for componentwise asynchronous reads.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For stale reads \(\hat x_i^k=x_i^{k-d_{k,i}}\), the process is in a uniformly bounded-delay regime if there exists a finite integer \(\tau\ge 0\) such that \(0\le d_{k,i}\le\min\{\tau,k\}\) for every update time \(k\) and every component \(i\) read at that update. Equivalently, no update applied at time \(k\) may use information older than logical time \(\max\{0,k-\tau\}\). The bound is pathwise and uniform: the same \(\tau\) applies to all realized update histories, components, and times.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All information used by any update is at most a fixed finite number of logical updates old.
assumptions_latex: \(d_{k,i}\) is the nonnegative integer age of component \(i\) used at time \(k\).

children.title: Unbounded Random-Delay Regimes
children.top_down_role: Asynchronous settings with random lags lacking deterministic bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Random-Delay Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random delays without an almost-sure uniform finite bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_{k,i}\) be the random age of component \(i\) used at update \(k\). An unbounded random-delay regime satisfies \(D_{k,i}\in\{0,\ldots,k\}\) almost surely and has no deterministic uniform bound: for every finite \(r\), some admissible pair \((k,i)\) satisfies \(\mathbb P(D_{k,i}>r)>0\). A common integrable subclass additionally requires a uniform moment bound \(\sup_{k,i}\mathbb E[D_{k,i}^{q}]<\infty\) for some \(q>0\), or an explicitly controlled tail \(\sup_{k,i}\mathbb P(D_{k,i}>r)\le\psi(r)\) with \(\psi(r)\to0\). These tail conditions do not convert the regime into bounded delay.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delays can be arbitrarily large with positive probability, while moments or tails may still be uniformly controlled.
assumptions_latex: \(D_{k,i}\) is measurable and takes integer values between \(0\) and \(k\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The basic distinction from uniformly bounded delay is plausible, but the proposed moment and uniform-tail subclasses require a source specifying their exact quantifiers and role in asynchronous convergence theory.

children.title: Heterogeneous Clock-Frequency Regimes

children.title: Local Component Clocks
children.top_down_role: Component-specific event counts used to index local stochastic updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Component Clocks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise counters induced by a global sequence of asynchronous updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given global update indices \(k=0,1,\ldots\) and selected blocks \(i_k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), the local clock of block \(i\) before update \(k\) is \(N_i(k)=\sum_{t=0}^{k-1}\mathbf 1\{i_t=i\}\). Thus \(N_i(0)=0\) and \(N_i(k+1)=N_i(k)+\mathbf 1\{i_k=i\}\). If block \(i\) uses a local stepsize schedule \((a_{i,n})_{n\ge0}\), its update at global time \(k\) uses \(a_{i,N_i(k)}\). The identity \(\sum_{i=1}^m N_i(k)=k\) holds when exactly one block is selected per global update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each component maintains a counter equal to its number of completed updates, and may index its stepsizes by that counter.
assumptions_latex: \(i_k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and exactly one block is selected at each global time.

notation.meaning: local update count of block i before global update k
stepsize for the nth update of block i

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local and Global Time Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Temporal model for each processor in an asynchronous computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each processor \(i\), let \(t_i\) denote local time and \(\tau\) external global time. Assume distinct global times correspond to distinct local times and conversely. Then \(\tau=h_i(t_i)\) for a strictly increasing function \(h_i\). The correspondence \(h_i\) need not be known by any processor and does not affect the implemented algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each processor has a local clock whose times correspond one-to-one and in order with an external global clock. Global time is a strictly increasing function of local time, but processors need not know this function and the algorithm cannot depend on it.
assumptions_latex: \(i\) is a processor with local time \(t_i\), while \(\tau\) is external global time.
Distinct global times correspond to distinct local times, and conversely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau=h_i(t_i)\) for some strictly increasing \(h_i\), unknown to the processor and operationally irrelevant to the algorithm.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asynchronous Event Regularity Assumptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event and reception assumptions for processor-local timelines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume: (a) every processor event is instantaneous; (b) distinct events at the same processor occur at distinct local times; (c) only finitely many events occur in every finite-length time interval; and (d) distinct messages received by the same processor arrive at distinct local times. Consequently, every message-induced event is caused by exactly one message.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Events take zero time, separate events at one processor have different local times, finite time intervals contain only finitely many events, and different messages received by one processor have different reception times. Thus each message-induced event has exactly one triggering message.
assumptions_latex: Distinct events at processor \(i\) have distinct local times.
Every finite-length time interval contains finitely many events.
Distinct messages received by the same processor have distinct local reception times.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Each message-induced event is induced by exactly one message.}

children.title: Unequal Update Frequencies
children.top_down_role: Persistent differences in component or worker participation rates.

knowledge_statements.title: Unequal Update Frequencies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotically unequal positive component frequencies under heterogeneous update clocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m<\infty\), suppose exactly one block is selected at each global update, and let \(N_i(k)\) count selections of block \(i\in\{1,ldots,m\}\) before time \(k\). The update sequence has unequal positive limiting frequencies if there are constants \(p_1,ldots,p_m\in(0,1]\) such that \(N_i(k)/k\to p_i\) as \(k\to\infty\) for every \(i\), and \(p_i\ne p_j\) for at least one pair \(i,j\). Under single-block updates, the limits necessarily satisfy \(\sum_{i=1}^m p_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Components have unequal positive update frequencies when every component's fraction of global updates converges to a positive limit and at least two of those limits differ.
assumptions_latex: \(m<\infty\), and exactly one block is selected at each global update.
\(N_i(k)\) counts selections of block \(i\) before time \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_i(k)/k\to p_i>0\) for every \(i\), \(\sum_{i=1}^m p_i=1\), and \(p_i\ne p_j\) for some \(i,j\).

notation.meaning: number of selections of block i before global time k
limiting update frequency of block i
